-<!-- SECTIONS 1, 3, 5, 6 PENDING — epidemiology/diagnosis, endurance & capacity,
-     softball-specific workload, and the mitigation plan. -->
+## Section 5 — Softball-specific evidence and workload
+### 5.1 The softball TOS literature barely exists
+PubMed `"thoracic outlet"[TIAB] AND softball[TIAB]` returns **exactly 6 records**:
+- **2 case reports in softball athletes**, both **structural/congenital first-rib
+  pathology** — a fracture nonunion and a congenital pseudarthrosis. **Neither

+  identifies the patient as a pitcher.** `[External]` Young BL, et al. *J Shoulder Elbow Surg* 2016;25(11):e353-7. PMID 27742249. / Gibson TW, Carson L. *JBJS Case Connect* 2021;11(3). PMID 34329202.
+- **4 cohort studies where softball is pooled with baseball** or given only as a
+  prevalence.
+A systematic review of Paget-Schroetter syndrome in athletes **does not contain
+the word "softball"** — zero softball effort-thrombosis cases in the systematic
+literature. `[External]` Keller RE, et al. *J Shoulder Elbow Surg* 2020;29(11):2417-25. PMID 32868012.
+**Net: no peer-reviewed paper attributes TOS or effort thrombosis in a softball
+pitcher to the pitching motion.** The design ceiling across the entire softball
+TOS literature is the single case report. Every mechanistic claim must be
+extrapolated from baseball, and the extrapolation should be stated.
+### 5.2 The windmill is not load-sparing
+| Measure | Value | Source |
+| Shoulder distraction, youth | **94% body weight** | Werner 2005, n=53 |
+| Shoulder distraction, elite/Olympic | **80% BW** | Werner 2006, n=24 |
+| Peak compression, shoulder & elbow | **70–98% BW** | Barrentine 1998, n=8 |
+| Shoulder extension/abduction torque | **9–10% BW × height** | Barrentine 1998 |
+| **Peak biceps activation, windmill vs overhand (velocity-matched)** | **38% vs 19%** | Rojas 2009 |
+| Scapular excursion through the pitch | 5–22° per plane | Holtz 2026, n=17 |

+`[External]` Werner SL, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2005;33(4):552-60. PMID 15722291; 2006;34(4):597-603. PMID 16282576. / Barrentine SW, et al. *J Orthop Sports Phys Ther* 1998;28(6):405-15. PMID 9836172. / Rojas IL, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2009;37(3):558-65. PMID 19174551. / Holtz KA, et al. *Int J Sports Med* 2026;47(1):72-7. PMID 40738124.
+Three independent sources state windmill shoulder and elbow loads are **similar
+to baseball pitching**. Our own library says the same:
+`[Zotero: FGQAC8DL, p. 1]` — *"it is continually reported that the shoulder stress
+endured from the softball pitch is analogous to that of the baseball pitch,"* and
+shoulder injury rates and patterns are "comparable with those reported in the
+sport of baseball." Oliver GD, et al. *Orthop J Sports Med* 2019;7(8):2325967119865171.
+**The "windmill is a natural motion" belief is explicitly named as a
+misconception in the peer-reviewed literature.** At matched ball velocity, biceps
+demand is **double** the overhand throw.
+**Hyperabduction — label as inference.** The windmill carries the arm through
+full overhead elevation once per pitch, transiently and at high angular velocity.
+**No windmill study reports maximum shoulder elevation angle or time above 90°.**
+The plausible outlet link is cumulative repetition, not sustained positional
+narrowing.
+**The actionable lever is proximal.** Lower-extremity screening alone predicted
+**49.9%** of peak shoulder distraction variance in 46 collegiate pitchers, rising
+to **56.2%** with hip rotation strength. `[External]` Ulman SM, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2025;53(3):565-70. PMID 39844736.
+Our library adds the trunk side: at foot contact, increased trunk rotation toward
+the pitching arm, increased stride length and a posteriorly shifted COM explained
+**~33% of variance** in upper-extremity pain among 37 D1 softball pitchers.
+`[Zotero: FGQAC8DL, p. 1 and p. 4]`
+### 5.3 Workload — the strongest part of the case
+**Rules, verified: NCAA softball has NO pitch count limit and NO mandated rest.**
+Confirmed three ways (Zaremski 2025 states "no established pitch count guidelines
+for collegiate softball"; Freetly et al. Table 2 lists NCAA for both sports as
+"No restrictions / None"; the NCAA softball playing-rules page lists no such
+document). NCAA baseball likewise has none — but **NFHS Rule 6-2-6 requires every
+state association to adopt a baseball pitch-count restriction with mandated
+rest**, while NFHS softball is capped only by *innings*.
+*Caveat: the current NCAA rulebook PDF would not retrieve. Confirm against the
+current rulebook before publishing a rules claim.*
+**Collegiate workload** — 40 softball and 40 baseball College World Series teams,
+| | Softball | Baseball | Ratio |
+| Innings pitched/season (median) | **84.1** | 29.2 | **2.9×** |
+| Appearances/season | 23.0 | 16.0 | 1.4× |
+All p<0.0001. `[External]` Freetly T, et al. *J Womens Sports Med.* doi:10.53646/khdyxt64.
+**That roster structure is the one-pitcher-carries-the-staff pattern,
+quantified:** a softball staff is under one-third the size of a baseball staff,
+and each pitcher absorbs nearly 3× the innings.
+**The single most actionable workload finding:** 8,248 pitches tracked over 89
+varsity outings. Counting game pitches only, **25.6%** exceeded recommendations.
+**Including bullpen and warm-up: 51.2%** (P=0.001). **Roughly half of true pitch
+volume is invisible to a box score.** `[External]` Kamarajugadda S, et al. *J Sports Med Phys Fitness* 2025;65(10):1306-10. PMID 40673787.
+**Volume thresholds (youth/HS only — no collegiate pitch-count study exists):**
+>85 pitches/game → **>2× likelihood of seeking medical attention**; shoulder pain
+associated with **429 vs 219 pitches/week** and **19,195 vs 8,876 pitches/year**.
+`[External]` Gooch B, et al. *Sports Health* 2022;14(5):702-9. PMID 34672828.
+**Fatigue — mixed direction, read carefully:**
+- After **99 ± 21 pitches**: dominant-side deficits **11–22%** across hip,
+  scapula, shoulder, elbow, wrist; **velocity −3.4%**. `[External]` Corben JS, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2015;43(8):2035-41. PMID 26109610.
+- Kinetics **decreased** at shoulder, elbow and wrist in the last and doubleheader
+  innings — the pitcher produces *less* force, not more. `[External]` Fava AW, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2024;52(12):3118-29. PMID 39344907.
+- Consecutive-day tournament pitching raises fatigue (2.0 → 3.5) and pain
+  (1.3 → 2.5). `[External]` Skillington SA, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 2017;45(6):1413-9. PMID 28298058.
+- But post-game stride-leg knee extension and trunk flexion strength
+  **increased** in one study. `[External]` Pletcher ER, et al. *Sports Biomech* 2024;23(9):1210-8. PMID 34134606.
+Consistent reading: **proximal control and output degrade within and across
+days**, while isolated post-game strength tests can move either way. Do not
+present fatigue as a clean monotonic decline.
+### 5.4 Injury epidemiology
+- **NCAA softball overall: 3.92 per 1,000 AE. Shoulder is the #1 body part at
+  15.2%.** `[External]` Veillard KL, et al. PMID 34280289.
+- Game 4.30 vs practice 2.67 per 1,000 AE; **preseason practice 3.65 vs in-season
+  1.68.** `[External]` Marshall SW, et al. *J Athl Train* 2007;42(2):286-94. PMID 17710178.
+- **Collegiate pitchers specifically: 72.8% injured in one season** (n=181); 92 of
+  131 injuries chronic/overuse, 33 shoulder-related. `[External]` Hill JL, et al. *J Strength Cond Res* 2004;18(3):426-31. PMID 15320672.
+- **20 of 24 collegiate pitchers had injuries/complaints; 82% of time-loss
+  injuries were upper extremity.** `[External]` Loosli AR, et al. *Am J Sports Med* 1992;20(1):35-7. PMID 1554071.
+### 5.5 Prevention — an open field
+Effectively **no softball-specific prevention evidence exists.** A systematic
+review screened 1,605 articles, included 7, and found **only 1 described an
+injury-prevention program for softball players** — with no efficacy trial.
+`[External]` Paul J, Brown SM, Mulcahey MK. *Sports Health* 2021;13(4):390-5. PMID 33535878.
+Uptake is poor: **<46% of fastpitch coaches run any prevention program**, with
+unfamiliarity and staffing cited as barriers. `[External]` Nurrenbern J, et al. *Int J Sports Phys Ther* 2023;18(4):958-68. PMID 37547836.
+### 5.6 A number to stop repeating
+**"1,200–1,500 pitches in a 3-day tournament (vs 100–120 for baseball)."** This
+appears in a peer-reviewed paper — but is cited to a biomechanics study of 53
+youth pitchers that **reports no tournament volume at all**. The citation does not
+support the figure. The only other peer-reviewed tournament number, **95–381
+pitches/weekend**, is an order of magnitude lower and also describes youth
+pitchers. **Do not use 1,200–1,500.**
+## Section 6 — Mitigation, mapped to who owns each lever
+The point of this table is that **most of the modifiable exposure does not sit in
+the weight room.** That is not a deflection; it is where the evidence points.
+| Lever | Owner | Evidence strength | Action |

+| **Count all pitches — bullpen and warm-up included** | Pitching coach + AT | **Strong** — half of true volume is uncounted (Kamarajugadda 2025) | Track every pitch. This is the highest-yield, lowest-cost change available. |

+| **Innings distribution across the staff** | Head coach | **Strong** — 43.7% of collegiate softball pitchers exceed 100 IP/season on a 4.5-pitcher staff | Develop staff depth. No rule will do this for you. |
+| **Consecutive-day and doubleheader exposure** | Head coach | **Moderate** — fatigue and pain accumulate across tournament days (Skillington 2017) | Build rest into tournament plans. |

+| **Cervical mobility screening (CFRT, cervical flexion ROM)** | AT + S&C | **Moderate, in our exact population** — RR 9.38 for time-loss injury `[Zotero: F5YKF6B4]` | Add to preseason screen. Cheap, fast, defensible. |
+| **Pec minor resting length** | S&C | **Moderate mechanism, no TOS validation** | Measure (reliable method exists). Do not publish a cut-off. |

+| **Hip and trunk capacity / lower-extremity mechanics** | S&C | **Moderate** — LE screening predicts ~50–56% of shoulder distraction variance (Ulman 2025) | This is the strongest evidence-aligned S&C target for shoulder load in softball pitchers. |
+| **Scapular control and postural capacity** | S&C | **Plausible, unproven for TOS** | Do it — low cost, low risk, independently justified. Do not claim it prevents TOS. |
+| **Upper-quarter capacity monitoring (DNF endurance, SME, CKCUEST, UQYBT)** | S&C | **Weak for individual tracking** (SME MDC = 30.1 s) | Use as group screens. Never present as a TOS screen. |
+| **Lifting timing relative to throwing** | S&C | **No evidence either way** | Avoid upper-body work to failure and novel heavy eccentrics near high-intent throwing. Drop the blanket rule. |

+| **Diagnostic and referral pathway** | Sports medicine | **Strong** — ascertainment drives counts; 47–62% false-positive rate on EAST | Agree on criteria before counting cases. Consider the SVS ≥3-of-4 standard. |
+| **Year-round throwing / travel ball history** | Recruiting + sports medicine | **Moderate** | Capture prior throwing volume at intake. |
+## Appendix — what to say, and what not to say
+- "TOS is not separately coded in NCAA injury surveillance, so there is no peer
+  benchmark to compare against."
+- "With a population incidence around 2–3 per 100,000 per year, a roster our size
+  cannot generate a statistically meaningful rate. Two cases is within chance."
+- "The provocative test used most often is positive in roughly half of people who
+  don't have TOS. Case counts track how hard you look."
+- "Windmill pitching produces shoulder loads equal to baseball, and our pitchers
+  throw about three times the innings on a staff a third the size, with no pitch
+  count limit."
+- "About half of true pitch volume is bullpen and warm-up that nobody counts."
+- "Scalene muscle changes in TOS are type II atrophy and fibrosis — the opposite
+  of a weight-training adaptation."
+- "There is no research supporting a ban on lifting before throwing. The
+  defensible version is avoiding upper-body work to failure near high-intent
+  throwing."
+- "Building capacity is worth doing on general shoulder-health grounds. I won't
+  claim it prevents TOS, because that hasn't been shown."
+**Do not say:**
+- "TOS incidence is 3–80 per 1,000." *(Traces to a non-indexed source.)*
+- "Roos described 14 types of congenital bands." *(No Roos primary says 14.)*
+- "GIRD contributes to TOS." *(Zero literature. Three queries, no records.)*
+- "Softball pitchers throw 1,200–1,500 pitches per tournament weekend."
+  *(Citation does not support the figure.)*
+- "Droopy shoulder syndrome narrows the costoclavicular space." *(It is a
+  traction mechanism; symptoms improve with arm elevation.)*
+- "Scapular endurance deficits cause TOS." *(No study has measured scapular
+  endurance in a TOS population at all.)*
+- "TOS surgery ends pitching careers." *(Matched-control studies find decline no
+  faster than normal aging; RTP 74–81% at 9–11 months.)*
+## Open questions worth answering locally
+1. **What is our actual diagnostic pathway?** Which test findings triggered each
+   diagnosis, and did they meet the SVS ≥3-of-4 standard?
+2. **What are our real pitch counts**, bullpen and warm-up included? No
+   collegiate pitch-count figure exists in the literature — it has to be
+   measured locally.
+3. **What is each pitcher's prior throwing history** (travel ball volume,
+   year-round participation, previous first-rib or clavicle injury)?
+4. **Has anyone imaged for structural predisposition** in the affected athletes —
+   cervical rib, elongated C7 transverse process, first-rib abnormality?
+*Prepared by Eric Rash, Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics. All citations
+verified against PubMed/Europe PMC or publisher records on 2026-09-18. Local
+library sources marked `[Zotero: KEY]`; all others `[External]`.*

# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

content.text:
## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font on an off-white ground, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding: a bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`.

**Title**: Set a `<title>` at the top of the HTML — only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It names the artifact in the browser tab and gallery, so make it a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, distinctive to this page's subject so the reader can pick it out of a gallery of many — the way an app or a document gets named, never a generic category label, and never a name plus an appended explainer after a dash or colon. When a natural title pairs the name with a generic word, the name is the half that survives the trim — keeping the generic half and dropping the identity makes the title worse, not shorter. And trim only actual explainers: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished as it is. The explanation belongs in the `description` parameter instead: pass a one-sentence `description` — it becomes the gallery card's subtitle. For HTML publishes, a `title` parameter fills in when the file has no tag (Markdown pages always keep their filename identity). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (unpkg and esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it; always pin an exact version. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (~400px). Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, and give that element any vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units; let flex/grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow; put `max-width:100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and no `min-width` wider than the screen on anything. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container — the page body must never scroll horizontally.

**Theme-aware**: Pages render in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps nothing — only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Define the complete light palette as tokens on bare `:root` (dark-first designs swap the roles consistently); redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)`, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])`; redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` so the toggle wins in both directions. Never give a color its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and give `body` an explicit token background — the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body borrows the host's theme. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may skip the dark blocks but still paints background and colors explicitly.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page - what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in. Format is not part of this read: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it - a Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title and takes almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first - CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world - its materials, instruments, vernacular - is where distinctive choices come from. Whatever the treatment, carry at least one detail only this subject would have - its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art - as content, not ornament; it costs a plain page nothing. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the one font host the Artifact CSP admits - link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`); a face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI or it falls back silently. Either way, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Load libraries, don't paste them.** When the page genuinely needs a library - React, a charting or highlighting package - load its UMD build from cdnjs (only the script - a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined) with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global, instead of inlining the library's source or hand-writing a stand-in; the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images and its data ship with the page. Most pages need no library at all - reach for one only when it carries real weight.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject - the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states, not two: an explicit choice stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting stamps *nothing* - most viewers see the un-stamped document, where only `prefers-color-scheme` separates light from dark. Structure the CSS token-level for all three: the bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice beats a dark OS; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also wins in the other direction. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block - a color whose only definition sits behind `[data-theme]` never applies in the un-stamped state, and the page renders one theme's text on the other theme's ground. Two more rules keep each theme resolving as a set: the artifact composites over a ground the viewer paints in *its* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token - a transparent body silently borrows the host's ground; and every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never a literal that only works in one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it - a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first - don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme - then skip the media query and stamps entirely but still paint the background and every color explicitly, so the page holds on either host ground; make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width - set once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides - and let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (~400px). Images and any `aspect-ratio` box get `max-width: 100%`, and nothing gets a `min-width` wider than the screen; only wide tables, code and diagrams may run past it - each gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere but a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content clears the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding; a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` rather than `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that carries its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Compose repeated things as one object.** Cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, badges on siblings: same edges, baselines and inner padding from one to the next, and a recurring element sits in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over dead space or sits alone in a row. Text that can outgrow its track wraps or scrolls in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Not everything is a card.** Border, fill, radius and shadow each say "separate object" - spend them by role, lifting the one thing that needs it, instead of one radius and one shadow stamped on every block, which flattens the hierarchy. Lead with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to the scale.** One scale places marks, ticks and labels, and every label names a value the chart reaches; chart text takes its color from the theme tokens so it reads in both themes; marks, labels and edges stay clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds - in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Show the page at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, without scrolling to trigger it - that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all get. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never parked at `opacity: 0` waiting on an observer. Size a hero to what it holds, not to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the page itself out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state - the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, a form someone plausibly filled, plainly marked as examples and never passed off as the user's own figures - so the first look shows what it does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly - their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform carries form values, focus and scroll across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out - a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen - name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it - no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Name the page like a product, not a caption.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it sets the reader's first impression of care. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject - or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which is then the page's name. Stop at the name - a title that carries its own explainer after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it sits beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could sit on any of them fails as a name just as surely as an appended explainer. When a candidate title pairs the name with a generic word - a greeting, a category, a page-type label - the name is the half to keep; a trim that drops the identity and keeps the generic word produces exactly the title that could sit on any page. And the rule removes explainers, it does not impose brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. The one-sentence publish `description` is where the explanation belongs; the gallery shows it right under the title.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number - a pill, a chip, a severity stripe - so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Start with what the viewer should be able to do on the page, not only what they will read: if it should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user; a page that is only read needs none of that.

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan - a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4-6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles - a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

**Write, look once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once - one screenshot of the local file, or the Artifact tool's preview where it offers one - then one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look. For a page that charts real numbers, take that look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. Don't build a test loop around your own file: no repeated screenshots, no pulling the script out to run it through node, no scripts that probe the DOM. That loop spends the session re-checking what a careful write already settled, while the user waits for a link. Then publish, check once any `window.claude` call the preview couldn't run, and stop: the live page is the review surface, and further polish is the user's to ask for. If the user reports something visibly broken - a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing - fix that and republish once.

**Open viewers** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open - published changes reach them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state carried where possible. If your page holds state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world - headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

Applied Performance · Evidence Brief · 18 Sept 2026

Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Overhead Throwing Athletes

What causes it, what the research actually supports, and which levers belong to whom — prepared for softball performance staff.

Eric Rash · Baylor Athletics 109 sources, PubMed-verified Softball & baseball · collegiate
How to read the confidence labels. This brief separates what is Established (measured, replicated), Plausible (coherent mechanism, no direct test), and No evidence (asserted in practice, unsupported in literature). A claim presented as stronger than it is will not survive a second opinion — and it will cost the person making it credibility on the claims that are solid.
  1. 00 Bottom line
  2. 01 Base rates & the peer comparison
  3. 02 What actually causes it
  4. 03 The endurance question
  5. 04 Lifting before throwing
  6. 05 Softball & workload
  7. 06 Mitigation & ownership
  8. 07 What to say
00 — Summary

Bottom line up front

  1. The peer comparison cannot be made. TOS is not separately coded in the NCAA Injury Surveillance Program. There is no national softball TOS rate to compare against.
  2. TOS is rare enough that no program can estimate its own rate. Population incidence is roughly 2–3 per 100,000 per year for neurogenic TOS. On a 35-athlete roster, expected cases per season is about 0.0014. Two cases is a plausible chance cluster, not a signal.
  3. Diagnosis drives counts at least as much as biology does. There is no gold-standard test for neurogenic TOS. The provocative test most used in an athletic training room is positive in 47–62% of people who do not have TOS.
  4. The throwing motion is the exposure, and the histology does not implicate the weight room. The cocked position roughly doubles scalene stiffness. The scalene changes found in TOS patients are type II atrophy plus fibrosis — the opposite of a resistance-training signature.
  5. "Don't lift before throwing" has no research support, and the adjacent evidence leans against it. The defensible version is much narrower.
  6. The endurance hypothesis is coherent and worth acting on, but it is not established. The best supporting study found a 45% rotator endurance deficit in TOS patients — in 40-year-old non-athletes, with the direction of causation unresolved.
  7. The strongest modifiable exposure is workload, and it is not the strength coach's lever. Collegiate softball pitchers throw 2.9× the innings of baseball pitchers on a staff one-third the size, under no pitch count limit — and about half of true pitch volume is bullpen and warm-up nobody counts.
01 — Epidemiology

Base rates, diagnosis, and why the peer comparison fails

If the premise is "we have more TOS than our peers," the first question is whether that sentence can be evaluated at all. It cannot.

Three conditions, not one

TOS is compression of the brachial plexus, subclavian artery, or subclavian vein in one of three anatomical spaces. The subtypes behave very differently and should never be discussed as a single entity.

SubtypeGeneral populationAthletes
Neurogenic (nTOS)82–95%66–74%
Venous (Paget-Schroetter, effort thrombosis)3–16%26–34%
Arterial (aTOS)~1–2%~2%

Established Venous TOS is roughly 5- to 10-fold over-represented in athletes. The mechanism is chronic repetitive compression of the subclavian vein in the costoclavicular space.

[External] Illig KA, et al. Ann Vasc Surg 2021;70:263-72. PMID 32771464 · Chandra V, Little C, Lee JT. J Vasc Surg 2014;60(4):1012-7. PMID 24835692 · Chauhan A, et al. Am J Sports Med 2024;52(7):1692-9. PMID 38702964 · Gutman MJ, et al. Phys Sportsmed 2022;50(2):141-6. PMID 33472488 · Vemuri C, et al. J Vasc Surg Venous Lymphat Disord 2016;4(4):485-500. PMID 27639006

Caveat: every athlete proportion above is a referral-centre or treated-case proportion, not an incidence. They describe the mix among athletes who reached a TOS surgeon.

A statistic to stop repeating

The most commonly cited TOS incidence figure is "3–80 per 1,000." It does not survive tracing:

  1. StatPearls — where most clinicians land — says "3 to 80 cases per 1,000," citing…
  2. Jones MR, et al. Pain Ther 2019 (PMID 31037504), which says "Several articles report an incidence of 3–80/1000 [4]," citing…
  3. Citisli V. J Pain Relief 2015;4(2):1-7 — which is not indexed in PubMed/MEDLINE at all.

A 27-fold-wide range is itself the tell that nobody measured anything.

"The incidence of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome is completely unknown, and has been wildly overestimated in the past." — Illig & Rodriguez-Zoppi, Thorac Surg Clin 2021. PMID 33220767

2–3nTOS cases per 100,000 per year
0.5–1vTOS cases per 100,000 per year
100–2,700×Gap between the folklore figure and the measured one

There is no gold-standard test — and the field says so in its own documents

Established This is the most defensible section of the brief.

  • The SVS reporting standards define nTOS as ≥3 of 4 criteria, one of which is absence of other pathology (a diagnosis of exclusion) and one of which is response to a scalene block (a therapeutic trial, not a test). No imaging, electrodiagnostic or laboratory criterion exists. PMID 27565607
  • Sanders 2008: "there is no standard objective test to confirm clinical impressions… To date there is still no reliable objective test." PMID 19008742
  • Cochrane: "one of the most controversial diagnoses in clinical medicine." Only two RCTs worldwide met a 6-month follow-up bar. PMID 25427003
  • Wilbourn vs Roos, Muscle Nerve 1999 — "TOS is overdiagnosed" and "TOS is underdiagnosed," published back to back in the same issue of the same journal. PMID 9883870 / 9883869
  • Even at a dedicated TOS centre, only 150 of 183 (82%) of new nTOS referrals met an established criteria set. PMID 28735950

The circularity problem

A 2026 Delphi expert consensus exists precisely because criteria remain unsettled a decade after the SVS standards. Its fifth diagnostic criterion is "participation in work/exercise requiring repetitive arm stress (overhead athletes, throwing sports)."

Read that twice. Being an overhead athlete is itself a formal diagnostic criterion for nTOS. For a programme comparing its softball TOS rate to peers, that is circular — athlete status is an input to the diagnosis.

Wagner ER, et al. Orthop J Sports Med 2026;14(5):23259671261440925. PMID 42169800

False-positive rates of provocative tests in people who do not have TOS

TestRayan 1995
(200 asymptomatic limbs)		Plewa 1998
(53 healthy)		Nord 2008
(normals)
Adson's13.5% vascular / 2% neuro11% pulse9–20%
Costoclavicular47% vascular / 10% neuro11% / 15%16%
Wright's / hyperabduction57% vascular / 16.5% neuro——
Roos / EAST—62% pulse, 36% paresthesia47%
≥1 test positive——56% of normals

[External] Rayan GM, Jensen C. J Shoulder Elbow Surg 1995;4(2):113-7. PMID 7600161 · Plewa MC, Delinger M. Acad Emerg Med 1998;5(4):337-42. PMID 9562199 · Nord KM, et al. Electromyogr Clin Neurophysiol 2008;48(2):67-74. PMID 18435210 · Warrens AN, Heaton JM. Ann R Coll Surg Engl 1987;69(5):203-4. PMID 3674682 · Gillard J, et al. Joint Bone Spine 2001;68(5):416-24. PMID 11707008

Nord 2008 adds the decisive number: in carpal tunnel patients — who by definition do not have TOS — Roos/EAST was positive in 77%, and 94% had at least one positive TOS manoeuvre. Gillard 2001 reduces it to one figure: provocative tests have mean specificity 53%.

The Roos/EAST test — the one most likely to be used in an athletic training room — is positive in roughly half of people who do not have TOS. Screening a 35-athlete roster with EAST would be expected to flag 16–20 healthy athletes.

TOS is not coded in the NCAA ISP

Established The ISP releases body part affected, specific injury, and type of injury. The body-part list is coarse and anatomical — head/face, neck, shoulder, arm or elbow, hand/wrist, trunk, hip/groin, thigh, knee, lower leg, ankle, foot, other. There is no "thoracic outlet" site and no vascular or peripheral-nerve category. The diagnosis taxonomy is injury-type based — strains, sprains, contusions — not disease-entity based. TOS appears nowhere in the two most recent 5-year NCAA baseball and softball epidemiology reports.

[External] Kerr ZY, et al. J Athl Train 2014;49(4):552-60. PMID 24870292 · Boltz AJ, et al. 2021;56(7):742-9. PMID 34280265 · Veillard KL, et al. 2021;56(7):734-41. PMID 34280289

Honest limit: the Datalys ISP documentation page returned a 404, so no internal code string can be ruled out. What is demonstrable: TOS is not reported in any published NCAA ISP output and is not in the released taxonomies. A programme wanting certainty should submit a data request to the Datalys Center.

The one usable collegiate denominator — from a chart review, not the ISP

15,609NCAA Division I athletes, 21 sports, 7 years
76TOS cases (0.48% overall)
95.4%Returned to unrestricted competition
SportTOS prevalence
Tennis2.6%
Softball1.3%
Rowing1.3%
All sports0.48%

90.8% neurogenic, 9.2% venous; 96.0% managed without surgery. Softball sits above the all-sport baseline but below tennis — and outcomes are good.

[External] Talutis SD, et al. J Vasc Surg 2025;82(1):155-62. PMID 40132734

Why a roster-level comparison is statistically meaningless

At roughly 4 per 100,000 per year for all TOS combined, a 35-athlete roster observed for one season has an expected count of 0.0014 cases.

  • Zero cases tells you nothing. By the rule of three, 35 athlete-years with zero events puts the 95% upper bound at 3/35 ≈ 8.6% per athlete-season — four orders of magnitude above the true rate. A programme with no cases has no evidence it is below average.
  • One case looks catastrophic and means almost nothing. The exact Poisson 95% CI on a single observed event is (0.03, 5.6) events.
  • Two cases is a plausible chance cluster. Poisson 95% CI on 2 events: (0.24, 7.2). A peer with 0 and a peer with 3 are not statistically distinguishable at these counts.
  • Ascertainment dominates everything. Any observed between-programme difference is far more likely to measure the referral pathway than the underlying biology.

The framing to take into the room

TOS is rare enough that no single athletic programme generates a sample large enough to estimate its own rate, let alone compare it to a peer's. The meaningful question is not "is our rate high?" but "is our diagnostic and referral pathway appropriate, and are our modifiable exposures managed?"

Outcomes, for reassurance

Five independent professional-baseball return-to-play studies converge tightly: 74–81% return to play at 9–11 months.

StudynRTPPerformance conclusion
Thompson 201713 MLB pitchers77% @ 10.8 mo75% of 72 PitchF/x metrics unchanged; max velocity −0.6 mph
Gutman 202227 MLB pitchers74% @ 297 dERA worse (3.66→4.50); velocity unchanged
Arnold 202226 MLB pitchers81% @ 10 moNo difference vs matched controls
Chauhan 202452 pro (88% pitchers)79% @ 9.5 moDeclines present, but no faster than matched healthy controls aging normally

The narrative that TOS surgery collapses a pitcher's career is supported by exactly one study (Gutman's unmatched pre/post ERA comparison) and contradicted by the two that used matched controls. Chauhan 2024 — the only one using MLB's internal Health and Injury Tracking System rather than press reports — found the decline was no faster than in healthy pitchers aging normally. An unmatched pre/post design on a cohort with mean age ~29–30 will manufacture a decline out of ordinary aging.

[External] Thompson RW, et al. Ann Vasc Surg 2017;39:216-27. PMID 27522980 · Arnold MT, et al. Orthop J Sports Med 2022;10(4). PMID 35494495 · Chauhan A, et al. PMID 38702964

02 — Mechanism

What actually causes TOS in throwing athletes

Three anatomical spaces, a common and usually silent structural predisposition, and a muscle-fibre signature that points away from the weight room.

The three compression spaces

SpaceBoundariesContents
Interscalene triangleAnterior scalene (front), middle scalene (back), first rib (below)Plexus trunks, subclavian artery. The subclavian vein passes anterior to the anterior scalene and is not in this triangle.
Costoclavicular spaceClavicle and subclavius (above), first rib (below)Plexus divisions, subclavian artery and vein
Subcoracoid spacePectoralis minor and its coracoid insertion (front), chest wall (behind)Plexus cords, axillary artery and vein

Established For arterial compression the costoclavicular space is the discriminating site — imaging of 44 volunteers and 28 arterial-TOS patients found no significant stenosis in the interscalene triangle or retropectoralis minor space in either group, with 130° hyperabduction most discriminating. PMID 16439785

Plausible The common claim that the subcoracoid space is the space most implicated in throwers is unproven — no study compares the three spaces head-to-head in throwing athletes.

Structural predisposition — common, and usually silent

0.74%Cervical rib prevalence (1,352 chest radiographs; corroborated at 0.7% in 6,571)
2.21%Elongated C7 transverse process — 3× more common, and the more likely bony contributor
⅓Of 58 cadaver outlets had at least one fibromuscular band — in people who never had symptoms
60%Of 51 cadavers had the textbook plexus-between-scalenes arrangement

[External] Brewin J, Hill M, Ellis H. Clin Anat 2009;22(3):331-6. PMID 19280652 · Ezeofor SN, et al. Niger J Clin Pract 2016;19(4):513-6. PMID 27251970 · Roos DB. Am J Surg 1976;132(6):771-8. PMID 998867; Acta Chir Belg 1980;79(5):353-61. PMID 7223264 · Harry WG, et al. Clin Anat 1997;10(4):250-2. PMID 9213042 · Makhoul RG, Machleder HI. J Vasc Surg 1992;16(4):534-42. PMID 1404675

The honest caveat — and it matters

Predisposition is not causation. Roos found his bands in a third of asymptomatic cadavers. Makhoul & Machleder concluded morphology alone predicted the clinical syndrome only for Paget-Schroetter. The defensible framing: structural narrowing is common, usually silent, and becomes symptomatic when loaded. That makes TOS a screening and load-management problem — not an act of God, and not an exoneration.

The scalene histology — why the weight room is the wrong suspect

Established Two independent biopsy series of scalene muscles taken at surgery from TOS patients found the same pattern.

FindingMachleder 1986Sanders 1990
Type I (slow/tonic) fibre predominance85.1% ± 5.1%78% vs 53% in controls
Type II fibres—Atrophied
Connective tissue (fibrosis)—36% vs <15% in controls

[External] Machleder HI, Moll F, Verity MA. Arch Surg 1986;121(10):1141-4. PMID 3767646 · Sanders RJ, Jackson CG, Banchero N, Pearce WH. Am J Surg 1990;159(2):231-6. PMID 2301718

Resistance training produces type II hypertrophy. The scalene muscle in TOS shows type II atrophy plus fibrosis and type I predominance — the signature of chronic sustained tone and of injury, not of a training adaptation. If anyone argues that weight-room hypertrophy built the compressing muscle, the histology does not support it.

Throwing loads the outlet — measurably

Established Shear wave elastography on 30 collegiate baseball pitchers:

Arm positionAnterior scaleneMiddle scalene
Neutral9.4 ± 2.0 kPa10.9 ± 3.4 kPa
ABER (cocked)14.4 ± 3.8 kPa15.8 ± 5.0 kPa
ABER + neck rotation away18.1 ± 4.6 kPa15.8 ± 2.6 kPa

The cocked throwing position roughly doubles anterior scalene stiffness. This is the cleanest mechanistic link between the throwing motion itself and loading of the interscalene triangle — and it locates the exposure in the throw.

[External] Takaba K, et al. Orthop J Sports Med 2022;10(8):23259671221114930. PMID 36003968

In the largest athlete series: mean interscalene distance 5.6 ± 3.6 mm against cadaveric norms of 10.7–15 mm, and "hypertrophy of the serratus anterior and posterior scalene muscles was commonly observed in overhead athletes." Note which muscles — posterior scalene and serratus anterior are throwing-driven, not bench-press-driven. This is the one finding a critic could reach for, and it belongs in the brief with its context rather than omitted.

[External] Funakoshi T, et al. JSES Int 2024;8(3):620-9. PMID 38707577

Positional compression is normal

Established MR imaging of 35 asymptomatic volunteers and 54 TOS patients:

47%Of asymptomatic volunteers showed positional venous compression (vs 63% of patients)
72% / 0%Arterial compression, patients vs volunteers
7% / 0%Nerve compression, patients vs volunteers

Compression is a positional phenomenon — it does not exist at rest, and roughly half of healthy people compress when you put their arm overhead. Only arterial and nerve compression discriminated.

[External] Demondion X, et al. Radiology 2003;227(2):461-8. PMID 12637678 · Demirbag D, et al. Arch Phys Med Rehabil 2007;88(7):844-51. PMID 17601463

Posture — with one correction worth making

Established "Droopy shoulder syndrome" is frequently mis-described as costoclavicular narrowing. It is not. Swift & Nichols described low-set shoulders and a long neck, with symptoms that worsened with downward traction and improved when patients elevated their arms — the opposite of what compression predicts. This is a plexus traction mechanism. PMID 6538012

Established in healthy non-athletes: a short pectoralis minor resting length is associated with a scapula that stays anteriorly tipped at higher elevation angles and is more internally rotated at lower angles. Length can be measured reliably in the field (intrarater ICC 0.86–0.97). No validated numeric cut-off for "short" exists — report the measurement, not a threshold.

[External] Borstad JD, Ludewig PM. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2005;35(4):227-38. PMID 15901124 · Borstad JD. 2008;38(4):169-74. PMID 18434665 · Rosa DP, et al. Braz J Phys Ther 2016;20(2):176-83. PMID 26982455

Scope caveat: this work was done in healthy, asymptomatic, non-athlete adults and targeted subacromial impingement, not TOS. Extending it to throwers and from impingement to subcoracoid compression is a two-step inference.

The cervical contribution — from our own library

Established in college pitchers. 49 healthy college baseball pitchers measured in preseason and followed through the season:

9.4×Risk of >7-day time-loss shoulder/elbow injury with Cervical Flexion-Rotation Test ≤39° on the dominant side (RR 9.38, 95% CI 1.28–68.49)
83.6 vs 109.4Days played before injury, restricted vs unrestricted rotation (of 112)

Proposed mechanism: reduced upper cervical rotation requires compensatory mid-cervical motion, and "these combined motions may decrease the space for the nerve roots in the intervertebral foramina" with consequent myotomal changes impairing scapular and glenohumeral control.

[Zotero: F5YKF6B4, p. 1 & p. 6] Devaney LL, et al. Orthop J Sports Med 2020;8(5):2325967120920556. DOI 10.1177/2325967120920556

Read this carefully. Devaney is not a TOS study — it measured shoulder and elbow injury. But it establishes, in exactly our population, that neck mobility is a modifiable, screenable risk factor for throwing injury, with a mechanism adjacent to the TOS story. The wide confidence intervals (n=49, 10 injuries) mean the 9.4× point estimate should not be quoted as precise; the direction and the screening implication are the usable findings.

What the literature does not support

  • No evidence GIRD → TOS. Three separate PubMed queries return zero records. Any such link is speculation.
  • No evidence Resistance training causes TOS. No controlled or cohort evidence exists. What exists is case reports — a weightlifter with Paget-Schroetter attributed to bench pressing; a rower/weightlifter with well-developed scalenes; a weightlifter with subclavian occlusion confounded by anabolic steroid use.
  • The closest thing to support for a hypertrophy mechanism in a thrower is a Division I pitcher with axillary artery compression from "hypertrophy of the pectoralis minor and scalene muscles" — attributed to throwing, not to a documented lifting programme. PMID 19588212
  • A 2022 systematic review of TOS in sport located 78 articles: 40 case reports, 10 clinical studies, 28 reviews. That composition is the finding. PMID 35755427

The defensible statement

Pectoralis minor and scalene hypertrophy have been documented as the compressing structure in individual athlete case reports — in throwing, water polo, rowing and weightlifting. Whether training-induced hypertrophy raises TOS risk at a population level has never been tested.

03 — Capacity

Can a lack of endurance or muscle capacity cause TOS?

Direct answer: it is a coherent, mechanistically reasonable hypothesis with no direct empirical support. Act on it because it is cheap, safe and independently justified — not because the evidence establishes it.

The strongest supporting study

100 nTOS patients vs 100 healthy controls, isokinetic shoulder rotator testing, with an endurance test defined as 30 repetitions at 180°/s:

MeasureMedial rotatorsLateral rotators
Peak strength 60°/s−21%−29%
Peak strength 180°/s−23%−20%
Endurance (30 reps @ 180°/s)−45%−30%

All p≤.001, all correlated with disability score. The endurance deficit is roughly twice the strength deficit — the single most striking number in this review.

[External] Daley P, et al. Diagnostics (Basel) 2021;11(9):1529. PMID 34573871

Four constraints block a causal reading — state all four

  1. Direction of causation is unresolvable by this design. nTOS is brachial plexus compression. Reduced fatigue resistance is at least as plausibly a consequence — partial denervation, pain inhibition, disuse — as a cause. The authors make no causal claim.
  2. Wrong muscles. This measured glenohumeral rotators — not scapular stabilisers, not deep neck flexors.
  3. Wrong population. 71% female, mean age 39.4, clinic population. Every direct capacity study in TOS is a non-athlete, predominantly female, ~40-year-old cohort. None has ever been done in an athlete.
  4. The companion study argues for consequence. Grip −30%, key pinch −19.5% — the classic C8–T1 lower-plexus signature. That points to nerve compression producing weakness, not the reverse. PMID 34068245

The outright evidentiary blanks

  • None Scapular stabiliser endurance in TOS vs controls: no study exists.
  • None Deep neck flexor endurance in TOS: zero studies.
  • None EMG evidence of scalene overactivity during breathing in TOS. The one respiratory study found TOS patients had reduced respiratory muscle endurance — if anything the opposite of the hyperactive-accessory-breather story. PMID 32829949
  • None Nobody has measured costoclavicular or subcoracoid space before and after a fatigue protocol. That single experiment would convert this from plausibility to mechanism. It has not been run.
  • None No RCT of exercise therapy versus control for nTOS exists. The only nTOS RCT compared surgery to continued conservative care in patients already refractory — and all 25 conservative-arm patients applied for surgery at 3 months. PMID 35537641

The indirect chain — fatigue alters scapular position

Established in healthy subjects, acute lab fatigue, framed around subacromial impingement — not the thoracic outlet.

StudynFatigue protocolScapular result
Tsai 200330 healthyExternal rotation↓ posterior tilt, ↓ external rotation, ↓ upward rotation
Ebaugh 2006 (JOSPT)20 healthyExternal rotation↓ posterior tilt early; ↑ upward rotation mid-range
Ebaugh 2006 (JEK)20 healthyRepetitive overhead↑ upward and external rotation
Joshi 201125 overhead athletesGH external rotation↓ lower trapezius activity, ↑ upward rotation
Harrison 202130Serratus anterior↓ posterior tilt, ↑ internal rotation, no change in upward rotation

What replicates is decreased posterior tilt (increased anterior tilt) — four of five studies. Upward rotation does not replicate: one study found it decreased, three found it increased, one found no change. Do not assert a consistent upward-rotation deficit.

[External] Tsai NT, et al. Arch Phys Med Rehabil 2003;84(7):1000-5. PMID 12881824 · Ebaugh DD, et al. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 2006;36(8):557-71. PMID 16915977; J Electromyogr Kinesiol 2006;16(3):224-35. PMID 16125416 · Joshi M, et al. J Athl Train 2011;46(4):349-57. PMID 21944066 · Harrison N, et al. J Sport Rehabil 2021;30(8):1151-7. PMID 34294607

The inferred chain — label it as inferred. Scapular muscle fatigue → increased anterior tilt and internal rotation (measured, replicated) → coracoid moves inferoanteriorly, clavicle approaches the first rib (anatomically reasoned) → narrowing of the costoclavicular and subcoracoid spaces (spaces are real and position-dependent, but never measured under fatigue) → brachial plexus compression (never demonstrated).

What the treatment protocols actually target

A 2026 scoping review screened 1,381 studies and included 29. Exercise appeared in 17/19 (90%) of programmes: stretching (n=15) targeting scalenes and pectoralis; strengthening (n=14) targeting scapula (n=9), trapezius and serratus anterior (n=5); posture (n=13), manual therapy (n=10).

The premise is confirmed at the level of muscle selection — and fails at the level of muscle quality. The review's own conclusion: "The reporting of rehabilitation techniques for NTOS is generally poor, particularly regarding treatment intensity." No published nTOS protocol specifies sets, reps or loads in a way that would let you classify it as endurance training. Anyone asserting "the protocols target endurance specifically" is reading intent into silence.

[External] O'Sullivan J, et al. Hand Ther 2026;17589983251411877. PMID 41657761 · Watson LA, Pizzari T, Balster S. Man Ther 2010;15(4):305-14. PMID 20382063

Conservative success rates span a wide, selection-driven range

StudynResult
Novak 19954225 improved / 10 same / 7 worse (~60%); only 16/42 back to full work + recreation
Lindgren 199711988% satisfied at ~25 mo (uncontrolled, subjective endpoint)
Balderman 2019150Only 40 (27%) satisfactory with PT alone; 60% went to surgery
Fouasson-Chailloux 20251823-week inpatient rehab: rotator endurance +35–39% (uncontrolled)

27% and 88% are not in conflict — they are opposite ends of a selection spectrum. Neither is the number for an athlete. No cohort anywhere reports what fraction of throwing athletes with nTOS resolve with rehabilitation alone. For a strength-and-conditioning audience, that is the most important absence in the entire literature.

Does injury-prevention programming work in overhead athletes?

Mixed, and weaker than our field generally believes. Know this before citing it.

  • The handball risk-factor study found scapular dyskinesis OR 8.41 (95% CI 1.47–48.1) — then the same group's own replication failed, in a paper subtitled "previous findings could not be confirmed."
  • The flagship RCT (45 teams, 660 players) reduced any shoulder problem — OR 0.72, p=.038 — but not substantial problems: OR 0.78, p=.23.
  • The mechanism failed to move. An RCT of 8 weeks of external rotation band strengthening produced a between-group difference of 0.06 N/kg (95% CI −0.01 to 0.14): "The ER strength program improved neither the ER strength nor the ER:IR ratio."
  • The pooled result is null. 3 RCTs, n=747: OR 0.73 (95% CI 0.45–1.17).
  • Baseball's positive RCT (HR 1.940, p=.010) used 5 stretching + 2 dynamic mobility + 2 balance exercises, with no scapular strengthening at all.

[External] Clarsen B, et al. Br J Sports Med 2014;48(17):1327-33. PMID 24948083 · Andersson SH, et al. 2018;52(18):1191-8. PMID 28784621; 2017;51(14):1073-80. The line to use

"Building scapular and postural capacity is a mechanistically coherent, low-cost, low-risk intervention that is independently justified by general shoulder health. The claim that it prevents TOS specifically has no direct empirical support."

04 — Session timing

"Don't lift the pitchers before they throw" — is it supported?

Direct answer: no. There is no research supporting this recommendation, and the adjacent evidence leans against it.

No evidence Three structured PubMed queries returned no baseball study examining resistance training performed before throwing and its effect on velocity, accuracy, mechanics, kinematics, kinetics, or injury rates. On TOS specifically: zero papers connect resistance training timing to thoracic outlet syndrome.

The adjacent evidence leans the other way

StudyProtocolResult
Water polo, n=123×6 @ 80% 1RM (bench, row, half squat) 15 min before in-water testingNo difference in throwing velocity (14.67 vs 14.91 m/s), accuracy, tethered force, swim or jump (all p>0.05)
Tennis3×6 @ 75% 1RM, maximal intended velocity, not to failureNo change in serve/forehand/backhand velocity or accuracy at 3 min, 24 h or 48 h
Trained throwers, n=14Morning total-body resistance sessionAfternoon overhead throw distance improved (p<0.05), 4–6 h later

[External] Malliaros I, et al. Sports (Basel) 2025;13(11):378. PMID 41295761 — authors state such training "can be safely implemented 15 min prior to in-water training sessions." · Terraza-Rebollo M, Baiget E. PLoS One 2021;16(12):e0260825. PMID 34882729 · Ekstrand LG, et al. J Strength Cond Res 2013;27(1):101-6. PMID 22395279

The one study showing a decrement — and why it undercuts the rule

16 adolescent baseball pitchers: push-ups to failure and repeated countermovement jumps to failure each dropped pitch velocity ~2 km/h (p=0.005). PMID 38838214

  1. It used fatigue to failure, not a programmed lift.
  2. The recovery interval before re-test was not quantified. Pilot, non-randomised.
  3. Lower-body fatigue dropped velocity as much as upper-body fatigue. If the mechanism were loading the throwing arm, squatting should not have mattered equally. This contradicts the rationale the rule rests on.

The mechanistic chain breaks at the end

  • Established Fatigue degrades shoulder proprioception — robust and replicated.
  • But the deficit does not become functional. A 160% increase in joint repositioning error produced no change in motor control (Y-Balance Upper Quarter) or performance (Athletic Shoulder test). PMID 39461122
  • Recovery is fast. After throwing-to-fatigue in 16 collegiate players, scapulothoracic, glenohumeral, elbow and endpoint acuity recovered within 4–7 minutes. The one exception: glenohumeral acuity in the arm-cocked position had not recovered at 10 minutes. PMID 18174932
  • Counterweight: strength training is associated with better shoulder proprioception chronically. PMID 25594912
  • All the fatigue-alters-pitching-mechanics literature concerns fatigue from throwing itself.

That arm-cocked exception is the single most defensible mechanistic hook for the athletic training staff's concern. It is narrow, and it is about the cocked position specifically.

The defensible version

RationaleSupport
Manage total daily/weekly loadBest supported, but indirectly — the literature is about cumulative throwing load
Avoid heavy loading of the throwing shoulder specificallyNot supported, actively undercut
Proximity in hoursWeak — 15 min fine, 3 min fine, 4–6 h beneficial
Nothing at allClosest to the truth for the blanket rule

Recommended reframe

Not "no lifting before throwing," but: avoid taking the upper body to failure, and avoid novel heavy eccentric upper-body work, in the hours before a high-intent throwing session. A dose-and-proximity-to-failure statement. Every trial using a dosed, sub-failure lift found no impairment.

Present the current rule as conservative professional judgment — a legitimate basis for a decision — but not as research-backed. There is no NSCA or ACSM baseball-specific position statement, and no MLB/ASMI consensus, prescribing lifting-relative-to-throwing order.

05 — Softball

Softball-specific evidence and workload

The softball TOS literature barely exists. The exposure case, by contrast, is the strongest part of this brief.

The scarcity, quantified

A PubMed title/abstract search for thoracic outlet AND softball returns exactly 6 records:

  • 2 case reports in softball athletes — both structural/congenital first-rib pathology (a fracture nonunion and a congenital pseudarthrosis). Neither identifies the patient as a pitcher.
  • 4 cohort studies where softball is pooled with baseball or given only as a prevalence.

A systematic review of Paget-Schroetter syndrome in athletes does not contain the word "softball" — zero softball effort-thrombosis cases in the systematic literature. PMID 32868012

No peer-reviewed paper attributes TOS or effort thrombosis in a softball pitcher to the pitching motion. The design ceiling across the entire softball TOS literature is the single case report. Every mechanistic claim must be extrapolated from baseball, and the extrapolation should be stated.

The windmill is not load-sparing

MeasureValueSource
Shoulder distraction, youth94% body weightWerner 2005, n=53
Shoulder distraction, elite/Olympic80% BWWerner 2006, n=24
Peak compression, shoulder & elbow70–98% BWBarrentine 1998, n=8
Peak biceps activation, windmill vs overhand (velocity-matched)38% vs 19%Rojas 2009

Three independent sources state windmill shoulder and elbow loads are similar to baseball pitching. Our own library says the same: "it is continually reported that the shoulder stress endured from the softball pitch is analogous to that of the baseball pitch," with shoulder injury rates and patterns "comparable with those reported in the sport of baseball."

[Zotero: FGQAC8DL, p. 1] Oliver GD, et al. Orthop J Sports Med 2019;7(8):2325967119865171 · [External] Werner SL, et al. Am J Sports Med 2005;33(4):552-60. PMID 15722291; 2006;34(4):597-603. PMID 16282576 · Barrentine SW, et al. J Orthop Sports Phys Ther 1998;28(6):405-15. PMID 9836172 · Rojas IL, et al. Am J Sports Med 2009;37(3):558-65. PMID 19174551

The "windmill is a natural motion" belief is explicitly named as a misconception in the peer-reviewed literature. At matched ball velocity, biceps demand is double the overhand throw.

Inference Hyperabduction. The windmill carries the arm through full overhead elevation once per pitch, transiently and at high angular velocity. No windmill study reports maximum shoulder elevation angle or time above 90°. The plausible outlet link is cumulative repetition, not sustained positional narrowing.

The actionable lever is proximal. Lower-extremity screening alone predicted 49.9% of peak shoulder distraction variance in 46 collegiate pitchers, rising to 56.2% with hip rotation strength. PMID 39844736 Our library adds the trunk side: at foot contact, increased trunk rotation toward the pitching arm, increased stride length and a posteriorly shifted centre of mass explained ~33% of variance in upper-extremity pain among 37 D1 softball pitchers. [Zotero: FGQAC8DL, p. 1 & p. 4]

Workload — the strongest part of the case

Rules, verified

NCAA softball has no pitch count limit and no mandated rest. Confirmed three ways. NCAA baseball likewise has none — but NFHS Rule 6-2-6 requires every state association to adopt a baseball pitch-count restriction with mandated rest, while NFHS softball is capped only by innings.

Caveat: the current NCAA rulebook PDF would not retrieve. Confirm against the current rulebook before publishing a rules claim.

Collegiate workload — 40 softball and 40 baseball College World Series teams, 2016–2021:
