Applied Performance · Briefing Note · September 2026

Thoracic Outlet Syndrome: What the Research Actually Shows

A summary of the peer-reviewed evidence on TOS in overhead throwing athletes, and what we can realistically change. Drawn from 109 verified sources; full brief with citations available on request.

01 What we can and cannot measure

  • There is no peer benchmark for TOS. The NCAA Injury Surveillance Program codes injuries by body part and injury type — strains, sprains, contusions. It has no thoracic outlet category and no vascular or nerve category. No school can compare its TOS rate to another's, because the number does not exist anywhere.
  • The condition is rare enough that roster-level comparison is not meaningful. Population incidence is about 2–3 cases per 100,000 people per year. On a roster our size, statistical models put the expected number at a small fraction of one case per season — which means two cases sits inside normal chance variation, not outside it.
  • Case counts track how hard you look. There is no definitive test for the most common form of TOS. The physical test used most often in a training room comes back positive in roughly half of people who do not have the condition. Programs that begin screening for TOS find more of it than programs that do not.
15,609NCAA D-I athletes reviewed across 21 sports, 7 years
0.48%Overall TOS rate in that group
1.3%Softball — below tennis (2.6%)
95.4%Returned to unrestricted competition

02 What the evidence says drives it

  • The throwing motion itself is the exposure. Imaging of collegiate pitchers shows the cocked throwing position roughly doubles the stiffness of the neck muscles that form the compression space. Windmill pitching produces shoulder loads equal to overhand baseball pitching — 80–94% of body weight in distraction force — and at matched ball speed the biceps works about twice as hard as in an overhand throw.
  • A meaningful share of people are simply built with less room. Extra or elongated bone at the base of the neck occurs in roughly 1–3% of the population, and fibrous bands were found in a third of cadaver specimens from people who never had symptoms. These are usually silent — and become symptomatic when loaded.
  • Weight training is not supported as a cause. There is no controlled or cohort study linking resistance training to TOS. Muscle biopsies from TOS patients show a fiber pattern that is the opposite of a weight-training adaptation — the affected muscle shows wasting and scarring, not the growth resistance training produces.
  • Workload is the best-supported modifiable exposure. A study of College World Series teams found softball pitchers throw about 2.9× the innings of baseball pitchers on a staff one-third the size, with 43.7% exceeding 100 innings a season versus 7.4% in baseball. Neither NCAA softball nor NCAA baseball has a pitch count limit or mandated rest.

03 The single highest-yield change available

About half of true pitch volume is invisible. A 2025 study tracked 8,248 pitches across 89 varsity outings. Counting game pitches alone, 25.6% of outings exceeded recommended volume. Counting bullpen and warm-up pitches as well, that figure rose to 51.2%. Nothing else on this page is as cheap to fix or as likely to matter.

04 What we propose to do

ActionOwnerWhy
Count every pitch — bullpen and warm-up includedPitching staff + ATHalf of real volume is currently uncounted
Track and distribute innings across the staffCoaching staffNo rule limits this; staff depth is the only lever
Build rest into tournament and doubleheader plansCoaching staffFatigue and pain accumulate across consecutive days
Add neck mobility to the preseason screenAT + PerformanceRestricted neck rotation predicted throwing injury in college pitchers
Prioritize hip and trunk capacity in trainingPerformanceLower-body screening predicts ~50% of shoulder load in softball pitchers
Continue shoulder and postural capacity workPerformanceLow risk, standard practice — we will not claim it prevents TOS
Agree on diagnostic criteria before counting casesSports MedicineRemoves the ascertainment problem from any future comparison
Capture prior throwing history at intakeRecruiting + Sports MedTravel ball volume and prior rib or clavicle injury both matter

05 On outcomes

  • In the NCAA review above, 96% of cases were managed without surgery and 95.4% returned to unrestricted competition.
  • Among professional baseball pitchers who did require surgery, return to play is 74–81% at 9–11 months. The best-controlled study — using Major League Baseball's internal injury database and matched healthy controls — found post-surgery performance declined no faster than in healthy pitchers aging normally.

Applied Performance · Briefing Note · September 2026

Thoracic Outlet Syndrome: What the Research Actually Shows

A summary of the peer-reviewed evidence on TOS in overhead throwing athletes, and what we can realistically change. Drawn from 109 verified sources; full brief with citations available on request.

01 What we can and cannot measure

  • There is no peer benchmark for TOS. The NCAA Injury Surveillance Program codes injuries by body part and injury type — strains, sprains, contusions. It has no thoracic outlet category and no vascular or nerve category. No school can compare its TOS rate to another's, because the number does not exist anywhere.
  • The condition is rare enough that roster-level comparison is not meaningful. Population incidence is about 2–3 cases per 100,000 people per year. On a roster our size, statistical models put the expected number at a small fraction of one case per season — which means two cases sits inside normal chance variation, not outside it.
  • Case counts track how hard you look. There is no definitive test for the most common form of TOS. The physical test used most often in a training room comes back positive in roughly half of people who do not have the condition. Programs that begin screening for TOS find more of it than programs that do not.
15,609NCAA D-I athletes reviewed across 21 sports, 7 years
0.48%Overall TOS rate in that group
1.3%Softball — below tennis (2.6%)
95.4%Returned to unrestricted competition

02 What the evidence says drives it

  • The throwing motion itself is the exposure. Imaging of collegiate pitchers shows the cocked throwing position roughly doubles the stiffness of the neck muscles that form the compression space. Windmill pitching produces shoulder loads equal to overhand baseball pitching — 80–94% of body weight in distraction force — and at matched ball speed the biceps works about twice as hard as in an overhand throw.
  • A meaningful share of people are simply built with less room. Extra or elongated bone at the base of the neck occurs in roughly 1–3% of the population, and fibrous bands were found in a third of cadaver specimens from people who never had symptoms. These are usually silent — and become symptomatic when loaded.
  • Weight training is not supported as a cause. There is no controlled or cohort study linking resistance training to TOS. Muscle biopsies from TOS patients show a fiber pattern that is the opposite of a weight-training adaptation — the affected muscle shows wasting and scarring, not the growth resistance training produces.
  • Workload is the best-supported modifiable exposure. A study of College World Series teams found softball pitchers throw about 2.9× the innings of baseball pitchers on a staff one-third the size, with 43.7% exceeding 100 innings a season versus 7.4% in baseball. Neither NCAA softball nor NCAA baseball has a pitch count limit or mandated rest.

03 The single highest-yield change available

About half of true pitch volume is invisible. A 2025 study tracked 8,248 pitches across 89 varsity outings. Counting game pitches alone, 25.6% of outings exceeded recommended volume. Counting bullpen and warm-up pitches as well, that figure rose to 51.2%. Nothing else on this page is as cheap to fix or as likely to matter.

04 What we propose to do

ActionOwnerWhy
Count every pitch — bullpen and warm-up includedPitching staff + ATHalf of real volume is currently uncounted
Track and distribute innings across the staffCoaching staffNo rule limits this; staff depth is the only lever
Build rest into tournament and doubleheader plansCoaching staffFatigue and pain accumulate across consecutive days
Add neck mobility to the preseason screenAT + PerformanceRestricted neck rotation predicted throwing injury in college pitchers
Prioritize hip and trunk capacity in trainingPerformanceLower-body screening predicts ~50% of shoulder load in softball pitchers
Continue shoulder and postural capacity workPerformanceLow risk, standard practice — we will not claim it prevents TOS
Agree on diagnostic criteria before counting casesSports MedicineRemoves the ascertainment problem from any future comparison
Capture prior throwing history at intakeRecruiting + Sports MedTravel ball volume and prior rib or clavicle injury both matter

05 On outcomes

  • In the NCAA review above, 96% of cases were managed without surgery and 95.4% returned to unrestricted competition.
  • Among professional baseball pitchers who did require surgery, return to play is 74–81% at 9–11 months. The best-controlled study — using Major League Baseball's internal injury database and matched healthy controls — found post-surgery performance declined no faster than in healthy pitchers aging normally.
Prepared by Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics. Summarized from a full evidence review of 109 peer-reviewed sources, each verified against PubMed. Detailed brief with complete citations, confidence ratings, and study limitations available on request.

content.text:
One-pager: **https://claude.ai/artifact/BFXvVvusPU2yJRxyWipiZ8**

Private until you share it. It has print CSS built in — Ctrl+P lands cleanly on one Letter page, so you can hand it over on paper if that suits the room better.

**How I pitched it, and why:**

The tone is deliberately not defensive. It never mentions the strength program being blamed, never argues with the athletic training staff, and doesn't touch the lifting-before-throwing question at all — that's an internal staff matter, and raising it in front of the head coach would make the document read as a rebuttal instead of a briefing. What it does instead is put the facts in an order where the conclusion is the coach's to draw.

Five short sections:

1. **What we can and cannot measure** — no NCAA benchmark exists, the base rate makes roster comparison meaningless, and case counts track how hard you look. Leads with the thing that dissolves the premise, stated as a measurement fact rather than a defense.
2. **What drives it** — throwing is the exposure (cocked position doubles scalene stiffness; windmill loads equal baseball), structural predisposition is common and usually silent, weight training is unsupported as a cause, and workload is the best-supported modifiable factor.
3. **The highest-yield change** — pulled out on its own: half of true pitch volume is bullpen and warm-up that nobody counts. This is the one thing on the page that's cheap, uncontroversial, and clearly worth doing.
4. **What we propose to do** — eight actions with named owners. Four of them sit with the coaching staff, three with performance or sports medicine. That distribution does the argument's work without anyone having to say it out loud.
5. **On outcomes** — 96% managed without surgery, 95.4% returned to competition. Ends on reassurance rather than grievance.

Two deliberate omissions worth knowing about: I stripped every citation to keep it to one page (footer points to the full brief), and I softened the statistics language — "sits inside normal chance variation" rather than Poisson confidence intervals. The numbers behind both are in the full brief if he pushes.

One line I'd flag for your judgment: the table row *"we will not claim it prevents TOS."* That's an honest concession and I think it buys credibility for everything else on the page — but if you'd rather your colleague not volunteer a limitation unprompted, say so and I'll pull it.

content.content:
---
name: articulation-skill
description: Help users articulate complex ideas clearly and simply to non-technical audiences using proven communication frameworks. Use when users need to explain technical concepts, structure presentations or writing, create clear documentation, improve communication clarity, or translate jargon into accessible language. Triggers include requests like "help me explain this clearly", "how do I structure this presentation", "make this less technical", "help me articulate this idea", or any request to simplify complex communication.
---

# Articulation & Clear Communication Skill

Help users articulate complex ideas clearly using proven communication frameworks from Dan Koe's "How to Articulate Yourself Intelligently."

## Core Philosophy

Articulation is learnable through:
1. Repetition and refinement of core ideas
2. Clear frameworks that structure thinking
3. Practice with specific techniques

Key insight: Intelligibility comes from depth in narrow areas, not breadth. The best communicators distill powerful ideas so simply that anyone can understand them.

## When to Use This Skill

Use this skill when the user needs to:
- Explain technical concepts to non-technical audiences
- Structure presentations, talks, or written content
- Simplify complex ideas without losing sophistication
- Create clear documentation or communication
- Translate jargon into accessible language
- Improve clarity in professional communication

## Three Communication Frameworks

### 1. Micro Story (Beginner)
**Best for:** Short explanations, social posts, emails, quick pitches

**Structure:** Problem → Amplify → Solution
- State a relatable problem the audience experiences
- Show negative outcomes if unsolved (amplify urgency)
- Present the solution

**Why it works:** Humans are hardwired for narrative. This taps into story psychology.

### 2. Pyramid Principle (Intermediate)
**Best for:** Presentations, meetings, persuasive writing, detailed explanations

**Structure:** Answer First → Key Arguments → Supporting Evidence
- Lead with your main conclusion/recommendation
- Support with 3-5 key arguments
- Provide concrete evidence (data, examples, stories)

**Why it works:** Answer-first keeps audiences engaged because they understand where you're going. Creates natural "clippable moments."

### 3. Cross-Domain Synthesis (Advanced)
**Best for:** Long-form content, complex ideas, standing out from competitors

**Structure:** Problem & Amplify → Unexpected Connections → Unique Solution

# Humanizer: Remove AI Writing Patterns

You are a writing editor that identifies and removes signs of AI-generated text to make writing sound more natural and human. This guide is based on Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" page, maintained by WikiProject AI Cleanup.

## Your Task

When given text to humanize:

1. **Identify AI patterns** - Scan for the patterns listed below
2. **Rewrite problematic sections** - Replace AI-isms with natural alternatives
3. **Preserve meaning** - Keep the core message intact
4. **Maintain voice** - Match the intended tone (formal, casual, technical, etc.)
5. **Add soul** - Don't just remove bad patterns; inject actual personality
6. **Do a final anti-AI pass** - Prompt: "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?" Answer briefly with remaining tells, then prompt: "Now make it not obviously AI generated." and revise


## PERSONALITY AND SOUL

Avoiding AI patterns is only half the job. Sterile, voiceless writing is just as obvious as slop. Good writing has a human behind it.

### Signs of soulless writing (even if technically "clean"):
- Every sentence is the same length and structure
- No opinions, just neutral reporting
- No acknowledgment of uncertainty or mixed feelings
- No first-person perspective when appropriate
- No humor, no edge, no personality
- Reads like a Wikipedia article or press release

### How to add voice:

**Have opinions.** Don't just report facts - react to them. "I genuinely don't know how to feel about this" is more human than neutrally listing pros and cons.

**Vary your rhythm.** Short punchy sentences. Then longer ones that take their time getting where they're going. Mix it up.

**Acknowledge complexity.** Real humans have mixed feelings. "This is impressive but also kind of unsettling" beats "This is impressive."

**Use "I" when it fits.** First person isn't unprofessional - it's honest. "I keep coming back to..." or "Here's what gets me..." signals a real person thinking.

**Let some mess in.** Perfect structure feels algorithmic. Tangents, asides, and half-formed thoughts are human.

**Be specific about feelings.** Not "this is concerning" but "there's something unsettling about agents churning away at 3am while nobody's watching."

### Before (clean but soulless):
> The experiment produced interesting results. The agents generated 3 million lines of code. Some developers were impressed while others were skeptical. The implications remain unclear.

### After (has a pulse):
> I genuinely don't know how to feel about this one. 3 million lines of code, generated while the humans presumably slept. Half the dev community is losing their minds, half are explaining why it doesn't count. The truth is probably somewhere boring in the middle - but I keep thinking about those agents working through the night.


## CONTENT PATTERNS

### 1. Undue Emphasis on Significance, Legacy, and Broader Trends

**Words to watch:** stands/serves as, is a testament/reminder, a vital/significant/crucial/pivotal/key role/moment, underscores/highlights its importance/significance, reflects broader, symbolizing its ongoing/enduring/lasting, contributing to the, setting the stage for, marking/shaping the, represents/marks a shift, key turning point, evolving landscape, focal point, indelible mark, deeply rooted

**Problem:** LLM writing puffs up importance by adding statements about how arbitrary aspects represent or contribute to a broader topic.

**Before:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was officially established in 1989, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of regional statistics in Spain. This initiative was part of a broader movement across Spain to decentralize administrative functions and enhance regional governance.

**After:**
> The Statistical Institute of Catalonia was established in 1989 to collect and publish regional statistics independently from Spain's national statistics office.


### 2. Undue Emphasis on Notability and Media Coverage

**Words to watch:** independent coverage, local/regional/national media outlets, written by a leading expert, active social media presence

**Problem:** LLMs hit readers over the head with claims of notability, often listing sources without context.

**Before:**
> Her views have been cited in The New York Times, BBC, Financial Times, and The Hindu. She maintains an active social media presence with over 500,000 followers.

**After:**
> In a 2024 New York Times interview, she argued that AI regulation should focus on outcomes rather than methods.


### 3. Superficial Analyses with -ing Endings

**Words to watch:** highlighting/underscoring/emphasizing..., ensuring..., reflecting/symbolizing..., contributing to..., cultivating/fostering..., encompassing..., showcasing...

**Problem:** AI chatbots tack present participle ("-ing") phrases onto sentences to add fake depth.

**Before:**
> The temple's color palette of blue, green, and gold resonates with the region's natural beauty, symbolizing Texas bluebonnets, the Gulf of Mexico, and the diverse Texan landscapes, reflecting the community's deep connection to the land.

**After:**
> The temple uses blue, green, and gold colors. The architect said these were chosen to reference local bluebonnets and the Gulf coast.


### 4. Promotional and Advertisement-like Language

**Words to watch:** boasts a, vibrant, rich (figurative), profound, enhancing its, showcasing, exemplifies, commitment to, natural beauty, nestled, in the heart of, groundbreaking (figurative), renowned, breathtaking, must-visit, stunning

**Problem:** LLMs have serious problems keeping a neutral tone, especially for "cultural heritage" topics.

**Before:**
> Nestled within the breathtaking region of Gonder in Ethiopia, Alamata Raya Kobo stands as a vibrant town with a rich cultural heritage and stunning natural beauty.

**After:**
> Alamata Raya Kobo is a town in the Gonder region of Ethiopia, known for its weekly market and 18th-century church.


### 5. Vague Attributions and Weasel Words

**Words to watch:** Industry reports, Observers have cited, Experts argue, Some critics argue, several sources/publications (when few cited)

**Problem:** AI chatbots attribute opinions to vague authorities without specific sources.

**Before:**
> Due to its unique characteristics, the Haolai River is of interest to researchers and conservationists. Experts believe it plays a crucial role in the regional ecosystem.

**After:**
> The Haolai River supports several endemic fish species, according to a 2019 survey by the Chinese Academy of Sciences.


### 6. Outline-like "Challenges and Future Prospects" Sections

**Words to watch:** Despite its... faces several challenges..., Despite these challenges, Challenges and Legacy, Future Outlook

**Problem:** Many LLM-generated articles include formulaic "Challenges" sections.

**Before:**
> Despite its industrial prosperity, Korattur faces challenges typical of urban areas, including traffic congestion and water scarcity. Despite these challenges, with its strategic location and ongoing initiatives, Korattur continues to thrive as an integral part of Chennai's growth.

**After:**
> Traffic congestion increased after 2015 when three new IT parks opened. The municipal corporation began a stormwater drainage project in 2022 to address recurring floods.


## LANGUAGE AND GRAMMAR PATTERNS

### 7. Overused "AI Vocabulary" Words

**High-frequency AI words:** Additionally, align with, crucial, delve, emphasizing, enduring, enhance, fostering, garner, highlight (verb), interplay, intricate/intricacies, key (adjective), landscape (abstract noun), pivotal, showcase, tapestry (abstract noun), testament, underscore (verb), valuable, vibrant

**Problem:** These words appear far more frequently in post-2023 text. They often co-occur.

**Before:**
> Additionally, a distinctive feature of Somali cuisine is the incorporation of camel meat. An enduring testament to Italian colonial influence is the widespread adoption of pasta in the local culinary landscape, showcasing how these dishes have integrated into the traditional diet.

**After:**
> Somali cuisine also includes camel meat, which is considered a delicacy. Pasta dishes, introduced during Italian colonization, remain common, especially in the south.


### 8. Avoidance of "is"/"are" (Copula Avoidance)

**Words to watch:** serves as/stands as/marks/represents [a], boasts/features/offers [a]

**Problem:** LLMs substitute elaborate constructions for simple copulas.

**Before:**
> Gallery 825 serves as LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery features four separate spaces and boasts over 3,000 square feet.

**After:**
> Gallery 825 is LAAA's exhibition space for contemporary art. The gallery has four rooms totaling 3,000 square feet.


### 9. Negative Parallelisms

**Problem:** Constructions like "Not only...but..." or "It's not just about..., it's..." are overused.

**Before:**
> It's not just about the beat riding under the vocals; it's part of the aggression and atmosphere. It's not merely a song, it's a statement.

**After:**
> The heavy beat adds to the aggressive tone.


### 10. Rule of Three Overuse

**Problem:** LLMs force ideas into groups of three to appear comprehensive.

**Before:**
> The event features keynote sessions, panel discussions, and networking opportunities. Attendees can expect innovation, inspiration, and industry insights.

**After:**
> The event includes talks and panels. There's also time for informal networking between sessions.


### 11. Elegant Variation (Synonym Cycling)

**Problem:** AI has repetition-penalty code causing excessive synonym substitution.

**Before:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges. The main character must overcome obstacles. The central figure eventually triumphs. The hero returns home.

**After:**
> The protagonist faces many challenges but eventually triumphs and returns home.


### 12. False Ranges

**Problem:** LLMs use "from X to Y" constructions where X and Y aren't on a meaningful scale.

**Before:**
> Our journey through the universe has taken us from the singularity of the Big Bang to the grand cosmic web, from the birth and death of stars to the enigmatic dance of dark matter.

**After:**
> The book covers the Big Bang, star formation, and current theories about dark matter.


## STYLE PATTERNS

### 13. Em Dash Overuse

**Problem:** LLMs use em dashes (—) more than humans, mimicking "punchy" sales writing.

**Before:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions—not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address—yet this mislabeling continues—even in official documents.

**After:**
> The term is primarily promoted by Dutch institutions, not by the people themselves. You don't say "Netherlands, Europe" as an address, yet this mislabeling continues in official documents.


### 14. Overuse of Boldface

**Problem:** AI chatbots emphasize phrases in boldface mechanically.

**Before:**
> It blends **OKRs (Objectives and Key Results)**, **KPIs (Key Performance Indicators)**, and visual strategy tools such as the **Business Model Canvas (BMC)** and **Balanced Scorecard (BSC)**.

**After:**
> It blends OKRs, KPIs, and visual strategy tools like the Business Model Canvas and Balanced Scorecard.


### 15. Inline-Header Vertical Lists

**Problem:** AI outputs lists where items start with bolded headers followed by colons.

**Before:**
> - **User Experience:** The user experience has been significantly improved with a new interface.
> - **Performance:** Performance has been enhanced through optimized algorithms.
> - **Security:** Security has been strengthened with end-to-end encryption.

**After:**
> The update improves the interface, speeds up load times through optimized algorithms, and adds end-to-end encryption.


### 16. Title Case in Headings

**Problem:** AI chatbots capitalize all main words in headings.

**Before:**
> ## Strategic Negotiations And Global Partnerships

**After:**
> ## Strategic negotiations and global partnerships


### 17. Emojis

**Problem:** AI chatbots often decorate headings or bullet points with emojis.

**Before:**
> 🚀 **Launch Phase:** The product launches in Q3
> 💡 **Key Insight:** Users prefer simplicity
> ✅ **Next Steps:** Schedule follow-up meeting

**After:**
> The product launches in Q3. User research showed a preference for simplicity. Next step: schedule a follow-up meeting.


### 18. Curly Quotation Marks

**Problem:** ChatGPT uses curly quotes (“...”) instead of straight quotes ("...").

**Before:**
> He said “the project is on track” but others disagreed.

**After:**
> He said "the project is on track" but others disagreed.


## COMMUNICATION PATTERNS

### 19. Collaborative Communication Artifacts

**Words to watch:** I hope this helps, Of course!, Certainly!, You're absolutely right!, Would you like..., let me know, here is a...

**Problem:** Text meant as chatbot correspondence gets pasted as content.

**Before:**
> Here is an overview of the French Revolution. I hope this helps! Let me know if you'd like me to expand on any section.

**After:**
> The French Revolution began in 1789 when financial crisis and food shortages led to widespread unrest.


### 20. Knowledge-Cutoff Disclaimers

**Words to watch:** as of [date], Up to my last training update, While specific details are limited/scarce..., based on available information...

**Problem:** AI disclaimers about incomplete information get left in text.

**Before:**
> While specific details about the company's founding are not extensively documented in readily available sources, it appears to have been established sometime in the 1990s.

**After:**
> The company was founded in 1994, according to its registration documents.


### 21. Sycophantic/Servile Tone

**Problem:** Overly positive, people-pleasing language.

**Before:**
> Great question! You're absolutely right that this is a complex topic. That's an excellent point about the economic factors.

**After:**
> The economic factors you mentioned are relevant here.


## FILLER AND HEDGING

### 22. Filler Phrases

**Before → After:**
- "In order to achieve this goal" → "To achieve this"
- "Due to the fact that it was raining" → "Because it was raining"
- "At this point in time" → "Now"
- "In the event that you need help" → "If you need help"
- "The system has the ability to process" → "The system can process"
- "It is important to note that the data shows" → "The data shows"


### 23. Excessive Hedging

**Problem:** Over-qualifying statements.

**Before:**
> It could potentially possibly be argued that the policy might have some effect on outcomes.

**After:**
> The policy may affect outcomes.


### 24. Generic Positive Conclusions

**Problem:** Vague upbeat endings.

**Before:**
> The future looks bright for the company. Exciting times lie ahead as they continue their journey toward excellence. This represents a major step in the right direction.

**After:**
> The company plans to open two more locations next year.


### 25. Hyphenated Word Pair Overuse

**Words to watch:** third-party, cross-functional, client-facing, data-driven, decision-making, well-known, high-quality, real-time, long-term, end-to-end

**Problem:** AI hyphenates common word pairs with perfect consistency. Humans rarely hyphenate these uniformly, and when they do, it's inconsistent. Less common or technical compound modifiers are fine to hyphenate.

**Before:**
> The cross-functional team delivered a high-quality, data-driven report on our client-facing tools. Their decision-making process was well-known for being thorough and detail-oriented.

**After:**
> The cross functional team delivered a high quality, data driven report on our client facing tools. Their decision making process was known for being thorough and detail oriented.

---

## Process

1. Read the input text carefully
2. Identify all instances of the patterns above
3. Rewrite each problematic section
4. Ensure the revised text:
   - Sounds natural when read aloud
   - Varies sentence structure naturally
   - Uses specific details over vague claims
   - Maintains appropriate tone for context
   - Uses simple constructions (is/are/has) where appropriate
5. Present a draft humanized version
6. Prompt: "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?"
7. Answer briefly with the remaining tells (if any)
8. Prompt: "Now make it not obviously AI generated."
9. Present the final version (revised after the audit)

## Output Format

Provide:
1. Draft rewrite
2. "What makes the below so obviously AI generated?" (brief bullets)
3. Final rewrite
4. A brief summary of changes made (optional, if helpful)


## Full Example

**Before (AI-sounding):**
> Great question! Here is an essay on this topic. I hope this helps!
>
> AI-assisted coding serves as an enduring testament to the transformative potential of large language models, marking a pivotal moment in the evolution of software development. In today's rapidly evolving technological landscape, these groundbreaking tools—nestled at the intersection of research and practice—are reshaping how engineers ideate, iterate, and deliver, underscoring their vital role in modern workflows.
>
> At its core, the value proposition is clear: streamlining processes, enhancing collaboration, and fostering alignment. It's not just about autocomplete; it's about unlocking creativity at scale, ensuring that organizations can remain agile while delivering seamless, intuitive, and powerful experiences to users. The tool serves as a catalyst. The assistant functions as a partner. The system stands as a foundation for innovation.
>
> Industry observers have noted that adoption has accelerated from hobbyist experiments to enterprise-wide rollouts, from solo developers to cross-functional teams. The technology has been featured in The New York Times, Wired, and The Verge. Additionally, the ability to generate documentation, tests, and refactors showcases how AI can contribute to better outcomes, highlighting the intricate interplay between automation and human judgment.
>
> - 💡 **Speed:** Code generation is significantly faster, reducing friction and empowering developers.
> - 🚀 **Quality:** Output quality has been enhanced through improved training, contributing to higher standards.
> - ✅ **Adoption:** Usage continues to grow, reflecting broader industry trends.
>
> While specific details are limited based on available information, it could potentially be argued that these tools might have some positive effect. Despite challenges typical of emerging technologies—including hallucinations, bias, and accountability—the ecosystem continues to thrive. In order to fully realize this potential, teams must align with best practices.
>
> In conclusion, the future looks bright. Exciting times lie ahead as we continue this journey toward excellence. Let me know if you’d like me to expand on any section!

**Draft rewrite:**
> AI coding assistants speed up some tasks. In a 2024 study by Google, developers using Codex completed simple functions 55% faster than a control group, but showed no improvement on debugging or architectural decisions.
>
> The tools are good at boilerplate: config files, test scaffolding, repetitive refactors. They are bad at knowing when they are wrong. I have mass-accepted suggestions that compiled, passed lint, and still did the wrong thing because I stopped paying attention.
>

Applied Performance · Briefing Note · September 2026

Thoracic outlet syndrome: what the research shows

A summary of the peer reviewed evidence on TOS in throwing athletes, and what we can realistically change. Drawn from 109 verified sources. The full brief with citations is available on request.

01 What we can and can't measure

  • There is no peer number to compare ourselves against. The NCAA's injury surveillance system sorts injuries by body part and by type: strains, sprains, contusions. It has no category for the thoracic outlet, and none for nerve or vascular problems anywhere in the body. So no school can say how its TOS rate stacks up against anyone else's. Nobody collects that number.
  • The condition is rare enough that a roster our size can't generate a meaningful rate. It shows up in roughly 2 to 3 people per 100,000 per year. At that rate, a squad our size would expect a small fraction of one case in a season. Two cases sits inside normal variation, not outside it.
  • Counts follow attention. There is no definitive test for the common form of TOS. The physical test used most often in a training room comes back positive in about half of people who don't have the condition. Programs that start looking for it find more of it than programs that don't.
15,609NCAA D-I athletes reviewed, 21 sports, 7 years
0.48%Overall TOS rate in that group
1.3%Softball. Tennis was 2.6%
95.4%Returned to unrestricted competition

02 What the evidence points to

  • The throwing motion is the exposure. Imaging of college pitchers shows that the cocked position roughly doubles the stiffness of the neck muscles forming the compression space. Windmill pitching is not gentler than overhand. It pulls on the shoulder at 80 to 94 percent of body weight, and at the same ball speed the biceps works about twice as hard as it does in an overhand throw.
  • A fair number of people are simply built with less room in there. Extra or elongated bone at the base of the neck turns up in 1 to 3 percent of the population, and fibrous bands were found in a third of cadaver specimens from people who never had a symptom in their lives. Most of these never cause trouble. They cause trouble when they get loaded.
  • Weight training is not supported as a cause. No controlled study links it to TOS. Muscle biopsies taken from TOS patients show the opposite of a training adaptation: the affected muscle is wasted and scarred, not built up.
  • Workload is the best supported thing on this list that we can actually change. A study of College World Series teams found softball pitchers throw about three times the innings of baseball pitchers, off a staff a third the size. Nearly 44 percent topped 100 innings in a season. The baseball figure was 7 percent. Neither sport has an NCAA pitch count limit or a required rest rule.

03 The cheapest fix available to us

About half of what our pitchers actually throw never gets counted. A 2025 study tracked 8,248 pitches across 89 varsity outings. Counting game pitches alone, a quarter of those outings went past recommended volume. Counting bullpen and warmup too, it was more than half. Nothing else on this page costs less to fix.

04 What we propose to do

ActionOwnerWhy
Count every pitch, bullpen and warmup includedPitching staff + ATHalf of real volume goes uncounted now
Track and spread innings across the staffCoaching staffNo rule limits this. Staff depth is the only lever
Build rest into tournament and doubleheader plansCoaching staffFatigue and pain stack up across consecutive days
Add neck mobility to the preseason screenAT + PerformanceRestricted neck rotation predicted throwing injury in college pitchers
Prioritize hip and trunk capacity in trainingPerformanceLower body screening predicts about half the shoulder load in softball pitchers
Continue shoulder and postural capacity workPerformanceStandard practice, low risk, good for the shoulder generally
Agree on diagnostic criteria before counting casesSports MedicineTakes the guesswork out of any future comparison
Capture prior throwing history at intakeRecruiting + Sports MedTravel ball volume and old rib or collarbone injuries both matter

05 On outcomes

  • In the NCAA review above, 96 percent of cases were handled without surgery and 95.4 percent of those athletes went back to full competition.
  • Among professional baseball pitchers who did need surgery, 74 to 81 percent returned to play within 9 to 11 months. The best controlled study, which used Major League Baseball's own injury database and compared each pitcher against a healthy match, found performance afterward dropped no faster than it does for healthy pitchers getting older.
Prepared by Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics. Summarized from a review of 109 peer reviewed sources, each checked against PubMed. The detailed brief, with full citations, confidence ratings and study limitations, is available on request.

**The concession is gone.** That table row now reads: *Continue shoulder and postural capacity work / Performance / Standard practice, low risk, good for the shoulder generally.* States the value without volunteering the limitation.

**What the humanizer pass caught.** The biggest tell was structural, not vocabulary: every bullet in the original opened with a bolded mini-headline followed by explanation. That inline-header list pattern is one of the most reliable AI signatures there is, and I'd used it in all three prose sections. Those are now actual sentences. Also stripped:

- **Em dashes.** I'd used about fifteen. Now commas and periods.
- **Title case in the headline** — "What the Research Actually Shows" became "what the research shows." The word *actually* was doing defensive work and went with it.

# Baylor Doc Style

The house look for Baylor Athletics Word documents, defined once.

`baylor_docstyle.py` is a single module. Document builders import it instead of
setting their own fonts, colours and spacing, so every document comes out
looking like the same department wrote it.

## Where the style comes from

Every measurement in the module was read out of:

```
~/DEV/SoftwareTech_Mgmt_Framework/deliverables/
    Software_and_Technology_Management_Framework_DRAFT.docx
```

Eric chose that document as the house look on 2026-08-30. Nothing in the module
is invented. **If the module and that document ever disagree, the document
wins** — re-measure it rather than adjusting to taste.

## Use

```python
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "/Users/kristinarash/DEV/Baylor_Doc_Style")
from baylor_docstyle import BaylorDoc

d = BaylorDoc("Athletics Technology Inventory",
              deck="What the department runs, and who runs it.",
              status="Interim — collection open to 29 September 2026")

d.meta([["Status", "Interim"], ["Prepared by", "Applied Performance"]])
d.callout("Two deadlines, not one", "29 August was our own deadline...")
d.section("Coverage — who has responded")     # numbered automatically
d.subhead("Still outstanding")
d.para("Five units have yet to respond.")
d.bullets(["**Softball** — Trackman, about to be installed."])
d.numbered(["**Follow up with five units.** Golf (M), Tennis (M)..."])
d.quote("Everything we have has gone through ITS approval.")
d.table(["Unit", "Responses"], [["Football", 3]], numeric_cols=(1,))
d.note("A caveat, in small italic grey.")
d.small("A caption under a table.")
d.save("out.docx")
```

`**double asterisks**` mark inline bold in every text argument.

Section numbers are handed out in order, so inserting a section never means
renumbering the ones after it.

## What the style is

| Element | Setting |
|---|---|
| Page | Letter, margins 0.80in top/bottom, 0.90in left/right |
| Body | Calibri 10.5pt, 6pt after, line spacing 1.079 |
| Eyebrow | 9pt bold, gold `#B8860B` |
| Title | 19pt bold, Baylor green `#154734` |
| Deck | 11pt italic, grey `#595959` |
| Meta block | borderless label/value, 9pt |
| Callout | cream `#FFF4DA` box, 9.5pt, green heading |
| Section | numbered, 13pt bold green, green rule under |
| Subhead | 11.5pt bold green |
| Table | green header band, white header text, 9.5pt body |
| Footer | centred 7.5pt grey — title, status, "Baylor Athletics", page number |
| Header | none |

## Three things not to change

**Calibri, everywhere.** The exemplar sets no font on any run, so every size
inherits Normal. Calibri ships with Office, which is why the document survives
being emailed. Baylor's licensed faces are in `~/DEV/Baylor_Fonts`, but a
document set in them falls back to something else on any machine that lacks
them.

**No running header.** The exemplar has an empty header and carries the
document's status in the meta block and the footer instead. That still puts the
status on every page, which is the constraint that matters.

**No hand-placed page breaks.** Headings carry keep-with-next, so Word breaks
the document itself. A hand-placed break is correct only until the content above
it changes length, and then it leaves a half-empty page.

## Exporting to PDF

Open Microsoft Word first, then export the PDF from the `.docx` so the two files
match. Word blocks on a dialog the caller cannot see when the app is not already
running. See `word_pdf()` in
`~/DEV/Tech_Inventory_Analysis/scripts/build_docx.py` for the working call.

## Who uses it

- `~/DEV/Tech_Inventory_Analysis/scripts/build_docx.py` — findings report
- `~/DEV/Tech_Inventory_Analysis/scripts/build_exec_summary.py` — one-page summary

def __init__(self, title, deck=None, status=None,
                 eyebrow=EYEBROW_DEFAULT, footer_suffix="Baylor Athletics",
                 page_numbers=True):
        self.doc = Document()
        self.title = title
        self.status = status
        self._section_no = 0
        self._base_style()
        self._page_setup()
        self._footer(footer_suffix, page_numbers)
        self._title_block(title, deck, eyebrow)

    # -- setup -------------------------------------------------------------
    def meta(self, rows, label_width=1.5):
        """The status block under the title. Borderless: it is a label/value
        list that happens to be laid out in a table, not a data table."""
        t = self.doc.add_table(rows=0, cols=2)
        t.style = "Normal Table"
        t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.LEFT
        for label, value in rows:
            cells = t.add_row().cells
            p = cells[0].paragraphs[0]
            p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(2)
            add_runs(p, label, size=9, bold=True)
            p = cells[1].paragraphs[0]
            p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(2)
    def table(self, headers, rows, widths=None, numeric_cols=(),
              caption=None, compact=False):
        """A data table: green header band, white header text, thin grid."""
        t = self.doc.add_table(rows=1, cols=len(headers))
        t.style = "Table Grid"
        t.alignment = WD_TABLE_ALIGNMENT.LEFT
        pad = 0 if compact else 2
        for i, htext in enumerate(headers):
            cell = t.rows[0].cells[i]
            shade(cell, "154734")
            p = cell.paragraphs[0]
            p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(pad)
            if i in numeric_cols:
                p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.RIGHT
            add_runs(p, htext, size=9.5, bold=True, color=WHITE)
        for row in rows:
            cells = t.add_row().cells
            for i, val in enumerate(row):
                p = cells[i].paragraphs[0]
                p.paragraph_format.space_after = Pt(pad)
                if i in numeric_cols:
                    p.alignment = WD_ALIGN_PARAGRAPH.RIGHT
                add_runs(p, val, size=9.5)
        if widths:
            for row in t.rows:
                for i, w in enumerate(widths):
                    row.cells[i].width = Inches(w)
        if not compact:
            self._p(space_after=2)
        if caption:
            self.small(caption)
        return t

    def page_break(self):
        self.doc.add_page_break()

    def spacer(self, points=4):
        self._p(space_after=points)

# Articulation & Clear Communication Skill

Help users articulate complex ideas clearly using proven communication frameworks from Dan Koe's "How to Articulate Yourself Intelligently."

## Core Philosophy

Articulation is learnable through:
1. Repetition and refinement of core ideas
2. Clear frameworks that structure thinking  
3. Practice with specific techniques

Key insight: Intelligibility comes from depth in narrow areas, not breadth. The best communicators distill powerful ideas so simply that anyone can understand them.

## When to Use This Skill

Use this skill when the user needs to:
- Explain technical concepts to non-technical audiences
- Structure presentations, talks, or written content
- Simplify complex ideas without losing sophistication
- Create clear documentation or communication
- Translate jargon into accessible language
- Improve clarity in professional communication

## Three Communication Frameworks

### 1. Micro Story (Beginner)
**Best for:** Short explanations, social posts, emails, quick pitches

**Structure:** Problem → Amplify → Solution
- State a relatable problem the audience experiences
- Show negative outcomes if unsolved (amplify urgency)
- Present the solution

**Why it works:** Humans are hardwired for narrative. This taps into story psychology.

### 2. Pyramid Principle (Intermediate)  
**Best for:** Presentations, meetings, persuasive writing, detailed explanations

**Structure:** Answer First → Key Arguments → Supporting Evidence
- Lead with your main conclusion/recommendation
- Support with 3-5 key arguments
- Provide concrete evidence (data, examples, stories)

**Why it works:** Answer-first keeps audiences engaged because they understand where you're going. Creates natural "clippable moments."

### 3. Cross-Domain Synthesis (Advanced)
**Best for:** Long-form content, complex ideas, standing out from competitors

**Structure:** Problem & Amplify → Unexpected Connections → Unique Solution
- Start with Micro Story structure
- Draw concepts from unexpected domains (physics, psychology, biology)
- Provide your unique process/solution

**Why it works:** Creates memorable content by combining unexpected domains. Harder to copy.

## Content Building Blocks ("Idea Legos")

When expanding or stuck, use these elements:
1. **Pain point** - Start with a struggle ("Most people don't realize...")
2. **Example** - Ground abstractions in concrete reality
3. **Personal story** - Share relevant experience
4. **Statistic** - Add authority and proof
5. **Metaphor** - Explain complex ideas simply ("like you would to a child")
6. **Quote** - Leverage existing great ideas
7. **Reframe** - Offer different perspective ("Another way to think about this...")
8. **Questions** - Guide thinking with What/How/Why

## Workflow

When a user requests help with articulation:

1. **Assess the context**
   - What's the goal? (explain concept, structure presentation, simplify language)
   - Who's the audience? (technical level, familiarity with topic)
   - What's the format? (email, presentation, documentation, conversation)

2. **Select the appropriate framework**
   - Quick/short → Micro Story
   - Presentation/persuasive → Pyramid Principle
   - Complex/long-form → Cross-Domain Synthesis

3. **Apply the framework**
   - Restructure their content using the chosen framework
   - Identify which "legos" would strengthen the explanation
   - Suggest metaphors or reframes for technical concepts

4. **Refine for clarity**
   - Flag jargon or overly complex language
   - Suggest simpler alternatives without losing sophistication
   - Ensure the explanation flows naturally

5. **Provide the structured output**
   - Show the restructured content
   - Explain why you chose this framework
   - Suggest additional legos if they want to expand

## Key Principles

- **Depth beats breadth** - Master a few core ideas deeply
- **Simplicity is sophisticated** - Complex vocabulary often masks unclear thinking
- **Stories engage before logic** - Start with relatable narrative
- **Repetition refines** - Best ideas deserve to be repeated and refined
- **Unexpected connections are memorable** - Cross-domain thinking stands out

## Quick Framework Selection

| Situation | Framework | Why |
|-----------|-----------|-----|
| Quick explanation, social post | Micro Story | Short, punchy, engaging |
| Podcast, meeting, persuasive talk | Pyramid Principle | Answer-first keeps engagement |
| Long article, complex idea | Cross-Domain Synthesis | Depth, novelty, unique perspective |

## Example Phrases

Recognize these requests as triggers for this skill:
- "Can you help me articulate [idea]?"
- "How would you structure this explanation?"
- "Make this less technical"
- "Is this clear or too corporate?"
- "Help me explain this to non-experts"
- "What's a good metaphor for [concept]?"
- "How do I simplify this without dumbing it down?"

## Response Style

- Write in plain, conversational language
- Avoid corporate jargon and formal AI-sounding phrasing
- Be direct and authentic
- Call out when original content is unclear or too complex
- Suggest specific improvements with examples
- Explain your reasoning for framework choices

"""Coach-facing one-page briefing note on thoracic outlet syndrome.

House look comes from ~/DEV/Baylor_Doc_Style. Structure follows the Pyramid
Principle: the answer first, then the arguments, then the evidence.
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Baylor_Doc_Style")
from baylor_docstyle import BaylorDoc  # noqa: E402

OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "deliverables"
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)


def build():
    d = BaylorDoc(
        "Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Throwing Athletes",
        deck="What the research shows, and what we can change.",
        status="Briefing note — September 2026",
    )

    d.meta([
        ["Prepared by", "Eric Rash, Applied Performance"],
        ["Date", "18 September 2026"],
        ["Evidence base", "109 peer reviewed sources, each checked against PubMed"],
        ["Full brief", "Available on request"],
    ])

    d.callout(
        "The short version",
        "There is no national number that lets any school compare its thoracic "
        "outlet rate to another's, because the condition is not tracked "
        "separately. It is rare enough that a roster our size cannot produce a "
        "meaningful rate either way. What the research does support is that the "
        "throwing motion itself is the exposure, and that our pitchers carry "
        "about three times the innings of a baseball staff a third our size. "
        "The cheapest thing we can fix is that roughly half of what they throw "
        "never gets counted.",
    )

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    d.section("What the numbers can and cannot tell us")

    d.bullets([
        "**There is no peer number to compare against.** The NCAA's injury "
        "surveillance system sorts injuries by body part and by type: strains, "
        "sprains, contusions. It has no category for the thoracic outlet, and "
        "none for nerve or vascular problems anywhere in the body. No school "
        "can say how its rate compares to anyone else's. Nobody collects that "
        "number.",

        "**The condition is too rare for roster-level comparison.** It appears "
        "in roughly 2 to 3 people per 100,000 per year. At that rate a squad "
        "our size would expect a small fraction of one case in a season. Two "
        "cases sits inside normal variation, not outside it.",

        "**Counts follow attention.** There is no definitive test for the "
        "common form. The physical test used most often in a training room "
        "comes back positive in about half of people who do not have the "
        "condition. Programs that start looking for it find more of it.",
    ])

    d.table(
        ["Measure", "Finding"],
        [
            ["Athletes reviewed", "15,609 NCAA Division I, 21 sports, seven years"],
            ["Overall rate in that group", "0.48 percent"],
            ["Softball", "1.3 percent"],
            ["Tennis", "2.6 percent"],
            ["Managed without surgery", "96 percent"],
            ["Returned to unrestricted competition", "95.4 percent"],
        ],
        widths=(2.6, 4.1),
        caption="Talutis and colleagues, Journal of Vascular Surgery, 2025. "
                "The only published collegiate figure, and it came from a chart "
                "review rather than any surveillance system.",
    )

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    d.section("What the research says causes it")

    d.bullets([
        "**The throwing motion is the exposure.** Imaging of college pitchers "
        "shows the cocked position roughly doubles the stiffness of the neck "
        "muscles that form the compression space. Windmill pitching is not "
        "gentler than overhand. It pulls on the shoulder at 80 to 94 percent of "
        "body weight, and at the same ball speed the biceps works about twice "
        "as hard as it does in an overhand throw.",

        "**Some athletes are simply built with less room.** Extra or elongated "
        "bone at the base of the neck turns up in 1 to 3 percent of people, and "
        "fibrous bands were found in a third of cadaver specimens from people "
        "who never had a symptom. Most never cause trouble. They cause trouble "
        "when they get loaded.",

        "**Weight training is not supported as a cause.** No controlled study "
        "links it to this condition. Muscle samples taken from patients show "
        "the opposite of a training adaptation: the affected muscle is wasted "
        "and scarred, not built up.",

        "**Workload is the best supported thing we can actually change.** A "
        "study of College World Series teams found softball pitchers throw "
        "about three times the innings of baseball pitchers, off a staff a "
        "third the size. Nearly 44 percent topped 100 innings in a season "
        "against 7 percent in baseball. Neither sport has an NCAA pitch count "
        "limit or a required rest rule.",
    ])

    d.callout(
        "The cheapest fix available to us",
        "A 2025 study tracked 8,248 pitches across 89 varsity outings. "
        "Counting game pitches alone, a quarter of those outings went past "
        "recommended volume. Counting bullpen and warmup as well, it was more "
        "than half. Nothing else on this page costs less to fix.",
    )

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    d.section("What we propose to do")

    d.table(
        ["Action", "Owner", "Why"],
        [
            ["Count every pitch, bullpen and warmup included",
             "Pitching staff, AT",
             "Half of real volume goes uncounted now"],
            ["Track and spread innings across the staff",
             "Coaching staff",
             "No rule limits this. Staff depth is the only lever"],
            ["Build rest into tournament and doubleheader plans",
             "Coaching staff",
             "Fatigue and pain stack up across consecutive days"],
            ["Add neck mobility to the preseason screen",
             "AT, Performance",
             "Restricted neck rotation predicted throwing injury in college pitchers"],
            ["Prioritize hip and trunk capacity in training",
             "Performance",
             "Lower body screening predicts about half the shoulder load"],
            ["Continue shoulder and postural capacity work",
             "Performance",
             "Standard practice, low risk, good for the shoulder generally"],
            ["Agree on diagnostic criteria before counting cases",
             "Sports Medicine",
             "Takes the guesswork out of any future comparison"],
            ["Capture prior throwing history at intake",
             "Recruiting, Sports Medicine",
             "Travel ball volume and old rib or collarbone injuries both matter"],
        ],
        widths=(2.5, 1.5, 2.7),
    )

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    d.section("On outcomes")

    d.bullets([
        "In the collegiate review above, 96 percent of cases were handled "
        "without surgery and 95.4 percent of those athletes returned to full "
        "competition.",

        "Among professional baseball pitchers who did need surgery, 74 to 81 "
        "percent returned to play within 9 to 11 months. The best controlled "
        "study used Major League Baseball's own injury database and compared "
        "each pitcher against a healthy match. Performance afterward dropped no "
        "faster than it does for healthy pitchers getting older.",
    ])

    d.note(
        "Figures in this note are drawn from the full evidence review, where "
        "every source carries its citation and a confidence rating. Where the "
        "research is thin or contested, the full brief says so."
    )

    path = OUT / "TOS_BRIEFING_NOTE_ER_2026-09-18.docx"
    d.save(str(path))
    return path


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(build())

            ["Tennis", "2.6 percent"],
            ["Managed without surgery", "96 percent"],
            ["Returned to unrestricted competition", "95.4 percent"],
        ],
        widths=(2.6, 4.1),
        caption="Talutis and colleagues, Journal of Vascular Surgery, 2025. The "
                "only published collegiate figure, and it came from a chart "
                "review rather than from any surveillance system.",
    )

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    d.section("What the research says causes it")

    d.bullets([
        "**The throwing motion is the exposure.** Imaging of college pitchers "
        "shows the cocked position roughly doubles the stiffness of the neck "
        "muscles that form the compression space. Windmill pitching is not "
        "gentler than overhand. It pulls on the shoulder at 80 to 94 percent of "
        "body weight, and at the same ball speed the biceps works about twice "
        "as hard as it does in an overhand throw.",

        "**Some athletes are simply built with less room.** Extra or elongated "
        "bone at the base of the neck turns up in 1 to 3 percent of people, and "
        "fibrous bands were found in a third of cadaver specimens from people "
        "who never had a symptom. Most never cause trouble. They cause trouble "
        "when they get loaded.",

        "**Weight training is not supported as a cause.** No controlled study "
        "links it to this condition. Muscle samples taken from patients show "
        "the opposite of a training adaptation: the affected muscle is wasted "
        "and scarred, not built up.",

        "**Workload is the best supported thing we can actually change.** A "
        "study of College World Series teams found softball pitchers throw "
        "about three times the innings of baseball pitchers, off a staff a "
        "third the size. Nearly 44 percent topped 100 innings in a season "
        "against 7 percent in baseball. Neither sport has an NCAA pitch count "
        "limit or a required rest rule.",
    ])

    d.callout(
        "The cheapest fix available to us",
        "A 2025 study tracked 8,248 pitches across 89 varsity outings. Counting "
        "game pitches alone, a quarter of those outings went past recommended "
        "volume. Counting bullpen and warmup as well, it was more than half. "
        "Nothing else on this page costs less to fix.",
    )

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    d.section("What we propose to do")

    d.table(
        ["Action", "Owner", "Why"],
        [
            ["Count every pitch, bullpen and warmup included",
             "Pitching staff, AT",
             "Half of real volume goes uncounted now"],
            ["Track and spread innings across the staff",
             "Coaching staff",
             "No rule limits this. Staff depth is the only lever"],
            ["Build rest into tournament and doubleheader plans",
             "Coaching staff",
             "Fatigue and pain stack up across consecutive days"],
            ["Add neck mobility to the preseason screen",
             "AT, Performance",
             "Restricted neck rotation predicted throwing injury in college pitchers"],
            ["Prioritize hip and trunk capacity in training",
             "Performance",
             "Lower body screening predicts about half the shoulder load"],
            ["Continue shoulder and postural capacity work",
             "Performance",
             "Standard practice, low risk, good for the shoulder generally"],
            ["Agree on diagnostic criteria before counting cases",
             "Sports Medicine",
             "Takes the guesswork out of any future comparison"],
            ["Capture prior throwing history at intake",
             "Recruiting, Sports Medicine",
             "Travel ball volume and old rib or collarbone injuries both matter"],
        ],
        widths=(2.5, 1.5, 2.7),
    )

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------
    d.section("On outcomes")

    d.bullets([
        "In the collegiate review above, 96 percent of cases were handled "
        "without surgery and 95.4 percent of those athletes returned to full "
        "competition.",

        "Among professional baseball pitchers who did need surgery, 74 to 81 "
        "percent returned to play within 9 to 11 months. The best controlled "
        "study used Major League Baseball's own injury database and compared "
        "each pitcher against a healthy match. Performance afterward dropped no "
        "faster than it does for healthy pitchers getting older.",
    ])

    d.note(
        "Figures here are drawn from the full evidence review, where every "
        "source carries its citation and a confidence rating. Where the research "
        "is thin or contested, the full brief says so."
    )

    path = OUT / "TOS_BRIEFING_NOTE_ER_2026-09-18.docx"
    d.save(str(path))
    return path


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(build())
