Reasonable means a coherent mechanism nobody has tested directly. No evidence
means the claim is common in practice and absent from the literature.
"""
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, r"C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Baylor_Doc_Style")
from baylor_docstyle import BaylorDoc  # noqa: E402

OUT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "deliverables"
OUT.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)


def build():
    d = BaylorDoc(
        "Thoracic Outlet Syndrome in Overhead Throwing Athletes",
        deck="An evidence review for softball performance and sports medicine staff.",
        status="Evidence review — September 2026",
    )

    d.meta([
        ["Prepared by", "Eric Rash, Applied Performance"],
        ["Date", "18 September 2026"],
        ["Sources", "109 peer reviewed, each verified against PubMed or Europe PMC"],
        ["Audience", "Softball performance staff, sports medicine, coaching staff"],
    ])

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("In brief")

    d.para(
        "This review was prepared because our softball programme believes it "
        "has a higher rate of thoracic outlet syndrome than peer institutions. "
        "The short answer is that the comparison cannot be made, and that the "
        "exposure most worth managing is throwing volume rather than anything "
        "happening in the weight room."
    )

    d.numbered([
        "**The peer comparison is not possible.** Thoracic outlet syndrome is "
        "not separately coded in the NCAA Injury Surveillance Program. No "
        "national softball rate exists to compare against.",

        "**No programme can estimate its own rate.** Neurogenic thoracic outlet "
        "syndrome occurs in roughly 2 to 3 people per 100,000 per year. On a "
        "35-athlete roster the expected count is about 0.0014 cases a season. "
        "Two cases is a chance cluster, not a signal.",

        "**Diagnosis drives counts as much as biology does.** There is no gold "
        "standard test. The provocative test used most often in an athletic "
        "training room is positive in 47 to 62 percent of people who do not "
        "have the condition.",

        "**The throwing motion is the exposure, and the muscle biology does not "
        "implicate lifting.** The cocked position roughly doubles scalene "
        "stiffness. Scalene muscle taken from patients at surgery shows type II "
        "fibre atrophy and fibrosis, which is the opposite of a resistance "
        "training signature.",

        "**The instruction not to lift before throwing has no research behind "
        "it.** Three structured literature searches found no baseball study on "
        "the question and no paper at all linking training timing to this "
        "condition. The adjacent evidence leans against the rule.",

        "**The endurance hypothesis is reasonable but unproven.** The strongest "
        "supporting study found a 45 percent rotator endurance deficit in "
        "patients, but in 40-year-old non-athletes, with the direction of cause "
        "unresolved.",

        "**Workload is the dominant modifiable exposure, and it is not a "
        "strength and conditioning lever.** Collegiate softball pitchers throw "
        "2.9 times the innings of baseball pitchers off a staff a third the "
        "size, under no pitch count limit, and roughly half of true pitch "
        "volume is bullpen and warmup that nobody counts.",
    ])

    d.note(
        "Confidence wording in this document is deliberate. Established means "
        "measured and replicated. Reasonable means a coherent mechanism that "
        "nobody has tested directly. No evidence means the claim is common in "
        "practice and absent from the literature. A claim presented as stronger "
        "than it is will not survive a second opinion, and it will cost the "
        "person making it credibility on the claims that are solid."
    )

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("How common it is, and why we cannot compare")

    d.subhead("Three conditions, not one")

    d.para(
        "Thoracic outlet syndrome is compression of the brachial plexus, the "
        "subclavian artery, or the subclavian vein in one of three anatomical "
        "spaces. The three subtypes behave differently and should not be "
        "discussed as a single entity."
    )

    d.table(
        ["Subtype", "General population", "Athletes"],
        [
            ["Neurogenic", "82 to 95 percent", "66 to 74 percent"],
            ["Venous, also called effort thrombosis", "3 to 16 percent", "26 to 34 percent"],
            ["Arterial", "about 1 to 2 percent", "about 2 percent"],
        ],
        widths=(3.1, 1.8, 1.8),
        caption="Illig 2021; Chandra 2014; Chauhan 2024; Gutman 2022. Every "
                "athlete figure is a treated-case proportion, not an incidence. "
                "It describes the mix among athletes who reached a surgeon.",
    )

    d.para(
        "**Established.** Venous thoracic outlet syndrome is roughly five to ten "
        "times over-represented in athletes. The mechanism is chronic repetitive "
        "compression of the subclavian vein in the costoclavicular space "
        "(Vemuri 2016)."
    )

    d.subhead("A statistic to stop repeating")

    d.para(
        "The most commonly cited incidence figure is 3 to 80 per 1,000. It does "
        "not survive tracing. StatPearls cites Jones 2019, which says several "
        "articles report that range and cites Citisli 2015 in the Journal of "
        "Pain Relief. That article is not indexed in PubMed or MEDLINE at all. "
        "A 27-fold-wide range is itself the tell that nobody measured anything."
    )

    d.quote(
        "The incidence of neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome is completely "
        "unknown, and has been wildly overestimated in the past."
    )

    d.small("Illig and Rodriguez-Zoppi, Thoracic Surgery Clinics, 2021.")

    d.para(
        "Their prospective referral database gives 2 to 3 cases per 100,000 per "
        "year for the neurogenic form and 0.5 to 1 for the venous form. The gap "
        "between the folklore figure and the measured one is a factor of 100 to "
        "2,700."
    )

    d.subhead("Why roster-level comparison is meaningless")

    d.para(
        "At roughly 4 per 100,000 per year for all subtypes combined, a "
        "35-athlete roster observed for one season has an expected count of "
        "about 0.0014 cases."
    )

    d.bullets([
        "**Zero cases tells you nothing.** By the rule of three, 35 athlete "
        "years with no events puts the 95 percent upper bound at about 8.6 "
        "percent per athlete season, four orders of magnitude above the true "
        "rate. A programme with no cases has no evidence it is below average.",

        "**One case looks alarming and means almost nothing.** The exact "
        "Poisson 95 percent interval on a single observed event runs from 0.03 "
        "to 5.6 events.",

        "**Two cases is a plausible chance cluster.** The interval on two events "
        "runs from 0.24 to 7.2. A peer with none and a peer with three are not "
        "statistically distinguishable at these counts.",

        "**Ascertainment dominates.** Any difference between programmes is far "
        "more likely to measure the referral pathway, meaning whether a school "
        "has a relationship with a thoracic outlet centre, than the underlying "
        "biology.",
    ])

    d.subhead("The surveillance system does not track it")

    d.para(
        "**Established.** The NCAA Injury Surveillance Program releases body "
        "part affected, specific injury, and type of injury. The body part list "
        "is coarse and anatomical: head and face, neck, shoulder, arm or elbow, "
        "hand or wrist, trunk, hip and groin, thigh, knee, lower leg, ankle, "
        "foot, other. There is no thoracic outlet site and no vascular or "
        "peripheral nerve category. The diagnosis taxonomy is injury-type based, "
        "not disease based. The condition appears nowhere in the two most recent "
        "five-year NCAA baseball and softball epidemiology reports."
    )

    d.note(
        "Honest limit: the Datalys documentation page returned an error, so no "
        "internal code string can be ruled out. What is demonstrable is that the "
        "condition is not reported in any published NCAA output and is not in "
        "the released taxonomies. A programme wanting certainty should submit a "
        "data request to the Datalys Center."
    )

    d.para(
        "The one usable collegiate denominator came from a chart review rather "
        "than surveillance: 15,609 NCAA Division I athletes across 21 sports "
        "and seven years, yielding 76 cases, an overall rate of 0.48 percent "
        "(Talutis 2025)."
    )

    d.table(
        ["Sport", "Prevalence"],
        [
            ["Tennis", "2.6 percent"],
            ["Softball", "1.3 percent"],
            ["Rowing", "1.3 percent"],
            ["All sports", "0.48 percent"],
        ],
        widths=(3.4, 3.3),
        numeric_cols=(1,),
        caption="Softball sits above the all-sport baseline and below tennis. "
                "In the same series 96 percent were managed without surgery and "
                "95.4 percent returned to unrestricted competition.",
    )

    d.subhead("Outcomes, for reassurance")

    d.table(
        ["Study", "Group", "Return to play", "Performance finding"],
        [
            ["Thompson 2017", "13 MLB pitchers", "77 percent at 10.8 months",
             "75 percent of 72 pitch-tracking metrics unchanged"],
            ["Gutman 2022", "27 MLB pitchers", "74 percent at 297 days",
             "ERA worse; velocity unchanged"],
            ["Arnold 2022", "26 MLB pitchers", "81 percent at 10 months",
             "No difference against matched controls"],
            ["Chauhan 2024", "52 professionals", "79 percent at 9.5 months",
             "Decline no faster than healthy controls aging normally"],
        ],
        widths=(1.3, 1.5, 1.7, 2.2),
    )

    d.para(
        "The belief that this surgery ends pitching careers rests on one study, "
        "an unmatched before-and-after ERA comparison, and is contradicted by "
        "the two that used matched controls. Chauhan 2024, the only one drawing "
        "on Major League Baseball's internal injury database rather than press "
        "reports, found decline no faster than in healthy pitchers getting "
        "older. An unmatched before-and-after design on a group averaging 29 or "
        "30 years old will manufacture a decline out of ordinary aging."
    )

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("How it is diagnosed, and why counts vary")

    d.para(
        "**Established, and this is the most defensible section of the review.** "
        "There is no gold standard test for the neurogenic form, and the field "
        "says so in its own documents."
    )

    d.bullets([
        "The Society for Vascular Surgery reporting standards define the "
        "neurogenic form as three of four criteria, one being absence of other "
        "pathology that explains the symptoms, which makes it a diagnosis of "
        "exclusion, and one being response to a scalene block, which is a "
        "treatment trial rather than a test. No imaging, electrodiagnostic or "
        "laboratory criterion exists (Illig 2016).",

        "Sanders 2008 states there is no standard objective test to confirm "
        "clinical impressions, and that to date there is still no reliable "
        "objective test.",

        "The Cochrane review calls it one of the most controversial diagnoses in "
        "clinical medicine, and had to rely entirely on the diagnosis of the "
        "condition by the investigators in the reviewed studies. Only two "
        "randomised trials worldwide met a six-month follow-up bar (Povlsen 2014).",

        "Wilbourn and Roos published *Thoracic outlet syndrome is overdiagnosed* "
        "and *Thoracic outlet syndrome is underdiagnosed* back to back in the "
        "same 1999 issue of Muscle and Nerve.",

        "Even at a dedicated centre, only 150 of 183 new referrals, 82 percent, "
        "met an established criteria set (Balderman 2017).",
    ])

    d.callout(
        "A circularity worth naming",
        "A 2026 Delphi consensus exists because criteria remain unsettled a "
        "decade after the vascular surgery standards. Its fifth diagnostic "
        "criterion is participation in work or exercise requiring repetitive arm "
        "stress, naming overhead athletes and throwing sports. Being an overhead "
        "athlete is itself an input to the diagnosis. For a programme comparing "
        "its softball rate against peers, that is circular.",
    )

    d.subhead("False positive rates in people without the condition")

    d.table(
        ["Test", "Rayan 1995", "Plewa 1998", "Nord 2008"],
        [
            ["Adson", "13.5 percent vascular", "11 percent", "9 to 20 percent"],
            ["Costoclavicular", "47 percent vascular", "11 percent", "16 percent"],
            ["Wright, or hyperabduction", "57 percent vascular", "not tested", "not tested"],
            ["Roos, also called EAST", "not tested", "62 percent", "47 percent"],
            ["At least one test positive", "not reported", "not reported", "56 percent"],
        ],
        widths=(2.2, 1.6, 1.4, 1.5),
    )

    d.para(
        "Nord 2008 adds the decisive number. In carpal tunnel patients, who by "
        "definition do not have thoracic outlet syndrome, the Roos test was "
        "positive in 77 percent and 94 percent had at least one positive "
        "manoeuvre. Gillard 2001 reduces it to one figure: provocative tests "
        "have a mean specificity of 53 percent."
    )

    d.quote(
        "The test most likely to be used in an athletic training room is "
        "positive in roughly half of people who do not have the condition. "
        "Screening a 35-athlete roster with it would be expected to flag 16 to "
        "20 healthy athletes."
    )

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("What causes it in throwing athletes")

    d.subhead("The three compression spaces")

    d.table(
        ["Space", "Boundaries", "Contents"],
        [
            ["Interscalene triangle",
             "Anterior scalene in front, middle scalene behind, first rib below",
             "Plexus trunks and the subclavian artery. The vein passes in front of the anterior scalene and is not in this triangle"],
            ["Costoclavicular space",
             "Clavicle and subclavius above, first rib below",
             "Plexus divisions, subclavian artery and vein"],
            ["Subcoracoid space",
             "Pectoralis minor and its coracoid insertion in front, chest wall behind",
             "Plexus cords, axillary artery and vein"],
        ],
        widths=(1.5, 2.2, 3.0),
    )

    d.para(
        "**Established.** For arterial compression the costoclavicular space is "
        "the discriminating site. Imaging of 44 volunteers and 28 patients found "
        "no significant stenosis in the interscalene triangle or the "
        "retropectoralis minor space in either group, with 130 degrees of "
        "hyperabduction most discriminating (Demondion 2006)."
    )

    d.para(
        "**Reasonable but unproven.** The common claim that the subcoracoid "
        "space is the one most implicated in throwers has never been tested. No "
        "study compares the three spaces head to head in throwing athletes."
    )

    d.subhead("Structural predisposition is common, and usually silent")

    d.table(
        ["Finding", "Prevalence"],
        [
            ["Cervical rib", "0.74 percent of 1,352 chest radiographs; 0.7 percent of 6,571 in a second series"],
            ["Elongated C7 transverse process", "2.21 percent, about three times more common than a cervical rib"],
            ["Fibromuscular bands", "Present in a third of 58 cadaver outlets from people who had no symptoms"],
            ["Textbook plexus-between-scalenes arrangement", "Present in only 60 percent of 51 cadavers"],
            ["Developmental anomaly in surgical series", "66 percent of 200 consecutive cases"],
        ],
        widths=(2.6, 4.1),
    )

    d.callout(
        "Predisposition is not exoneration",
        "Roos found his bands in a third of cadavers from people who never had a "
        "symptom. Makhoul and Machleder concluded that morphology alone "
        "predicted the clinical syndrome only for effort thrombosis. The "
        "defensible framing is that structural narrowing is common, usually "
        "silent, and becomes symptomatic when loaded. That makes this a "
        "screening and load management problem rather than an act of God.",
    )

    d.subhead("The muscle biology argues against blaming the weight room")

    d.para(
        "**Established, and the single most useful finding in this review.** Two "
        "independent biopsy series of scalene muscle taken at surgery found the "
        "same pattern."
    )

    d.table(
        ["Finding", "Machleder 1986", "Sanders 1990"],
        [
            ["Type I, slow fibre, predominance", "85.1 percent", "78 percent against 53 percent in controls"],
            ["Type II fibres", "not reported", "atrophied"],
            ["Connective tissue, meaning fibrosis", "not reported", "36 percent against under 15 percent in controls"],
        ],
        widths=(2.3, 2.0, 2.4),
    )

    d.para(
        "Machleder read this as an extraordinary adaptive transformation in the "
        "type I fibre system reflecting chronic increased tone or motor neuron "
        "stimulation."
    )

    d.quote(
        "Resistance training produces type II hypertrophy. The scalene muscle in "
        "these patients shows type II atrophy, fibrosis and type I predominance. "
        "That is the signature of chronic sustained tone and of injury, not of a "
        "training adaptation."
    )

    d.subhead("Throwing loads the outlet, measurably")

    d.table(
        ["Arm position", "Anterior scalene", "Middle scalene"],
        [
            ["Neutral", "9.4 kPa", "10.9 kPa"],
            ["Cocked, the throwing position", "14.4 kPa", "15.8 kPa"],
            ["Cocked plus neck rotation away", "18.1 kPa", "15.8 kPa"],
        ],
        widths=(2.7, 2.0, 2.0),
        numeric_cols=(1, 2),
        caption="Takaba 2022, shear wave elastography in 30 collegiate baseball "
                "pitchers. The cocked position roughly doubles anterior scalene "
                "stiffness. This measures muscle stiffness rather than nerve "
                "compression, but it places the exposure in the throw.",
    )

    d.para(
        "In the largest athlete series the mean interscalene distance was 5.6 "
        "millimetres against cadaveric norms of 10.7 to 15, and hypertrophy of "
        "the serratus anterior and posterior scalene was commonly observed "
        "(Funakoshi 2024). Note which muscles those are. Posterior scalene and "
        "serratus anterior are driven by throwing rather than by pressing. This "
        "is the one finding a critic could reach for, and it belongs here with "
        "its context rather than left out."
    )

    d.subhead("Positional compression is normal")

    d.para(
        "**Established.** Magnetic resonance imaging of 35 asymptomatic "
        "volunteers and 54 patients found positional venous compression in 47 "
        "percent of the volunteers against 63 percent of patients. Arterial "
        "compression appeared in 72 percent of patients and none of the "
        "volunteers; nerve compression in 7 percent of patients and none of the "
        "volunteers. Except for venous thrombosis, compression appeared only "
        "with the arm elevated (Demondion 2003). Compression is positional, and "
        "roughly half of healthy people show it."
    )

    d.subhead("Posture, with one correction worth making")

    d.para(
        "**Established.** Droopy shoulder syndrome is often described as "
        "costoclavicular narrowing. It is not. Swift and Nichols described "
        "low-set shoulders and a long neck, with symptoms that worsened under "
        "downward traction and improved when patients raised their arms, which "
        "is the opposite of what compression predicts. It is a traction "
        "mechanism."
    )

    d.para(
        "**Established in healthy non-athletes.** A short pectoralis minor "
        "resting length goes with a scapula that stays anteriorly tipped at "
        "higher elevation angles and sits more internally rotated at lower ones "
        "(Borstad 2005). Length can be measured reliably in the field, with "
        "intrarater reliability of 0.86 to 0.97. No validated cut-off for short "
        "exists, so report the measurement rather than a threshold. This work "
        "was done in asymptomatic non-athletes and targeted subacromial "
        "impingement, so carrying it to throwers and to neurovascular "
        "compression is a two-step inference."
    )

    d.subhead("The cervical contribution, from our own library")

    d.para(
        "**Established in college pitchers.** Forty-nine healthy college "
        "baseball pitchers were measured in preseason and followed through the "
        "season. A cervical flexion-rotation test finding at or below 39 degrees "
        "on the dominant side carried 9.4 times the risk of a time-loss shoulder "
        "or elbow injury lasting more than seven days, with a confidence "
        "interval from 1.28 to 68.49. Pitchers with restricted rotation were "
        "injured earlier, playing 83.6 of 112 days against 109.4 (Devaney 2020)."
    )

    d.para(
        "The authors propose that reduced upper cervical rotation forces "
        "compensatory mid-cervical motion, and that these combined motions may "
        "decrease the space for the nerve roots in the intervertebral foramina, "
        "with knock-on effects on scapular and glenohumeral control."
    )

    d.note(
        "Read this carefully. Devaney did not study thoracic outlet syndrome. It "
        "measured shoulder and elbow injury. What it establishes, in exactly our "
        "population, is that neck mobility is a modifiable and screenable risk "
        "factor for throwing injury, by a mechanism next door to this one. With "
        "49 pitchers and 10 injuries the confidence intervals are wide, so the "
        "9.4 figure should not be quoted as precise. The direction and the "
        "screening implication are what to use."
    )

    d.subhead("What the literature does not support")

    d.bullets([
        "**No evidence for a link between glenohumeral internal rotation "
        "deficit and this condition.** Three separate literature searches "
        "returned nothing at all. Any such claim is speculation.",

        "**No evidence that resistance training causes it.** There is no "
        "controlled or cohort study. What exists is case reports: a weightlifter "
        "with effort thrombosis attributed to bench pressing, a rower and "
        "weightlifter with well-developed scalenes, and a weightlifter with "
        "subclavian occlusion whose case was confounded by anabolic steroid use.",

        "**The closest thing to support** is a Division I pitcher with axillary "
        "artery compression from hypertrophy of the pectoralis minor and scalene "
        "muscles, which the authors attributed to throwing rather than to any "
        "documented lifting programme (Ligh 2009).",

        "**The evidence base is case reports.** A 2022 systematic review of this "
        "condition in sport located 78 articles: 40 case reports, 10 clinical "
        "studies, 28 reviews. That composition is itself the finding.",
    ])

    d.para(
        "The defensible statement is this. Pectoralis minor and scalene "
        "hypertrophy have been documented as the compressing structure in "
        "individual athlete case reports, across throwing, water polo, rowing "
        "and weightlifting. Whether training-induced hypertrophy raises risk at "
        "a population level has never been tested."
    )

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("Muscle capacity and endurance")

    d.para(
        "The question put to us was whether a deficit in muscular endurance or "
        "capacity can cause this condition. The answer is that it is a coherent "
        "and reasonable hypothesis with no direct empirical support. It is worth "
        "acting on because the intervention is cheap, safe and justified on "
        "other grounds, not because the evidence establishes it."
    )

    d.subhead("The strongest supporting study")

    d.table(
        ["Measure", "Medial rotators", "Lateral rotators"],
        [
            ["Peak strength at 60 degrees per second", "minus 21 percent", "minus 29 percent"],
            ["Peak strength at 180 degrees per second", "minus 23 percent", "minus 20 percent"],
            ["Endurance, 30 repetitions at 180 degrees per second", "minus 45 percent", "minus 30 percent"],
        ],
        widths=(3.1, 1.8, 1.8),
        caption="Daley 2021, 100 patients against 100 healthy controls. All "
                "differences significant and correlated with disability score. "
                "The endurance deficit is roughly twice the strength deficit.",
    )

    d.para("**Four constraints block a causal reading. State all four.**")

    d.numbered([
        "**The direction of cause cannot be resolved by this design.** This "
        "condition is nerve compression. Reduced fatigue resistance is at least "
        "as plausibly a consequence, through partial denervation, pain "
        "inhibition or disuse, as a cause. The authors make no causal claim.",

        "**Wrong muscles.** The study measured glenohumeral rotators, not "
        "scapular stabilisers and not deep neck flexors.",

        "**Wrong population.** Seventy-one percent female, mean age 39.4, a "
        "clinic population. Every direct capacity study in this condition is a "
        "non-athlete, mostly female, roughly 40-year-old clinic group. None has "
        "ever been done in an athlete.",

        "**The companion study argues for consequence.** Grip strength was down "
        "30 percent and key pinch 19.5 percent, which is the classic lower "
        "plexus signature. That points to compression producing weakness rather "
        "than the reverse.",
    ])

    d.subhead("What has never been measured")

    d.bullets([
        "Scapular stabiliser endurance in patients against controls. No study "
        "exists.",
        "Deep neck flexor endurance in this population. No study exists.",
        "Electromyographic evidence of scalene overactivity during breathing. "
        "The one respiratory study found patients had reduced respiratory muscle "
        "endurance, which if anything runs opposite to the accessory-breathing "
        "explanation.",
        "**The decisive missing experiment:** nobody has measured the "
        "costoclavicular or subcoracoid space before and after a fatigue "
        "protocol. That single study would move this from plausibility to "
        "mechanism.",
        "A randomised trial of exercise therapy against a control. The only "
        "randomised trial compared surgery against continued conservative care "
        "in patients already refractory, and all 25 in the conservative arm "
        "applied for surgery at three months.",
    ])

    d.subhead("The indirect chain, and where it breaks")

    d.para(
        "**Established in healthy subjects, under acute laboratory fatigue, and "
        "framed around subacromial impingement rather than the thoracic "
        "outlet.** What replicates across four of five studies is decreased "
        "posterior tilt, meaning increased anterior tilt. Upward rotation does "
        "not replicate: one study found it decreased, three found it increased, "
        "one found no change. Do not assert a consistent upward rotation deficit."
    )

    d.para(
        "The chain runs: scapular muscle fatigue, then increased anterior tilt "
        "and internal rotation, which is measured and replicated; then the "
        "coracoid moving forward and down and the clavicle approaching the first "
        "rib, which is reasoned from anatomy; then narrowing of the "
        "costoclavicular and subcoracoid spaces, which are real and position "
        "dependent but have never been measured under fatigue; then nerve "
        "compression, which has never been demonstrated."
    )

    d.subhead("What the treatment protocols actually target")

    d.para(
        "A 2026 scoping review screened 1,381 studies and included 29. Exercise "
        "appeared in 90 percent of programmes: stretching aimed at the scalenes "
        "and pectoralis, strengthening aimed at the scapula, trapezius and "
        "serratus anterior. So the premise holds at the level of muscle "
        "selection and fails at the level of muscle quality. The review's own "
        "conclusion is that reporting of rehabilitation technique is generally "
        "poor, particularly on treatment intensity. No published protocol "
        "specifies sets, repetitions or loads in a way that would let anyone "
        "classify it as endurance training."
    )

    d.table(
        ["Study", "Patients", "Result"],
        [
            ["Novak 1995", "42", "25 improved, 10 unchanged, 7 worse. Only 16 back to full work and recreation"],
            ["Lindgren 1997", "119", "88 percent satisfied at about 25 months. Uncontrolled, subjective endpoint"],
            ["Balderman 2019", "150", "Only 40, or 27 percent, satisfactory with physical therapy alone; 60 percent went to surgery"],
            ["Fouasson-Chailloux 2025", "182", "Three-week inpatient rehabilitation raised rotator endurance 35 to 39 percent. Uncontrolled"],
        ],
        widths=(1.6, 0.9, 4.2),
    )

    d.para(
        "Twenty-seven percent and 88 percent are not in conflict. They are "
        "opposite ends of a selection spectrum. Neither is the number for an "
        "athlete. No cohort anywhere reports what fraction of throwing athletes "
        "resolve with rehabilitation alone, which for a performance audience is "
        "the most important absence in the literature."
    )

    d.subhead("Whether prevention programmes work at all")

    d.para(
        "**Mixed, and weaker than our field generally believes. Know this before "
        "citing it.**"
    )

    d.bullets([
        "The handball risk factor study found scapular dyskinesis at an odds "
        "ratio of 8.41, then **the same group's own replication failed**, in a "
        "paper subtitled *previous findings could not be confirmed*.",

        "The flagship randomised trial, 45 teams and 660 players, reduced any "
        "shoulder problem at an odds ratio of 0.72, but **did not** reduce "
        "substantial problems, where the result was not significant.",

        "**The mechanism failed to move.** A randomised trial of eight weeks of "
        "external rotation strengthening produced a between-group difference of "
        "0.06 newtons per kilogram. The authors concluded the programme improved "
        "neither external rotation strength nor the strength ratio.",

        "**The pooled result is null.** Three trials, 747 players, odds ratio "
        "0.73 with an interval from 0.45 to 1.17.",

        "Baseball's one clearly positive trial used five stretching, two "
        "mobility and two balance exercises, **with no scapular strengthening "
        "at all**.",
    ])

    d.subhead("Field tests, and their limits")

    d.table(
        ["Test", "Normative data", "Reliability", "Limit"],
        [
            ["Deep neck flexor endurance",
             "Men 38.9 seconds, women 29.4",
             "0.66, moderate at best",
             "Age and activity did not affect performance"],
            ["Scapular muscle endurance",
             "None published",
             "0.67, smallest detectable change 30.1 seconds",
             "Change threshold is large relative to hold times, so not usable for tracking an individual"],
            ["Closed kinetic chain upper extremity stability",
             "Collegiate baseball values exist",
             "not reported here",
             "Measures closed chain stability, not endurance"],
            ["Upper quarter Y balance",
             "High school baseball and softball composite 87.2",
             "not reported here",
             "Measures mobility and stability, not endurance"],
        ],
        widths=(1.6, 1.6, 1.6, 1.9),
    )

    d.para(
        "**None of these has ever been validated against this condition.** None "
        "has been administered to a patient population and none has a cut-point "
        "for risk. Use them as general upper quarter monitoring. Presenting any "
        "of them as a thoracic outlet screen would be unsupported."
    )

    d.callout(
        "The line to use",
        "Building scapular and postural capacity is a mechanistically coherent, "
        "low cost, low risk intervention that is justified on general shoulder "
        "health grounds. The claim that it prevents thoracic outlet syndrome "
        "specifically has no direct empirical support.",
    )

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("Lifting before throwing")

    d.para(
        "Our athletic training staff have recommended that pitchers not lift "
        "before they throw. **There is no research supporting this "
        "recommendation, and the adjacent evidence leans against it.**"
    )

    d.para(
        "Three structured literature searches returned no baseball study "
        "examining resistance training performed before throwing and its effect "
        "on velocity, accuracy, mechanics or injury rates. On this condition "
        "specifically, no paper connects resistance training timing to it at all."
    )

    d.table(
        ["Study", "Protocol", "Result"],
        [
            ["Water polo, 12 players",
             "Three sets of six at 80 percent of one repetition maximum, bench press, row and half squat, fifteen minutes before testing in the water",
             "No difference in throwing velocity, accuracy, tethered force, swimming or jumping"],
            ["Tennis, competitive juniors",
             "Three sets of six at 75 percent, at maximal intended velocity, not to failure",
             "No change in serve, forehand or backhand velocity or accuracy at three minutes, 24 hours or 48 hours"],
            ["Trained throwers, 14 athletes",
             "Morning total body resistance session",
             "Afternoon overhead throw distance improved"],
        ],
        widths=(1.5, 2.8, 2.4),
    )

    d.subhead("The one study showing a decrement, and why it undercuts the rule")

    d.para(
        "Sixteen adolescent baseball pitchers performed push-ups to failure and "
        "repeated jumps to failure. Each dropped pitch velocity by about two "
        "kilometres per hour. Three things about it matter."
    )

    d.numbered([
        "It used fatigue to failure, not a programmed lift.",
        "The authors state the recovery interval before the velocity retest was "
        "not quantified. It is a non-randomised pilot.",
        "**Lower body fatigue dropped velocity as much as upper body fatigue "
        "did.** If the mechanism were loading the throwing arm, squatting should "
        "not have mattered equally. This contradicts the rationale the rule "
        "rests on.",
    ])

    d.subhead("The mechanism breaks at the last link")

    d.bullets([
        "**Fatigue degrades shoulder proprioception.** Robust and replicated.",

        "**The deficit does not become functional.** A 160 percent increase in "
        "joint repositioning error produced no change in motor control or in "
        "shoulder performance testing.",

        "**Recovery is fast.** After a throwing-to-fatigue protocol in 16 "
        "collegiate players, scapulothoracic, glenohumeral, elbow and endpoint "
        "acuity recovered within four to seven minutes. The one exception was "
        "glenohumeral acuity in the arm-cocked position, which had not recovered "
        "at ten minutes. That exception is the single most defensible "
        "mechanistic hook for the staff's concern, and it is narrow.",

        "**Strength training is associated with better shoulder proprioception "
        "chronically.**",

        "All the fatigue-alters-mechanics literature concerns fatigue from "
        "throwing itself, not from lifting.",
    ])

    d.table(
        ["Possible rationale", "How well the evidence supports it"],
        [
            ["Manage total daily and weekly load",
             "Best supported, though indirectly. The literature concerns cumulative throwing load"],
            ["Avoid heavy loading of the throwing shoulder specifically",
             "Not supported, and actively undercut by the lower body result"],
            ["Proximity in hours",
             "Weak. Fifteen minutes was fine, three minutes was fine, four to six hours was beneficial"],
            ["Nothing at all",
             "Closest to the truth for the blanket rule"],
        ],
        widths=(2.7, 4.0),
    )

    d.callout(
        "A defensible reframe",
        "Not no lifting before throwing, but this: avoid taking the upper body "
        "to failure, and avoid novel heavy eccentric upper body work, in the "
        "hours before a high intent throwing session. That is a statement about "
        "dose and proximity to failure. Every trial using a dosed, sub-failure "
        "lift found no impairment. The current rule should be presented as "
        "conservative professional judgment, which is a legitimate basis for a "
        "decision, but not as research backed. No NSCA or ACSM position stand "
        "and no consensus statement prescribes an order.",
    )

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("Softball, and the workload picture")

    d.subhead("The softball literature barely exists")

    d.para(
        "A literature search for this condition in softball returns exactly six "
        "records. Two are case reports in softball athletes, both structural or "
        "congenital first rib problems, and **neither patient is identified as a "
        "pitcher**. Four are cohort studies where softball is pooled with "
        "baseball or given only as a prevalence. A systematic review of effort "
        "thrombosis in athletes does not contain the word softball."
    )

    d.quote(
        "No peer reviewed paper attributes thoracic outlet syndrome or effort "
        "thrombosis in a softball pitcher to the pitching motion. Every "
        "mechanistic claim has to be extrapolated from baseball, and the "
        "extrapolation should be stated."
    )

    d.subhead("The windmill is not load sparing")

    d.table(
        ["Measure", "Value"],
        [
            ["Shoulder distraction, youth pitchers", "94 percent of body weight"],
            ["Shoulder distraction, elite and Olympic pitchers", "80 percent of body weight"],
            ["Peak compression at shoulder and elbow", "70 to 98 percent of body weight"],
            ["Peak biceps activation, windmill against overhand at matched ball speed", "38 percent against 19 percent"],
            ["Scapular excursion through the pitch", "5 to 22 degrees per plane"],
        ],
        widths=(4.3, 2.4),
        caption="Werner 2005 and 2006; Barrentine 1998; Rojas 2009; Holtz 2026.",
    )

    d.para(
        "Three independent sources state that windmill shoulder and elbow loads "
        "are similar to baseball pitching. Our own library says the same: it is "
        "continually reported that the shoulder stress endured from the softball "
        "pitch is analogous to that of the baseball pitch, with comparable "
        "injury rates and patterns (Oliver 2019). **The belief that the windmill "
        "is a natural motion is named as a misconception in the peer reviewed "
        "literature.**"
    )

    d.para(
        "The actionable lever is proximal. Lower extremity screening alone "
        "predicted 49.9 percent of peak shoulder distraction variance in 46 "
        "collegiate pitchers, rising to 56.2 percent with hip rotation strength "
        "(Ulman 2025). Our library adds the trunk: at foot contact, increased "
        "trunk rotation toward the pitching arm, increased stride length and a "
        "posteriorly shifted centre of mass explained about a third of the "
        "variance in upper extremity pain among 37 Division I softball pitchers."
    )

    d.subhead("Workload")

    d.para(
        "**NCAA softball has no pitch count limit and no mandated rest.** NCAA "
        "baseball has none either, but the high school federation requires every "
        "state association to adopt a baseball pitch count restriction with "
        "mandated rest, while softball is capped only by innings."
    )

    d.table(
        ["Measure", "Softball", "Baseball", "Ratio"],
        [
            ["Innings pitched per season, median", "84.1", "29.2", "2.9 times"],
            ["Appearances per season", "23.0", "16.0", "1.4 times"],
            ["Innings per game", "3.6", "1.6", "2.3 times"],
            ["Pitchers per roster", "4.5, or 21 percent", "15.7, or 44 percent", "one third the staff"],
            ["Share exceeding 100 innings per season", "43.7 percent", "7.4 percent", "6 times"],
        ],
        widths=(2.5, 1.5, 1.5, 1.2),
        numeric_cols=(1, 2),
        caption="Freetly 2024, 40 College World Series teams per sport, 2016 to "
                "2021. All differences highly significant. This is the "
                "one-pitcher-carries-the-staff pattern, quantified.",
    )

    d.callout(
        "The most actionable finding in this review",
        "A 2025 study tracked 8,248 pitches across 89 varsity outings. Counting "
        "game pitches alone, 25.6 percent of outings exceeded recommended "
        "volume. Counting bullpen and warmup as well, 51.2 percent did. Roughly "
        "half of true pitch volume is invisible to a box score.",
    )

    d.para(
        "Volume thresholds exist only for youth and high school, since no "
        "collegiate pitch count study has been published. In high school "
        "pitchers, more than 85 pitches in a game more than doubled the "
        "likelihood of seeking medical attention, and shoulder pain went with "
        "429 against 219 pitches a week and 19,195 against 8,876 a year."
    )

    d.para(
        "**Fatigue findings run in mixed directions, so read them carefully.** "
        "After about 99 pitches, dominant side deficits of 11 to 22 percent "
        "appeared across hip, scapula, shoulder, elbow and wrist, with velocity "
        "down 3.4 percent. Kinetics decreased at shoulder, elbow and wrist in "
        "the last and doubleheader innings, meaning the pitcher produces less "
        "force rather than more. Consecutive day tournament pitching raised "
        "fatigue and pain. But one study found stride-leg knee extension and "
        "trunk flexion strength increased after 105 pitches. The consistent "
        "reading is that proximal control and output degrade within and across "
        "days, while isolated post-game strength tests can move either way."
    )

    d.subhead("Injury epidemiology and prevention")

    d.table(
        ["Measure", "Finding"],
        [
            ["NCAA softball overall injury rate", "3.92 per 1,000 athlete exposures"],
            ["Shoulder share of injuries", "15.2 percent, the single most injured body part"],
            ["Game against practice rate", "4.30 against 2.67 per 1,000 exposures"],
            ["Preseason against in-season practice", "3.65 against 1.68 per 1,000 exposures"],
            ["Collegiate pitchers injured in one season", "72.8 percent of 181 pitchers"],
            ["Upper extremity share of pitcher time-loss injuries", "82 percent"],
        ],
        widths=(3.4, 3.3),
    )

    d.para(
        "There is effectively no softball specific prevention evidence. A "
        "systematic review screened 1,605 articles, included seven, and found "
        "only one describing an injury prevention programme for softball "
        "players, with no efficacy trial. Fewer than 46 percent of fastpitch "
        "coaches run any programme at all."
    )

    d.note(
        "One number to stop repeating: 1,200 to 1,500 pitches in a three-day "
        "tournament. It appears in a peer reviewed paper but is cited to a "
        "biomechanics study of 53 youth pitchers that reports no tournament "
        "volume at all. The only other peer reviewed tournament figure, 95 to "
        "381 pitches a weekend, is an order of magnitude lower and also "
        "describes youth pitchers."
    )

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("What we propose, and who owns each part")

    d.para(
        "Most of the modifiable exposure does not sit in the weight room. That "
        "is not a deflection. It is where the evidence points."
    )

    d.table(
        ["Lever", "Owner", "Evidence", "Action"],
        [
            ["Count every pitch, bullpen and warmup included", "Pitching coach, AT", "Strong",
             "Half of true volume is uncounted. Highest yield, lowest cost change available"],
            ["Innings distribution across the staff", "Head coach", "Strong",
             "Develop staff depth. No rule will do this for you"],
            ["Consecutive day and doubleheader exposure", "Head coach", "Moderate",
             "Build rest into tournament plans"],
            ["Cervical mobility screening", "AT, Performance", "Moderate, our exact population",
             "Add to the preseason screen. Cheap, fast, defensible"],
            ["Pectoralis minor resting length", "Performance", "Mechanism only",
             "Measure it. Do not publish a cut-off"],
            ["Hip and trunk capacity", "Performance", "Moderate",
             "Predicts about half of shoulder distraction. The strongest evidence-aligned target we have"],
            ["Scapular control and postural capacity", "Performance", "Unproven for this condition",
             "Do it. Low cost, low risk, justified on other grounds"],
            ["Upper quarter capacity monitoring", "Performance", "Weak for individuals",
             "Group screens only. Never present as a thoracic outlet screen"],
            ["Lifting timing relative to throwing", "Performance", "No evidence either way",
             "Avoid upper body work to failure near high intent throwing. Drop the blanket rule"],
            ["Diagnostic and referral pathway", "Sports Medicine", "Strong",
             "Agree criteria before counting cases"],
            ["Prior throwing history at intake", "Recruiting, Sports Medicine", "Moderate",
             "Capture travel ball volume and previous rib or clavicle injury"],
        ],
        widths=(1.7, 1.3, 1.4, 2.3),
    )

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("Language to use, and language to avoid")

    d.subhead("Claims that survive scrutiny")

    d.bullets([
        "This condition is not separately coded in NCAA injury surveillance, so "
        "there is no peer benchmark to compare against.",
        "At an incidence around 2 to 3 per 100,000 per year, a roster our size "
        "cannot generate a statistically meaningful rate. Two cases is within "
        "chance.",
        "The provocative test used most often is positive in roughly half of "
        "people who do not have the condition. Case counts track how hard you "
        "look.",
        "Windmill pitching produces shoulder loads equal to baseball, and our "
        "pitchers throw about three times the innings on a staff a third the "
        "size, with no pitch count limit.",
        "About half of true pitch volume is bullpen and warmup that nobody "
        "counts.",
        "Scalene muscle changes in patients are type II atrophy and fibrosis, "
        "the opposite of a weight training adaptation.",
        "There is no research supporting a ban on lifting before throwing.",
        "Building capacity is worth doing on general shoulder health grounds. I "
        "will not claim it prevents this condition, because that has not been "
        "shown.",
    ])

    d.subhead("Claims that will not survive scrutiny")

    d.table(
        ["Do not say", "Why not"],
        [
            ["Incidence is 3 to 80 per 1,000",
             "Traces to a source not indexed in PubMed"],
            ["Roos described 14 types of congenital band",
             "No Roos primary says 14. It is seven in 1976 and nine in 1980"],
            ["Internal rotation deficit contributes to it",
             "Zero literature. Three searches, no records"],
            ["Softball pitchers throw 1,200 to 1,500 pitches a tournament weekend",
             "The citation does not support the figure"],
            ["Droopy shoulder syndrome narrows the costoclavicular space",
             "It is a traction mechanism. Symptoms improve with arm elevation"],
            ["Scapular endurance deficits cause it",
             "No study has measured scapular endurance in this population at all"],
            ["This surgery ends pitching careers",
             "Matched control studies find decline no faster than normal aging, with return to play of 74 to 81 percent"],
        ],
        widths=(3.0, 3.7),
    )

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("Open questions for us to answer locally")

    d.numbered([
        "**What is our actual diagnostic pathway?** Which test findings "
        "triggered each diagnosis, and did they meet the three-of-four vascular "
        "surgery standard?",

        "**What are our real pitch counts**, bullpen and warmup included? No "
        "collegiate figure exists in the literature, so it has to be measured "
        "locally.",

        "**What is each pitcher's prior throwing history**, meaning travel ball "
        "volume, year-round participation, and any previous first rib or "
        "clavicle injury?",

        "**Has anyone imaged for structural predisposition** in the affected "
        "athletes, meaning cervical rib, elongated C7 transverse process, or "
        "first rib abnormality?",
    ])

    # ==================================================================
    d.section("Sources")

    d.para(
        "All 109 sources were verified against PubMed, Europe PMC or the "
        "publisher record on 18 September 2026. The ones carrying the arguments "
        "above are listed here. Items marked Zotero are held in the Applied "
        "Performance research library."
    )

    d.table(
        ["Claim", "Source"],
        [
            ["Subtype proportions and incidence",
             "Illig, Annals of Vascular Surgery 2021, PMID 32771464; Illig and Rodriguez-Zoppi, Thoracic Surgery Clinics 2021, PMID 33220767"],
            ["Athlete subtype mix",
             "Chandra, Journal of Vascular Surgery 2014, PMID 24835692; Chauhan, American Journal of Sports Medicine 2024, PMID 38702964; Gutman, Physician and Sportsmedicine 2022, PMID 33472488"],
            ["Collegiate prevalence, 15,609 athletes",
             "Talutis, Journal of Vascular Surgery 2025, PMID 40132734"],
            ["No gold standard, diagnostic criteria",
             "Illig, Journal of Vascular Surgery 2016, PMID 27565607; Sanders, Neurologist 2008, PMID 19008742; Povlsen, Cochrane 2014, PMID 25427003; Wagner, Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 2026, PMID 42169800"],
            ["Provocative test false positives",
             "Rayan, Journal of Shoulder and Elbow Surgery 1995, PMID 7600161; Plewa, Academic Emergency Medicine 1998, PMID 9562199; Nord, Electromyography and Clinical Neurophysiology 2008, PMID 18435210; Gillard, Joint Bone Spine 2001, PMID 11707008"],
            ["NCAA surveillance taxonomy",
             "Kerr, Journal of Athletic Training 2014, PMID 24870292; Boltz 2021, PMID 34280265; Veillard 2021, PMID 34280289"],
            ["Scalene histology",
             "Machleder, Archives of Surgery 1986, PMID 3767646; Sanders, American Journal of Surgery 1990, PMID 2301718"],
            ["Scalene stiffness in the cocked position",
             "Takaba, Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 2022, PMID 36003968"],
            ["Structural predisposition",
             "Brewin, Clinical Anatomy 2009, PMID 19280652; Roos, American Journal of Surgery 1976, PMID 998867; Makhoul and Machleder, Journal of Vascular Surgery 1992, PMID 1404675"],
            ["Positional compression in healthy people",
             "Demondion, Radiology 2003, PMID 12637678; Demondion, Journal of Ultrasound in Medicine 2006, PMID 16439785"],
            ["Cervical mobility and throwing injury",
             "Devaney, Orthopaedic Journal of Sports Medicine 2020, DOI 10.1177/2325967120920556 (Zotero)"],
            ["Endurance deficit in patients",
             "Daley, Diagnostics 2021, PMID 34573871; Fouasson-Chailloux, Diagnostics 2021, PMID 34068245"],
            ["Rehabilitation protocol content",
             "O'Sullivan, Hand Therapy 2026, PMID 41657761; Watson, Manual Therapy 2010, PMID 20382063; Balderman, Journal of Vascular Surgery 2019, PMID 30852035"],
            ["Prevention programme evidence",
             "Clarsen, British Journal of Sports Medicine 2014, PMID 24948083; Andersson 2017, PMID 27313171 and 2018, PMID 28784621; Fredriksen, JOSPT 2021, PMID 33789429; Yonneau 2025, PMID 41035524; Sakata, AJSM 2019, PMID 31336051"],
            ["Lifting before throwing",
             "Malliaros, Sports 2025, PMID 41295761; Terraza-Rebollo, PLoS One 2021, PMID 34882729; Ekstrand, JSCR 2013, PMID 22395279; Tremblay, JSCR 2024, PMID 38838214"],
            ["Fatigue and proprioception",
             "Carpenter, AJSM 1998, PMID 9548121; Tripp, Journal of Athletic Training 2007, PMID 18174932; Hadjisavvas, Human Movement Science 2024, PMID 39461122"],
            ["Windmill biomechanics",
             "Werner, AJSM 2005, PMID 15722291 and 2006, PMID 16282576; Barrentine, JOSPT 1998, PMID 9836172; Rojas, AJSM 2009, PMID 19174551; Oliver, OJSM 2019, DOI 10.1177/2325967119865171 (Zotero)"],
            ["Softball workload and pitch counting",
             "Freetly, Journal of Women's Sports Medicine 2024, DOI 10.53646/khdyxt64; Kamarajugadda, Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness 2025, PMID 40673787; Gooch, Sports Health 2022, PMID 34672828"],
            ["Softball case reports and reviews",
             "Young, JSES 2016, PMID 27742249; Gibson, JBJS Case Connector 2021, PMID 34329202; Keller, JSES 2020, PMID 32868012; Garraud, Frontiers in Physiology 2022, PMID 35755427"],
            ["Largest overhead athlete series",
             "Funakoshi, JSES International 2024, PMID 38707577; Funakoshi, JBJS 2019, PMID 31094981"],
        ],
        widths=(2.1, 4.6),
    )

    path = OUT / "TOS_EVIDENCE_REVIEW_ER_2026-09-18.docx"
    d.save(str(path))
    return path

    d = BaylorDoc(

        status="Briefing note — September 2026",

        ["Prepared by", "Eric Rash, Applied Performance"],
        ["Evidence base",

    ])

        "outlet rate to another's, because the condition is not tracked "
        "separately. It is also rare enough that a roster our size cannot "
        "produce a meaningful rate either way. What the research does support "
        "is that the throwing motion itself is the exposure, and that our "
        "pitchers carry roughly three times the innings of a baseball staff a "
        "third our size.",
    )

        "surveillance system sorts injuries by body part and by type: strains, "

        "percent against 2.6 percent for tennis.",

            ["Agree diagnostic criteria before counting cases",
             "Sports Medicine", "Removes guesswork from any comparison"],
            ["Capture prior throwing history at intake",

        "returned within 9 to 11 months, and performance afterward dropped no "
        "faster than for healthy pitchers getting older."

    path = OUT / "TOS_BRIEFING_NOTE_ER_2026-09-18.docx"
    d.save(str(path))
    return path


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(build())

entries.name: ExitWorktree
entries.description:
Exit a worktree session created by EnterWorktree and return the session to the original working directory.

## Scope

This tool ONLY operates on worktrees created by EnterWorktree in this session. It will NOT touch:
- Worktrees you created manually with `git worktree add`
- Worktrees from a previous session (even if created by EnterWorktree then)
- The directory you're in if EnterWorktree was never called

If called outside an EnterWorktree session, the tool is a **no-op**: it reports that no worktree session is active and takes no action. Filesystem state is unchanged.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly asks to "exit the worktree", "leave the worktree", "go back", or otherwise end the worktree session
- Do NOT call this proactively — only when the user asks

## Parameters

- `action` (required): `"keep"` or `"remove"`
  - `"keep"` — leave the worktree directory and branch intact on disk. Use this if the user wants to come back to the work later, or if there are changes to preserve.
  - `"remove"` — delete the worktree directory and its branch. Use this for a clean exit when the work is done or abandoned.
- `discard_changes` (optional, default false): only meaningful with `action: "remove"`. If the worktree has uncommitted files or commits not on the original branch, the tool will REFUSE to remove it unless this is set to `true`. If the tool returns an error listing changes, confirm with the user before re-invoking with `discard_changes: true`.

## Behavior

- Restores the session's working directory to where it was before EnterWorktree
- Clears CWD-dependent caches (system prompt sections, memory files, plans directory) so the session state reflects the original directory
- If a tmux session was attached to the worktree: killed on `remove`, left running on `keep` (its name is returned so the user can reattach)
- Once exited, EnterWorktree can be called again to create a fresh worktree

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree and branch on disk; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required true when action is "remove" and the worktree has uncommitted files or unmerged commits. The tool will refuse and list them otherwise.

Done. Rebuilt clean from its permanent location, Drive refreshed, worktree cleaned up.

**Where everything lives now:**

| What | Path |
|---|---|
| Project (scripts, deliverables, sources) | `~/Desktop/DEV/TOS_Evidence_Brief/` |
| DOCX + PDF, both docs | `…/TOS_Evidence_Brief/deliverables/` |
| Same four files on Drive | `G:\My Drive\00_Primary_Storage_Drive\04_RESEARCH\TOS_Evidence_Brief_2026-09\` |
| Long-form markdown | SecondBrain `Knowledge/sport-science/` |
| Rescued HTML artifact sources | `…/TOS_Evidence_Brief/artifacts/` |

That last row matters: the HTML sources were sitting in the job scratch directory and would have been deleted with this job. They're now saved alongside everything else.

**The two documents**, both built through `baylor_docstyle.py` — the genuine Word pipeline, not a lookalike:

- **`TOS_BRIEFING_NOTE_ER_2026-09-18`** — one page, confirmed by Word's own page count.
- **`TOS_EVIDENCE_REVIEW_ER_2026-09-18`** — 14 pages, 11 numbered sections, 25 tables, closing with a claim-to-source table so any figure can be traced.

**On the articulation skill**, I used the Pyramid Principle for both: answer first, then arguments, then evidence. The full review now opens with a section called "In brief" that states the seven conclusions before any supporting material, which is a real restructure — the old version made you read to section 5 before learning the endurance answer. It also happens to match how your tech inventory exec summary opens, so the convergence was free.

**One thing worth flagging.** Getting the briefing note to one page took five rebuilds, and the cause wasn't what I assumed. I kept cutting prose while the real culprits were structural: long table cells wrap to two lines and cost far more vertical space than the same words in a paragraph, and Word silently inserts an empty paragraph after a table that ends the document body — that phantom paragraph alone was creating page 2 after the content already fit. The note now adds that paragraph explicitly so pagination is deterministic across rebuilds. Both traps are written into the README, and `export_pdfs.py` flags the page count on every build so it can't regress quietly.

The cost of fitting one page: the structural-predisposition bullet and the outcomes paragraph came out of the briefing note. Both are intact in the full review.

**Nothing is committed.** `~/DEV`'s `.gitignore` starts with `/*`, so the new project isn't tracked and `git status` is empty. I didn't add a negation rule since that changes your thin-repo policy — say the word if you want it tracked.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\research-in-5

# Research in 5

The procedure, content rules, and build tooling live in the project repo, not here.
This skill gets you into the repo and carries the lessons that are easy to relearn
the hard way.

## Start

1. Project root: `~/Desktop/DEV/Weekly_Research_Review` (Windows) or
   `~/DEV/Weekly_Research_Review` (Mac). Missing on this machine:
   `gh repo clone erash11/Weekly_Research_Review` into DEV.
2. `git pull`, then read `docs/STATUS.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `docs/WORKFLOW.md`, and
   `docs/CONTENT_SPEC.md`. Follow WORKFLOW.md step by step; it owns the process.
3. Background session: work in a worktree of that repo, open a PR, merge only when
   Eric says so.

Build and QA: `pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/NNN_slug -NoDrive`, read every
`dark-slideN.png` and `light-slideN.png`, then publish without `-NoDrive`.
Deliverables land in `07_EDUCATION/Research_in_5/NNN_slug/` on the Google Drive
primary storage drive.

## Gotchas

- **Check Zotero for the full text before settling for an abstract.** A new item's PDF may not be indexed yet: run `sync_zotero_library` with `include_fulltext: true`, then `get_paper` and look at `attachments`. #001 was first built from the abstract while the PDF sat in Zotero.
- **Article-in-press papers often have no public PDF.** Springer's PDF URL 404s even in Chrome. Ask Eric for the PDF or check Zotero; set `paper.full_text: false` only as a last resort and say so in the post.
- **Every number comes from the paper's tables, with a page, as reported.** Write `notes.md` first. Plot and tabulate exact values; never display a computed difference. Flag contradictions inside the paper (a conclusion stronger than its own limitations, a mislabeled table) in notes.md.
- **Slides carry one idea each; detail goes to the post.** Slide-facing fields have tight limits that build.js enforces (question 90, fact 26, summary 110, role line 70, takeaway 60, bottom line 55). Write those short first. `did.bullets`, `results.bullets`, extra limitations, and the discussion question are post-only.
- **Department names:** Athletic Performance (not strength and conditioning), Athletic Medicine (not sports medicine), Applied Performance (not sport science). build.js rejects others.
- **Baylor Bears Font has only A to Z, 0 to 9, space and `. : ! - #`.** It sets display text only; `headline` must fit that set. Section titles are caps statements because there is no `?`. Agency FB sets everything people read and has no `→`.
- **"Calibri" in the PDF font list is expected.** PowerPoint cannot embed Bears (OpenType-CFF) and draws it as outlines with a Calibri-tagged text layer. Only `Agency FB embedded: False` is a real failure. Both fonts must be installed before building on a new machine (`DEV/Baylor_Fonts`).
- **Run the humanizer skill on the audience copy before the final build.** Keep facts, pages, and limits; cut rule-of-three lists, "not X, but Y" lines, and stacked rhetorical questions.
- **Revisions get a new `version`** (outputs `_vN`) so the files Eric may already have shared stay on Drive. Only overwrite in place for a same-day correction, and say so.
- **publish.ps1 needs Windows PowerShell COM (installed PowerPoint) for the PDF export.** On the Mac, `node tools/build.js` still builds the pptx files and posts; export and publish from the Windows laptop.
- **Eric prefers the dark deck.** Both themes build every run; send the dark PDF first.

## Examples

```
User: "Research in 5 on this one: Saraee 2026, J Orthop Surg Res, alignment and jumper's knee"
→ cd into the repo, pull, read STATUS
→ Zotero: search, sync with full text, read every page; write notes.md
→ review.json (next number), humanizer pass, publish.ps1 -NoDrive, read all PNGs
→ publish, commit on a branch, PR; send the dark PDF, teams.md, email.txt
```

=== WORKFLOW.md ===
# Weekly workflow

One paper in, one review out: a dark deck, a light deck, a Teams post, and an email,
all generated from the same `review.json`. Steps run in order; do not skip the QA gate.
The `/research-in-5` skill starts this workflow from any folder.

## 1. Intake

Eric hands over the paper one of three ways:

| Input | How to read it |
|---|---|
| PDF in `_DRIVE/07_EDUCATION/Research_in_5/_Inbox/` or a path | Read the full text, page by page. Best source. |
| DOI or URL | Fetch the article page. Articles in press often have no public PDF. If the full text is out of reach, ask Eric for the PDF; set `paper.full_text: false` and build from the abstract only as a last resort. |
| Zotero item (title, key, or tag) | `sync_zotero_library` with `include_fulltext: true`, then `search_papers` for the key, `get_paper` to confirm a PDF attachment, and `get_paper_pages` for page-located text. A just-attached PDF is not searchable until that sync runs. |

## 2. Set up the folder

- Number = highest existing `reviews/NNN_*` + 1 (`000_sample` does not count).
- Create `reviews/NNN_slug/` (slug: 2-4 lowercase words, e.g. `sleep-extension-sprint`).
- Copy `templates/review.template.json` to `reviews/NNN_slug/review.json`.

## 3. Extract to notes.md

Before writing anything for the audience, write `reviews/NNN_slug/notes.md`:

- Citation (authors, year, title, journal, DOI)
- Research question or aim, in the authors' words, with page
- Design, participants (n, sex, sport, level), duration, what was measured
- Main results: every number you might use, with page, copied from the tables as reported
- Limitations the authors state, plus any obvious ones they did not (label those "ours")
- Anything inside the paper that does not add up (a conclusion stronger than its own limitations section, a mislabeled table), and which source you used

Every number in review.json must appear here with a page number. This is what makes
the review defensible when a coach or physician asks "where did that come from?"
Never display a number you computed (a difference, a percent change); plot and
tabulate the reported values.

## 4. Write review.json

Follow `docs/CONTENT_SPEC.md`. Set `date` to the planned send date.

Write in this order, because the slides and the post use different fields:

1. **Slide fields, short.** `headline`, `hook`, `did.question`, `did.facts`,
   `results.stats[0]`, `results.chart` (or `results.table`), `meaning.summary`,
   `meaning.roles`, `trust.level` and `trust.limitations[0]`, `takeaways.bullets`,
   `takeaways.bottom_line`. These are set in large type; build.js enforces tight limits.
2. **Post-only fields, with the nuance.** `did.bullets`, the other `results.stats`,
   `results.bullets`, `trust.design`, `trust.sample`, the other limitations,
   `takeaways.question`. These appear in the Teams post and email, never on a slide.
3. **Humanizer pass** on all audience copy (the `humanizer` skill). Keep every
   number, page, and limit; cut rule-of-three lists, "not X, but Y" lines, and stacked
   rhetorical questions.

## 5. Build and QA locally

```
pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/NNN_slug -NoDrive
```

build.js validates first and stops on length, dash, department-name, or Baylor Bears
character errors. Fix the wording and rerun. It then writes both decks and the posts
to `build/NNN_slug/`, and publish.ps1 exports each deck to PDF and slide images.

Read all ten images, `dark-slide1.png` to `dark-slide5.png` and `light-slide1.png` to
`light-slide5.png`, and check:

- No text overflow, clipping, or overlap in either theme
- Every number on the slides matches notes.md and has a page (chart values match the paper's table)
- Slide 1 headline sits on one line; evidence scale matches the rubric
- Role lines are concrete, use department names, and only cover roles the paper touches
- Slide 5 has three takeaways and the Bottom line bar
- publish.ps1 prints `Agency FB embedded: True` for both PDFs. If False, recipients see a substitute font; do not send. "Calibri" inside the PDF is expected: it is the hidden text layer PowerPoint adds to Baylor Bears text
- `teams[_vN].md` and `email[_vN].txt` read cleanly and carry the detail the slides left out

Report PASS, FAIL (theme, slide numbers, and defects), or DEGRADED (PowerPoint export
unavailable, so slides were not visually checked). Do not call a DEGRADED review ready.
PDF export needs PowerPoint on Windows; on the Mac, `node tools/build.js` still builds
the pptx files and posts.

## 6. Publish

```
pwsh tools/publish.ps1 reviews/NNN_slug
```

Drive folder `07_EDUCATION/Research_in_5/NNN_slug/` receives:

| File | Use |
|---|---|
| `RI5-NNN_slug[_vN]_dark.pdf` | The deck to send (Eric's preferred theme) |
| `RI5-NNN_slug[_vN]_light.pdf` | Alternate for printing or bright rooms |
| `RI5-NNN_slug[_vN]_dark.pptx`, `..._light.pptx` | Editable decks |
| `teams[_vN].md` | Teams post |
| `email[_vN].txt` | Email, subject line on top |

`Research_in_5_Index.csv` at the top of `Research_in_5/` is refreshed too. Then move the
paper PDF from `_Inbox/` into the review folder as `paper.pdf`.

**Revisions:** bump `version` in review.json before rebuilding. Version 2 and up add
`_vN` to every file name, so copies Eric may already have shared stay on Drive. Only
overwrite in place for a same-day correction, and say so.

## 7. Commit

Commit `reviews/NNN_slug/` and `reviews/INDEX.md`, update docs/STATUS.md, push.
In a background session, work on a branch and open a PR; merge when Eric says so.

## 8. Eric sends

- Teams: paste `teams[_vN].md`, attach the dark PDF.
- Email: paste `email[_vN].txt` (subject line on top) to the training staff list, attach the dark PDF.
