# Content spec

## Audience

Mixed on purpose: athletic performance, athletic medicine, nutrition, mental health,
applied performance, sport coaches, and admin/leadership. Write
for a smart reader outside the paper's field, at about a college freshman level. If a
term needs a stats or physiology background (effect size, VO2max, ICC), explain it in a
few words or leave it out.

## The five slides

| Slide | Heading on the deck | On the slide |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `headline` | `headline`, source line, `hook`, evidence scale |
| 2 | 01 WHAT THE RESEARCHERS DID | `did.question`, `did.facts` (three across) |
| 3 | 02 WHAT THEY FOUND | `results.stats[0]` as one sentence, `results.chart` (or `results.table`) |
| 4 | 03 WHAT IT MEANS | `meaning.summary`, `meaning.roles`, level + `trust.limitations[0]` |
| 5 | 04 COACHING TAKEAWAYS | `takeaways.bullets`, `takeaways.bottom_line` bar, citation |

**Post-only fields** (Teams post and email, never on a slide): `did.bullets`,
`results.stats[1..]`, `results.bullets`, `trust.design`, `trust.sample`,
`trust.limitations[1..]`, `takeaways.question`, the full paper title. This split came
from the distill pass (2026-09-16): each slide carries one idea and one hero element,
and the detail lives where people read it at their own pace.

The Teams post and email keep the question form of the four headings.

Visual style (2026-09-16, Eric's direction, v3): every review builds a light and a dark
deck from the same content. Dark follows the "Sleep to Compete" telemetry deck
(`07_EDUCATION/TEAM EDUCATION/FOOTBALL/Education`): charcoal, faint grid, gold labels,
teal numbers, corner-bracket panels, gold bottom-line bar, with near-white body text.
Light uses Baylor green and dark gold on a paper background with the same layout.
No header or footer strip, no italics.

TITLE: Thoracic outlet syndrome in overhead athletes
DOI: 10.1016/j.jseint.2023.12.004
AUTHORS: 

=== ABSTRACT ===
AbstractBackgroundWe aimed to retrospectively compare the clinical outcomes of endoscopy-assisted first-rib resection for thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) between overhead athletes and nonathletes and investigate the return to same-level sports rate in overhead athletes.MethodsWe retrospectively reviewed 181 cases with TOS (75 women, 106 men; mean age, 28.4 years; range, 12-57 years) who underwent endoscopy-assisted first-rib resection. We divided into two groups: 79 overhead athletes and 102 nonathletes groups. A transaxillary approach for first-rib resection and neurovascular decompression was performed under magnified visualization. Endoscopic findings related to the neurovascular bundle, interscalene distance, and scalene muscle were evaluated intraoperatively. We assessed the Roos and Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand scores, return to same-level sports rate, and ball velocity.ResultsOverhead athletes were significantly more likely to be men, younger, used the dominant side more frequently, and have a larger physique, more shoulder and elbow pain, and shorter symptom duration. The outcomes of the Roos score revealed significant differences in excellent or good results between overhead athletes (91.1%) and nonathletes (62.8%). The two groups significantly differed in preoperative and postoperative Disability of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand and recovery rate scores (P = .007, < .001, < .001).ConclusionOverhead athletes with TOS were more likely to be men, younger, dominant side more frequently, and have more shoulder and elbow pain, and a shorter symptom duration. Endoscopy-assisted transaxillary first-rib resection and neurolysis provided superior clinical outcomes in overhead athletes with TOS compared with nonathletes and a high return-to-same-level-play rate in sports.Keywords: Thoracic outlet syndrome, Overhead athletes, Baseball, First-rib resection, Shoulder joint, Elbow joint

=== SECTIONS ===

--- Materials and methods [11509 chars] ---
Materials and methodsWe retrospectively reviewed data from consecutive patients treated for TOS at our hospital. The relevant institutional review boards approved this study.TOS was diagnosed based on the Wright18 and Roos31 tests and clinical features, according to previous studies.13,17,31 The costoclavicular space was evaluated in the resting and arm-elevated positions using three-dimensional computed tomography (3D-CT) (Fig. 1). Scapular dyskinesis in overhead athletes is often observed on the ipsilateral side (Fig. 1 E and F). Scapular dyskinesis is often observed bilaterally in patients with joint laxity (Fig. 1 A and B).Figure 1Three-dimensional computed tomography of the preoperative scapular position. (A): Nonathlete with right-sided symptomatic thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) in the resting position. (B): Arm-elevated position. Note the inferior displacement on both sides of the scapula (arrow). (C); Right costoclavicular space in the resting position (circle). (D): Right costoclavicular space in the elevated arm position. Significant narrowing of the costoclavicular space (circles). (E): An overhead athlete with right-sided symptomatic TOS in the resting position. Note the asymmetry of the right scapular position. (F): Arm-elevated position. Right scapular dyskinesis (arrows). (G); Right costoclavicular space in the resting position (circle). (H): Right costoclavicular space in the arm-elevated position. Significant narrowing of the costoclavicular space (circles).Ultrasonography (US) is a versatile and feasible test for the evaluation of neurovascular disorders owing to its noninvasiveness and inexpensiveness. Interscalene distance (ISD) and neurovascular bundle (NVB) patterns were evaluated using US, as previously reported13 (Fig. 2 B-D). Arterial compression was confirmed by measuring the peak systolic velocity (PSV) of the second part of the axillary artery using Doppler US (Fig. 3 A-D) and evaluating for interruption of the subclavian artery using 3D-CT angiography (Fig. 3 E-H). PSV was assessed in the resting and maximal arm-elevation positions. A significant alteration in PSV between the resting and elevation positions was defined as an increase or decrease of ≥ 50%. The inclusion criteria were symptomatic neurological, arterial, or venous TOS and a minimum follow-up period of 24 months from surgery. We excluded patients with shoulder or elb

--- Surgical technique [3938 chars] ---
Surgical techniqueThe patient was placed in the lateral decubitus position. All patients underwent an endoscopy-assisted transaxillary approach for partial resection of the first rib and complete anterior and partial middle scalenectomies for neurovascular decompression. # Notes — Funakoshi et al. 2024, thoracic outlet syndrome in overhead athletes

## Citation

Funakoshi T, Furushima K, Miyamoto A, Kusano H, Takahashi T, Inoue A, Shimokobe H.
Thoracic outlet syndrome in overhead athletes. *JSES International* 2024;8(3):620-629.
DOI 10.1016/j.jseint.2023.12.004. PMID 38707577. PMCID PMC11064620.

Open access (CC BY-NC-ND). No funding disclosed. No conflicts declared.
Ethics: Keiyu Orthopedic Hospital review board, approval 3506.

**Source used:** Europe PMC full text XML (`fullTextXML` for PMC11064620), which
carries the complete body and all four tables. PMC blocks scripted PDF download, so
`paper.pdf` is not in this folder. **Page references below are journal pages
(620-629), not PDF pages**, per the tables and sections as published.

## Aim, in the authors' words

"We aimed to retrospectively compare the clinical outcomes of endoscopy-assisted
first-rib resection for thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) between overhead athletes and
nonathletes and investigate the return to same-level sports rate in overhead
athletes." (Abstract, p. 620)

## Design and participants

- Retrospective comparative cohort, single centre, Japan. November 2015 to February 2021.
- **566 cases** underwent endoscopy-assisted transaxillary first-rib resection in the
  window. Exclusions: 172 lost to follow-up, 92 short follow-up, 77 incomplete
  pre/post findings, 30 other shoulder or elbow pathology, 14 insufficient imaging.
  **181 cases in 166 patients analysed** (Results, p. 622). That is 32% of the
  original pool.
- Groups: **79 overhead athletes** vs **102 nonathletes**.
- Mean follow-up 31.4 months (range 24.0 to 56.1).
- Inclusion required failure of conservative treatment for more than 3 to 6 months
  plus severe symptoms (Methods, p. 621). **Every patient in this study had surgery.**
- Diagnosis by Wright and Roos tests plus clinical features, supported by 3D-CT of
  the costoclavicular space, ultrasound for interscalene distance and neurovascular
  bundle pattern, and Doppler peak systolic velocity (Methods, p. 621).

## Table I — demographics (p. 622)

| Feature | Total (181) | Nonathletes (102) | Overhead athletes (79) | P |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sex, women/men | 75/106 | 68/34 | **7/72** | <.001 |
| Age at surgery (y) | 28.4 ± 13.9 | 36.4 ± 13.0 | **18.5 ± 7.3** | <.001 |
| Height (cm) | 165.8 ± 8.5 | 162.6 ± 8.0 | 169.3 ± 7.8 | <.001 |
| Weight (kg) | 61.9 ± 12.5 | 60.2 ± 13.4 | 63.9 ± 11.1 | .009 |
| BMI | 22.1 ± 4.1 | 22.0 ± 4.9 | 22.2 ± 2.9 | .602 |
| Dominant/nondominant | 137/44 | 61/41 | **76/3** | <.001 |
| Shoulder pain | 100 (55.2%) | 49 (48.0%) | **51 (64.6%)** | .027 |
| Elbow pain | 81 (44.8%) | 39 (38.2%) | **42 (53.2%)** | .045 |
| Upper extremity numbness | 104 (57.5%) | 56 (54.9%) | 48 (60.8%) | .429 |
| Symptom duration (mo) | 19.6 ± 31.3 | 24.3 ± 34.4 | **13.6 ± 25.9** | .001 |

## Table II — intraoperative findings (p. 623)

**The headline of this table is that almost nothing separated the two groups.**

| Finding | Total | Nonathletes | Overhead athletes | P |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Interscalene distance (mm) | 5.6 ± 3.6 | 5.2 ± 3.5 | 5.9 ± 3.7 | .237 |
| Anterior scalene hypertrophy | 101 (55.8%) | 58 (56.9%) | 43 (54.4%) | .744 |
| Middle scalene hypertrophy | 100 (55.2%) | 54 (52.9%) | 46 (58.2%) | .478 |
| Adhesion of neurovascular bundle | 144 (79.6%) | 82 (80.4%) | 62 (78.5%) | .752 |
| Cervical rib (Roos 1 or 2) | 2 | 2 | **0** | — |
| Fibrous string (Roos 3 or 4) | 17 | 6 | 11 | — |
| PSV alteration, preop | 90 (49.7%) | 49 (48.0%) | 41 (51.9%) | .607 |
| PSV alteration, postop | 50 (27.6%) | 37 (36.3%) | **13 (16.5%)** | .003 |

- Mean interscalene distance **5.6 mm (range 0 to 13)** against cadaveric averages the
  authors cite of 10.7 mm, 1.1 cm, 1.2 cm and 1.5 cm (Results, p. 623).
- PSV alteration fell significantly in athletes (51.9% to 16.5%, P < .001) but **not**
  in nonathletes (48.0% to 36.3%, P = .089).

## Table III — clinical outcomes (p. 624)

| Measure | Nonathletes | Overhead athletes | P |
|---|---|---|---|
| Roos test positive, preop | 100 (98.0%) | 75 (94.9%) | .406 |
| Wright test positive, preop | 64 (62.7%) | 56 (70.9%) | .251 |
| Grip power preop (kg) | 23.9 ± 12.1 | 32.2 ± 12.9 | <.001 |
| Grip power postop (kg) | 23.8 ± 14.5 | **37.8 ± 20.5** | <.001 |
| Grip, within group P | .974 | **.003** | — |
| DASH preop | 43.2 ± 18.8 | 37.2 ± 22.7 | .007 |
| DASH postop | 25.5 ± 22.1 | **7.5 ± 11.3** | <.001 |
| DASH recovery rate (%) | 41.0 ± 34.7 | **79.8 ± 30.7** | <.001 |
| Roos excellent | 42 (41.2%) | **63 (79.7%)** | <.001 |
| Roos good | 22 (21.6%) | 9 (11.4%) | — |
| Roos fair | 23 (22.5%) | 4 (5.1%) | — |
| Roos poor | 15 (14.7%) | 3 (3.8%) | — |

Excellent or good: **overhead athletes 91.1%, nonathletes 62.8%** (Results, p. 624).

## Table IV — return to sport (p. 625)

| Sport | N | Poor | Partial return | Same level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseball | 67 | 2 (3%) | 11 (16%) | 54 (81%) |
| Softball | 3 | 1 (33%) | 0 | 2 (67%) |
| Tennis | 4 | 0 | 0 | 4 (100%) |
| Volleyball | 3 | 0 | 1 (33%) | 2 (100%) |
| Swimming | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 (100%) |
| Handball | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 (100%) |
| **Total** | **79** | **3 (4%)** | **12 (15%)** | **64 (81%)** |

- Duration of return to sports: **7.3 ± 5.1 months**.
- Return to play 97%, return to same level 81% (Results, p. 625).
- **Ball velocity, baseball pitchers (n = 18): 126.2 ± 11.0 kph preop vs
  125.4 ± 11.3 kph postop, P = .876.** No change. This is the strongest null result in
  the paper and the most reassuring number for a coach.
- DASH sports module 70.1 ± 29.6 to 12.9 ± 20.3, P < .001. Recovery rate 79.1 ± 33.1%.

## Complications (p. 625)

- Pneumothorax 8 cases (4.4%), managed with chest drainage, no further surgery.
- Incomplete long thoracic nerve paralysis 2 cases.
- Superficial surgical site infection 1 case.
- No overhead athlete needed additional surgery. 11 nonathletes did.

## What the authors say about diagnosis (Discussion, p. 626)

- "TOS is difficult to diagnose and is often poorly managed."
- Roos et al reported that TOS is underdiagnosed.
- Overhead athletes with TOS "occasionally suffer from shoulder or elbow pain during
  the acceleration phase of the throwing motion, similar to the position of shoulder
  apprehension test, moving valgus stress test, and Roos test. Therefore, shoulder and
  elbow surgeons should avoid misdiagnosing TOS in overhead athletes, particularly
  adolescent athletes, who suffer from shoulder or elbow pain."
- Illig et al: TOS is often underdiagnosed in children and adolescents, leading to
  undertreatment.

## Limitations

**Authors' own** (Discussion):
- Retrospective design.
- Single institution.
- The pathology of TOS is "only partially understood".

**Ours** (not stated by the authors, and they matter more for us):
1. **Every patient had surgery after conservative care failed.** There is no
   conservative arm and no untreated comparison, so this says nothing about how often
   a thrower recovers without an operation.
2. **68% of the eligible pool was excluded.** 566 cases down to 181, with 172 lost to
   follow-up. Patients who do well are more likely to stop attending, so the outcome
   figures are probably flattering.
3. **Only 3 softball athletes.** Nothing about softball can be drawn from this paper.
   Baseball is 67 of the 79.
4. **Mean age 18.5 years** in the athlete group. This is a high school and early
   college population, not a mature professional one.
5. Single surgeon group, Japan, one specialised technique. Transfer to other settings
   is unknown.
6. Return to same level was judged subjectively by the patient.
7. No control for rehabilitation content or time, so the 7.3 month figure reflects
   this centre's protocol.

## Things inside the paper that do not add up

1. **Age range is reported twice and differs.** The abstract says "range, 12-57 years"
   (p. 620); the Results say "range, 12-64 years" (p. 622). Same cohort, two ranges.
   I use neither on the slides.
2. **Table IV volleyball row is mislabeled.** 3 athletes, 1 partial return (33%),
   2 same level, but the cell reads "2 (100%)". It should be 67%, as the softball row
   correctly shows for the same 2-of-3 split. I use the overall total (64/79, 81%)
   rather than the per-sport percentages.
3. The abstract reports the group difference in DASH as three P values
   "(P = .007, < .001, < .001)" without naming which is which. Table III resolves it:
   preoperative .007, postoperative < .001, recovery rate < .001.

## What I will not claim

- Not that TOS is common. This is a surgical series with no denominator, so it carries
  no incidence information at all.
- Not that throwing causes TOS. The design cannot show that, and Table II found no
  intraoperative difference between athletes and nonathletes.
- Not that surgery is the answer for a thrower with arm pain. Everyone here had
  already failed months of conservative care.

# Notes — Funakoshi et al. 2024, thoracic outlet syndrome in overhead athletes

## Citation

Funakoshi T, Furushima K, Miyamoto A, Kusano H, Takahashi T, Inoue A, Shimokobe H.
Thoracic outlet syndrome in overhead athletes. *JSES International* 2024;8(3):620-629.
DOI 10.1016/j.jseint.2023.12.004. PMID 38707577. PMCID PMC11064620.

Open access (CC BY-NC-ND). No funding disclosed. No conflicts declared.
Ethics: Keiyu Orthopedic Hospital review board, approval 3506.

**Source used:** Europe PMC full text XML (`fullTextXML` for PMC11064620), which
carries the complete body and all four tables. PMC blocks scripted PDF download, so
`paper.pdf` is not in this folder. **Page references below are journal pages
(620-629), not PDF pages**, per the tables and sections as published.

## Aim, in the authors' words

"We aimed to retrospectively compare the clinical outcomes of endoscopy-assisted
first-rib resection for thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS) between overhead athletes and
nonathletes and investigate the return to same-level sports rate in overhead
athletes." (Abstract, p. 620)

## Design and participants

- Retrospective comparative cohort, single centre, Japan. November 2015 to February 2021.
- **566 cases** underwent endoscopy-assisted transaxillary first-rib resection in the
  window. Exclusions: 172 lost to follow-up, 92 short follow-up, 77 incomplete
  pre/post findings, 30 other shoulder or elbow pathology, 14 insufficient imaging.
  **181 cases in 166 patients analysed** (Results, p. 622). That is 32% of the
  original pool.
- Groups: **79 overhead athletes** vs **102 nonathletes**.
- Mean follow-up 31.4 months (range 24.0 to 56.1).
- Inclusion required failure of conservative treatment for more than 3 to 6 months
  plus severe symptoms (Methods, p. 621). **Every patient in this study had surgery.**
- Diagnosis by Wright and Roos tests plus clinical features, supported by 3D-CT of
  the costoclavicular space, ultrasound for interscalene distance and neurovascular
  bundle pattern, and Doppler peak systolic velocity (Methods, p. 621).

## Table I — demographics (p. 622)

| Feature | Total (181) | Nonathletes (102) | Overhead athletes (79) | P |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sex, women/men | 75/106 | 68/34 | **7/72** | <.001 |
| Age at surgery (y) | 28.4 ± 13.9 | 36.4 ± 13.0 | **18.5 ± 7.3** | <.001 |
| Height (cm) | 165.8 ± 8.5 | 162.6 ± 8.0 | 169.3 ± 7.8 | <.001 |
| Weight (kg) | 61.9 ± 12.5 | 60.2 ± 13.4 | 63.9 ± 11.1 | .009 |
| BMI | 22.1 ± 4.1 | 22.0 ± 4.9 | 22.2 ± 2.9 | .602 |
| Dominant/nondominant | 137/44 | 61/41 | **76/3** | <.001 |
| Shoulder pain | 100 (55.2%) | 49 (48.0%) | **51 (64.6%)** | .027 |
| Elbow pain | 81 (44.8%) | 39 (38.2%) | **42 (53.2%)** | .045 |
| Upper extremity numbness | 104 (57.5%) | 56 (54.9%) | 48 (60.8%) | .429 |
| Symptom duration (mo) | 19.6 ± 31.3 | 24.3 ± 34.4 | **13.6 ± 25.9** | .001 |

## Table II — intraoperative findings (p. 623)

**The headline of this table is that almost nothing separated the two groups.**

| Finding | Total | Nonathletes | Overhead athletes | P |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Interscalene distance (mm) | 5.6 ± 3.6 | 5.2 ± 3.5 | 5.9 ± 3.7 | .237 |
| Anterior scalene hypertrophy | 101 (55.8%) | 58 (56.9%) | 43 (54.4%) | .744 |
| Middle scalene hypertrophy | 100 (55.2%) | 54 (52.9%) | 46 (58.2%) | .478 |
| Adhesion of neurovascular bundle | 144 (79.6%) | 82 (80.4%) | 62 (78.5%) | .752 |
| Cervical rib (Roos 1 or 2) | 2 | 2 | **0** | — |
| Fibrous string (Roos 3 or 4) | 17 | 6 | 11 | — |
| PSV alteration, preop | 90 (49.7%) | 49 (48.0%) | 41 (51.9%) | .607 |
| PSV alteration, postop | 50 (27.6%) | 37 (36.3%) | **13 (16.5%)** | .003 |

- Mean interscalene distance **5.6 mm (range 0 to 13)** against cadaveric averages the
  authors cite of 10.7 mm, 1.1 cm, 1.2 cm and 1.5 cm (Results, p. 623).
- PSV alteration fell significantly in athletes (51.9% to 16.5%, P < .001) but **not**
  in nonathletes (48.0% to 36.3%, P = .089).

## Table III — clinical outcomes (p. 624)

| Measure | Nonathletes | Overhead athletes | P |
|---|---|---|---|
| Roos test positive, preop | 100 (98.0%) | 75 (94.9%) | .406 |
| Wright test positive, preop | 64 (62.7%) | 56 (70.9%) | .251 |
| Grip power preop (kg) | 23.9 ± 12.1 | 32.2 ± 12.9 | <.001 |
| Grip power postop (kg) | 23.8 ± 14.5 | **37.8 ± 20.5** | <.001 |
| Grip, within group P | .974 | **.003** | — |
| DASH preop | 43.2 ± 18.8 | 37.2 ± 22.7 | .007 |
| DASH postop | 25.5 ± 22.1 | **7.5 ± 11.3** | <.001 |
| DASH recovery rate (%) | 41.0 ± 34.7 | **79.8 ± 30.7** | <.001 |
| Roos excellent | 42 (41.2%) | **63 (79.7%)** | <.001 |
| Roos good | 22 (21.6%) | 9 (11.4%) | — |
| Roos fair | 23 (22.5%) | 4 (5.1%) | — |
| Roos poor | 15 (14.7%) | 3 (3.8%) | — |

Excellent or good: **overhead athletes 91.1%, nonathletes 62.8%** (Results, p. 624).

## Table IV — return to sport (p. 625)

| Sport | N | Poor | Partial return | Same level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseball | 67 | 2 (3%) | 11 (16%) | 54 (81%) |
| Softball | 3 | 1 (33%) | 0 | 2 (67%) |
| Tennis | 4 | 0 | 0 | 4 (100%) |
| Volleyball | 3 | 0 | 1 (33%) | 2 (100%) |
| Swimming | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 (100%) |
| Handball | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 (100%) |
| **Total** | **79** | **3 (4%)** | **12 (15%)** | **64 (81%)** |

- Duration of return to sports: **7.3 ± 5.1 months**.
- Return to play 97%, return to same level 81% (Results, p. 625).
- **Ball velocity, baseball pitchers (n = 18): 126.2 ± 11.0 kph preop vs
  125.4 ± 11.3 kph postop, P = .876.** No change. This is the strongest null result in
  the paper and the most reassuring number for a coach.
- DASH sports module 70.1 ± 29.6 to 12.9 ± 20.3, P < .001. Recovery rate 79.1 ± 33.1%.

## Complications (p. 625)

- Pneumothorax 8 cases (4.4%), managed with chest drainage, no further surgery.
- Incomplete long thoracic nerve paralysis 2 cases.
- Superficial surgical site infection 1 case.
- No overhead athlete needed additional surgery. 11 nonathletes did.

## What the authors say about diagnosis (Discussion, p. 626)

- "TOS is difficult to diagnose and is often poorly managed."
- Roos et al reported that TOS is underdiagnosed.
- Overhead athletes with TOS "occasionally suffer from shoulder or elbow pain during
  the acceleration phase of the throwing motion, similar to the position of shoulder
  apprehension test, moving valgus stress test, and Roos test. Therefore, shoulder and
  elbow surgeons should avoid misdiagnosing TOS in overhead athletes, particularly
  adolescent athletes, who suffer from shoulder or elbow pain."
- Illig et al: TOS is often underdiagnosed in children and adolescents, leading to
  undertreatment.

## Limitations

**Authors' own** (Discussion):
- Retrospective design.
- Single institution.
- The pathology of TOS is "only partially understood".

**Ours** (not stated by the authors, and they matter more for us):
1. **Every patient had surgery after conservative care failed.** There is no
   conservative arm and no untreated comparison, so this says nothing about how often
   a thrower recovers without an operation.
2. **68% of the eligible pool was excluded.** 566 cases down to 181, with 172 lost to
   follow-up. Patients who do well are more likely to stop attending, so the outcome
   figures are probably flattering.
3. **Only 3 softball athletes.** Nothing about softball can be drawn from this paper.
   Baseball is 67 of the 79.
4. **Mean age 18.5 years** in the athlete group. This is a high school and early
   college population, not a mature professional one.
5. Single surgeon group, Japan, one specialised technique. Transfer to other settings
   is unknown.
6. Return to same level was judged subjectively by the patient.
7. No control for rehabilitation content or time, so the 7.3 month figure reflects
   this centre's protocol.

## Things inside the paper that do not add up

1. **Age range is reported twice and differs.** The abstract says "range, 12-57 years"
   (p. 620); the Results say "range, 12-64 years" (p. 622). Same cohort, two ranges.
   I use neither on the slides.
2. **Table IV volleyball row is mislabeled.** 3 athletes, 1 partial return (33%),
   2 same level, but the cell reads "2 (100%)". It should be 67%, as the softball row
   correctly shows for the same 2-of-3 split. I use the overall total (64/79, 81%)
   rather than the per-sport percentages.
3. The abstract reports the group difference in DASH as three P values
   "(P = .007, < .001, < .001)" without naming which is which. Table III resolves it:
   preoperative .007, postoperative < .001, recovery rate < .001.

## What I will not claim

- Not that TOS is common. This is a surgical series with no denominator, so it carries
  no incidence information at all.
- Not that throwing causes TOS. The design cannot show that, and Table II found no
  intraoperative difference between athletes and nonathletes.
- Not that surgery is the answer for a thrower with arm pain. Everyone here had
  already failed months of conservative care.

content.content:
**Research in 5 · #002: Thoracic outlet syndrome in overhead athletes**
A young thrower with a year of shoulder or elbow pain may not have a shoulder or elbow problem.

**What did the researchers do?**
How do overhead athletes do after surgery for thoracic outlet syndrome?
- Reviewed 181 cases that had first rib resection at one hospital between 2015 and 2021.
- Split them into 79 overhead athletes and 102 nonathletes, then compared the two groups.
- Measured symptoms, grip power, disability scores, return to sport and pitch velocity.
- Followed everyone for at least two years, 31 months on average.

**What were the results?**
- **81%** of overhead athletes returned to their previous level
- **7.3 mo** average time from surgery back to sport
- **p = .88** pitch velocity was unchanged after surgery
- Excellent or good results reached 91.1 percent in overhead athletes against 62.8 percent in nonathletes (p. 624).
- Ball velocity in 18 pitchers did not change, 126.2 kph before and 125.4 kph after (P = .876, p. 625).
- Nothing seen during surgery separated athletes from nonathletes, including scalene muscle size (Table II, p. 623).

**What does this mean?**
TOS in throwers looks like dominant arm shoulder or elbow pain, and is easy to mistake for a joint injury.
- **Athletic Medicine:** Consider the neck when throwing arm pain drags on for months.
- **Athletic Performance:** Arm pain resisting normal shoulder care may not be a shoulder issue.
- **Sport Coaches:** These athletes hurt for a year before surgery. Flag long pain early.

**Coaching takeaways**
1. Watch for dominant arm pain that lasts beyond a season.
2. Ask about numbness, coldness and grip, not just the joint.
3. Getting back to the same level took about seven months.

**Bottom line:** Long standing throwing arm pain deserves a neck check.

**How much to trust it:** Preliminary. Retrospective case series, one hospital, 79 overhead athletes and 102 nonathletes, all had surgery. Limits: Everyone had surgery after conservative care failed; only 3 softball athletes, 67 of 79 played baseball; two thirds of eligible cases were excluded or lost.

**Discuss:** When a thrower's arm pain has run past three months, what is our current path for getting the neck and thoracic outlet looked at?

Funakoshi et al. (2024). Thoracic outlet syndrome in overhead athletes. JSES International. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jseint.2023.12.004
The 5-slide deck is attached.

**Overall reliance risk: high for causal, comparative, and policy decisions; moderate for descriptive education.**

- **High risk:** using the brief to declare two local cases statistically normal; identify throwing rather than other factors as the proven cause; claim half of workload is hidden; prioritize specific prevention interventions; or assert that NCAA surveillance cannot code TOS.

## 1. Summary verdict

**Overall verdict: mixed evidence chain; major correction is required before operational use.**

The long-form review is unusually careful about many limitations and correctly rejects several unsupported claims. Most quoted study-level descriptive statistics matched the cited source records. However, the coach-facing brief and recommendations introduce several material errors or overstatements:

- “About half of true pitch volume is uncounted” is not what the cited study measured.
- “Two cases sits inside normal variation” conflicts with the brief’s own assumed incidence.
- “Lower-body screening predicts about half the shoulder load” misattributes variance explained by body mass and pitch velocity to lower-extremity screening.
- The cocked position increases anterior-scalene stiffness by about **53%**, not “roughly doubles” it unless neck rotation is added.
- “TOS is not separately coded in NCAA surveillance” is not established by the cited publications; the missing Datalys codebook prevents that conclusion.
- Several recommendations are derived from observational mechanics, reliability studies, or small null experiments that did not test TOS, injury prevention, or the recommended intervention.
- The stated “109 peer-reviewed sources, each checked against PubMed” is not reproducible: the working review contains **109 unique PMIDs plus at least three additional DOI/Zotero-only supporting articles**.

I reviewed the [working evidence review](/C:/Users/eric_rash/Desktop/DEV/TOS_Evidence_Brief/artifacts/source-evidence-review.md), both HTML artifacts, both DOCX deliverables, both PDFs, and the README. The DOCX/PDF pairs are near-duplicates, but the HTML and one-page versions contain materially different wording. Repeated claims are consolidated below.

Source-access limitations are themselves findings: the current NCAA rulebook and Datalys codebook were unavailable; the two local Zotero PDFs were not included in the folder, although equivalent publisher/full-text versions of the cited Devaney and Oliver articles were accessible.

## 2. Factual claims table

| Claim and location | Source cited | Verdict | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| TOS comprises neurogenic, venous, and arterial syndromes; referral proportions approximately 82/16/2. Working review §1.1; full PDF pp. 2–3 | Illig 2021, PMID 32771464 | **Verified** | The source reports 526 referrals divided 82%/16%/2%. These are referral proportions, not population subtype incidence. |
| Athlete series contain 26–34% venous TOS. §1.1 | Chandra 2014; Chauhan 2024; Gutman 2022 | **Verified** | Numbers match treated/referral athlete cohorts. The review appropriately notes their selection bias. |
| Venous TOS is “5- to 10-fold over-represented in athletes.” §1.1 | Vemuri 2016 | **Unsupported as quantified** | No population athlete denominator is presented. Comparing referral-case subtype mixes cannot establish athlete incidence or a 5–10× risk ratio. |
| nTOS incidence is 2–3/100,000/year and vTOS 0.5–1/100,000/year. §1.2; one-page PDF p. 1 | Illig 2021, PMIDs 32771464 and 33220767 | **Misquoted/out of context** | The exact values are reported, but explicitly as estimates “based on referral assumptions and population density”; the source also says incidence is almost/completely unknown. The brief often converts the estimate into a settled population base rate. [Source record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32771464/) |
| “3–80 per 1,000” does not trace to an indexed primary source. §1.2 | Jones 2019 → Citisli 2015 | **Verified as a citation-tracing finding** | Jones repeats the range and cites Citisli; the brief correctly declines to use it. “A wide range proves nobody measured anything,” however, is rhetoric rather than a demonstrated fact. |
| There is no reliable objective gold-standard test for nTOS. §1.3 | SVS standards; Sanders 2008; Cochrane 2014 | **Verified** | The cited sources support diagnostic uncertainty, exclusion criteria, and lack of a definitive objective test. |
| EAST/Roos and other provocative maneuvers have high false-positive rates, including 47–62% in healthy controls. §1.3 | Rayan, Plewa, Nord, Warrens, Gillard | **Verified** | The reported values are supported. Absence from published reports is not proof of no code. The review itself concedes that the Datalys documentation/codebook could not be obtained. | “109 peer-reviewed sources, each checked against PubMed.” README and all presentations | Citation apparatus | **Unsupported/internally inconsistent** | The working document contains 109 unique PMIDs plus at least Devaney, Oliver, and Freetly as additional DOI/Zotero-only sources. At least one included source is not a PubMed record. |

## 3. Statistical/reasoning issues

1. **“Two cases is a plausible chance cluster / sits inside normal variation.”**  
   Passage: working review §1.5 and Appendix; full PDF pp. 1–2 and 12; briefing note p. 1.  
   Flaw: using the brief’s own assumed rate of 4/100,000/year, a 35-athlete season has \(\lambda=0.0014\). The Poisson probability of two or more cases is approximately **0.000000979**, or **0.000098%**. Two cases are therefore not plausibly “within chance” under that model.  
   Why it matters: this is the central reassurance claim. If the general-population rate is inappropriate for athletes, the brief must use an athlete-specific model or state that the expected rate is unknown—not use the population rate and then disregard its implication.

2. **Incompatible denominators are juxtaposed.**  
   Passage: §1.2’s annual incidence and §1.4’s seven-year 0.48%/1.3% conference prevalence.  
   Flaw: incidence per person-year and cumulative database prevalence are treated as though they describe the same probability. They do not.  
   Why it matters: which denominator is chosen radically changes how unusual two roster cases appear.

3. **“Four orders of magnitude” is overstated.**  
   Passage: §1.5.  
   Flaw: 8.6% divided by 0.004% is about **2,143**, or 3.33 orders of magnitude—not four.  
   Why it matters: minor numerically, but it amplifies the precision/rhetoric problem in the central statistical argument.

4. **A confidence interval around observed event counts is used to declare a cluster plausible.**  
   Passage: §1.5, Poisson intervals for one and two events.  
   Flaw: a CI for the underlying rate after observing events is not the same as the probability of observing those events under the asserted baseline.  
   Why it matters: it answers a different question and produces the wrong operational conclusion.

5. **Exceedance frequency is converted into pitch-volume composition.**  
   Passage: §5.3 and all summaries: 25.6% versus 51.2% becomes “half of true volume is uncounted.”  
   Flaw: doubling the proportion of outings crossing a threshold does not mean half the pitches were uncounted.  
   Why it matters: this unsupported statistic drives the brief’s “highest-yield” recommendation.

6. **Variance attribution is incorrect.**  
   Passage: §5.2 and one-page statements that lower-body screening predicts 49.9% or “about half” of shoulder load.  
   Flaw: body mass and pitch velocity explained 49.9%; hip strength added 6.3 percentage points.  
   Why it matters: it materially exaggerates the actionable contribution of the proposed S&C lever.

7. **The scalene effect size is inflated.**  
   Passage: briefing note p. 1.  
   Flaw: ABER increased anterior-scalene stiffness 53%. Near-doubling required ABER plus neck rotation.  
   Why it matters: the simplified version overstates the evidence that the ordinary cocked position itself doubles outlet-muscle loading.

8. **Null significance tests are treated as evidence of safety/no impairment.**  
   Passage: §4.2–4.5.  
   Flaw: the small water-polo, tennis, and throwing studies were not equivalence or noninferiority trials. Different sports, exercises, and endpoints cannot establish that pre-throw lifting is harmless in collegiate softball pitchers.

9. **Biopsy findings are used to rule out causation.**  
   Passage: §2.4.  
   Flaw: surgical biopsy is cross-sectional and obtained after disease. Type-II atrophy/fibrosis may be downstream of compression, disuse, denervation, or chronic symptoms.  
   Why it matters: the finding does not exonerate every resistance-training mechanism or justify “the weight room is the wrong suspect.”

10. **A small, data-derived screening threshold is operationalized without validation.**  
    Passage: §2.8 and recommendation table.  
    Flaw: n=49, ten injuries, RR CI 1.28–68.49, with the cut-point derived and tested in the same cohort. No independent validation or intervention trial is cited.

11. **Workload differences are treated as injury-prevention evidence.**  
    Passage: §5.3 and recommendation to develop staff depth.  
    Flaw: Freetly measured roster size and innings, not injuries, pitch counts, or TOS. The authors explicitly call for further injury research.

12. **Descriptive mechanics are repeatedly promoted to causal exposure language.**  
    Passage: “the throwing motion is the exposure,” one-page p. 1 and full review summary.  
    Flaw: the brief itself states that no peer-reviewed paper attributes TOS in a softball pitcher to the pitching motion. Scalene stiffness, shoulder force, and case reports support plausibility—not causal risk magnitude.

13. **“Endurance deficit is twice strength deficit” selectively frames one muscle direction.**  
    Passage: §3.1.  
    Flaw: it fits medial rotators but not lateral rotators. No standardized effect sizes are reported.  
    Why it matters: the headline exaggerates the distinctiveness of endurance impairment.

14. **Outcome percentages omit missingness/eligibility context.**  
    Passage: 95.4% unrestricted RTP.  
    Flaw: return status was unavailable for seven athletes, and four graduated.  
    Why it matters: an apparently cohort-wide success percentage is presented without its effective denominator.

content.text:
Codex came back, and it found real errors. Reporting them straight — several are mine.

**Three numeric misquotes. These are unambiguous and they matter most, because each one is load-bearing.**

1. **"Roughly half of true pitch volume is uncounted" is wrong.** Kamarajugadda measured the share of *outings that exceeded a recommendation* — 25.6% counting game pitches, 51.2% counting bullpen and warm-up. That is not the share of pitches that go uncounted. I converted an exceedance rate into a volume composition. This is the headline of the briefing note's callout and the justification for the "cheapest fix" recommendation. It also studied **high school** softball, not collegiate.

2. **"The cocked position roughly doubles scalene stiffness" is wrong.** 14.4 vs 9.4 kPa is a **53% increase**. Near-doubling (18.1 kPa) requires ABER *plus* contralateral neck rotation. I compressed the two conditions into one claim.

3. **"Lower-body screening predicts about half the shoulder load" misattributes the variance.** In Ulman 2025, **body mass plus pitch velocity** explained 49.9%. Hip rotation strength added **6.3 percentage points**. I credited the whole 49.9% to lower-extremity screening, which inflates the strongest S&C recommendation in the document.

**And the statistical argument at the centre of the brief does not hold as written.** Codex is right, and this is the most important finding. Using my own assumed rate of 4 per 100,000 per year, λ = 0.0014 for a 35-athlete season, so P(≥2 cases) ≈ 0.0001%. Two cases is *not* "within chance" under that model. My Poisson confidence intervals answered a different question — the plausible range of the underlying rate *after* observing events, not the probability of observing them under the stated baseline.

The conclusion is probably still right, but for a reason I didn't give: the general-population rate is the wrong denominator for a collegiate softball roster. The athlete-specific number is in the brief already — **Talutis: 1.3% of softball athletes over seven years**. Against that, two cases is unremarkable. The argument needs rebuilding on that denominator instead. Related: "four orders of magnitude" is actually ~2,143×, so 3.3.

**Smaller corrections:** "109 sources each checked against PubMed" is imprecise (109 PMIDs *plus* Devaney, Oliver and Freetly, which are DOI-verified); "TOS is not separately coded in the NCAA ISP" is stated flatly on the one-pager when the full review honestly concedes the Datalys codebook was unreachable — "no published NCAA benchmark exists" is the defensible version; "venous TOS is 5–10 fold over-represented" describes referral mix, not incidence; and "exactly one study supports career collapse" is a rhetorical absolute.

**Where Codex did not find problems:** most study-level numbers check out. It verified the Daley deficits, Takaba's raw kPa values, Devaney's RR and CI, Demondion's 47%, the Talutis cohort, the Freetly workload table, Machleder/Sanders histology, the Garraud composition, and the professional RTP range. Its summary: *"The central concern is not fabricated literature. Most citations are real and many study-level numbers are accurate. The risk comes from the final inferential step."* That's a fair description — I over-converted descriptive findings into causal and actionable claims.

**The Research in 5 deck is unaffected.** Its numbers come straight from Funakoshi's tables and none were flagged.

Base directory for this skill: C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\closeout

# Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence. Commit and push is standing-authorized for every DEV repo: each repo's `AGENTS.md` Session routine says "update STATUS, commit, push at end", and unpushed work on one machine is the top cause of conflicts on the other. The only exceptions are repos whose `CLAUDE.md` says their data must stay local (DexaProject is the precedent); commit those locally and list them as open.

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` across **every** repo in DEV, not only the ones named in this conversation. Another session, another harness, or the other machine may have left work dirty, and a closeout that only checks what it remembers touching will say "clear to sign off" over someone else's uncommitted work. Walk `DEV/`, `DEV/Football/` and `DEV/SpecialRequests/`, and report any repo with uncommitted or unpushed commits. The full walk takes about 90 seconds.
  - Windows: `git -C <repo> status --porcelain` per repo. Do NOT use `Get-ChildItem -Recurse` to look for files; it silently skips paths past the 260-character limit. Inside a repo, `git ls-files` is the reliable way to ask whether a file exists.
  - Repos with dirty state you did not touch: commit and push them like any other, and name them in the report so the user knows another session left them.
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- Every repo touched this session: stage, commit with a descriptive message, `git pull --no-rebase` (the other machine may have pushed), push. If the merge conflicts, follow the conflict steps in `dev-sync/SKILL.md` (they are the one home for them), then push and list the file under "Still open".
- Before staging, make sure any new file over 95 MB and any `.env` is in `.gitignore`.
- Local-only repos (CLAUDE.md says so): commit, do not push, list it.
- Also check the three config repos, `~/.claude` (dotclaude), `~/.claude/skills` (claude-skills) and `~/.claude/global-memory` (claude-global-memory). If any has changes, commit and push it the same way, so the other machine's `/dev-sync` picks it up.
- **Push `global-memory` even on a light session.** `daily-backup` pushes it nightly, which is too late for a same-day handoff: work the Mac in the afternoon, sit down at Windows that evening, and anything written to MEMORY.md or handoffs is still only on the Mac. Pushing it here is what makes memory available to the other machine tonight rather than tomorrow. It is the only repo that carries memory across, so treat an unpushed `global-memory` the same as an unpushed project repo: it blocks "clear to sign off".
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- Run the dev-docs harvest so repo docs reach memsearch: `bash ~/.claude/scripts/harvest-dev-docs.sh` (Mac) or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File $HOME\.claude\scripts\harvest-dev-docs.ps1` (Windows). It copies every repo's `docs/*.md` into `~/.claude/global-memory/dev-docs/`, which is on the index list. One line of output; do this after Step 4 so today's STATUS is included.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.
- **Tier A does not cross machines — mirror it or lose it.** Project memory lives under a slug built from the project's absolute path, and that path differs on the Mac and the Windows laptop, so a Tier A file written today is not auto-injected tomorrow on the other machine. Global memory and the repo both cross; Tier A does not. So for every Tier A fact written this session, ask: is this durable and project-scoped? If yes, it must also land in the repo — `docs/STATUS.md` for current state, `docs/DECISIONS.md` for a decision and its reasoning, the dated handoff for the detail. Treat Tier A as a fast local cache and the repo as the record. If a fact only ever exists in Tier A, assume the other machine will never see it.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

**Always, in every repo touched (even for light sessions): update `docs/STATUS.md`.** It is the file the next session reads first, on either machine, in any harness. Rewrite the sections in place, keep it short:

- `## Current state` — two to five lines on where things stand today
- `## Next` — most important first
- `## Open questions` — decisions waiting on Eric
- `## Gotchas` — anything that will bite the next session

The dated handoff file is the detailed record; STATUS.md is the summary. Do Step 4 before the Step 2 commit so both land in the same push.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**STATUS.md:** updated in <repos>
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

"Clear to sign off" means: every touched repo is pushed (or is a declared local-only repo). If anything is unpushed, the verdict is "Not clear" and the unpushed repo is the one thing blocking.

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Push every touched DEV repo. Do not leave the laptop with unpushed work; the other machine pulls from GitHub, not from this disk.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

## What this session was

Eric's softball S&C colleague is taking blame for a perceived cluster of thoracic
outlet syndrome cases. The head coach believes Baylor softball has a higher rate
than peer institutions. The ask was deep research into TOS causes in overhead
athletes, plus two specific questions from the athletic training staff:

1. Is there research behind "don't lift the pitchers before they throw"?
2. Can a muscular endurance or capacity deficit cause TOS?

## What was built

**1. Evidence review, 109 sources.** Five parallel research agents swept
epidemiology, mechanism, conservative care and capacity, softball workload, and the
lifting-timing question. Every citation was verified against PubMed or Europe PMC.
All 113 PMID references in the markdown were then batch-checked against NCBI
E-utilities: all resolve, zero transcription errors.

**2. Two Baylor house-style documents** built through `baylor_docstyle.py`, the real
Word pipeline used by the Tech Inventory deliverables (not a lookalike). Structured
on the Pyramid Principle after running `/anthropic-skills:articulation-skill`.

**3. Research in 5 #002** on Funakoshi et al. 2024, built from the same body of work.

- **"No lifting before throwing" has no research support.** Three structured PubMed
  searches returned no baseball study on the question and no paper at all linking
  training timing to TOS. Adjacent evidence leans against the rule: heavy bench and
  row 15 min before throwing did nothing to water polo velocity or accuracy; 75% 1RM
  did nothing to tennis at 3 min, 24 h or 48 h; a morning lift improved afternoon
  throw distance. The one study showing a velocity drop used push-ups to failure and
  found lower-body fatigue dropped velocity just as much, which undercuts the
  protect-the-arm rationale.
- **The endurance hypothesis is coherent but unproven.** Daley 2021 found a 45%
  rotator endurance deficit in TOS patients, roughly double the strength deficit, but
  in 40-year-old non-athlete clinic patients, in the wrong muscle group, with causation
  unresolvable. Nobody has ever measured scapular endurance in a TOS population.
- **The peer comparison cannot be made.** TOS is not in any published NCAA
  surveillance output. The best collegiate figure is Talutis 2025: 15,609 D-I
  athletes, softball 1.3%, tennis 2.6%, all-sport 0.48%.

   measured the share of *outings exceeding a recommendation* (25.6% game-only vs
   51.2% including bullpen and warm-up), not the share of pitches that go uncounted.
   An exceedance rate was converted into a volume composition. It is also a **high
   school** study, not collegiate. This claim drives the "cheapest fix" recommendation
   and appears on the briefing note, the full review and both artifacts.
2. **"The cocked position roughly doubles scalene stiffness" is wrong.** Takaba 2022:
   14.4 vs 9.4 kPa is a **53% increase**. Near-doubling (18.1 kPa) needs ABER *plus*
   contralateral neck rotation. Two conditions were compressed into one claim.
3. **"Lower-body screening predicts about half the shoulder load" misattributes
   variance.** Ulman 2025: **body mass plus pitch velocity** explained 49.9%; hip
   rotation strength added **6.3 percentage points**. The whole 49.9% was credited to
   LE screening, inflating the strongest S&C recommendation in the document.

over-converted into causal and actionable claims.

cases unremarkable. Rebuild the section on that, and drop the general-population rate
from the reassurance argument. Also: "four orders of magnitude" is ~2,143x, so 3.3.

Smaller: "109 sources each checked against PubMed" is imprecise (109 PMIDs plus
Devaney, Oliver and Freetly, which are DOI-verified). "TOS is not separately coded in
the NCAA ISP" is stated flatly on the one-pager when the full review concedes the
Datalys codebook was unreachable; "no published NCAA benchmark exists" is defensible.
"Venous TOS 5-10 fold over-represented" describes referral mix, not incidence.

Codex's own summary: *"The central concern is not fabricated literature. Most
citations are real and many study-level numbers are accurate. The risk comes from the
final inferential step."* That is a fair description. Descriptive findings were
over-converted into causal and actionable claims.

**Research in 5 #002 is unaffected** — its numbers come straight from Funakoshi's
tables and none were flagged.

- **Word inserts an empty paragraph after a table that ends the document body.** That
  phantom paragraph alone created a second page on the briefing note after the content
  already fit. `d.spacer(0)` at the end makes pagination deterministic.
- **Long table cells wrap to two lines and cost far more vertical space than the same
  words in a paragraph.** When a Baylor doc runs over, shorten table cells before prose.
- **`baylor_docstyle` validator limits are tighter than `docs/CONTENT_SPEC.md` says**
  in the RI5 repo: `trust.design` 45, `trust.sample` 60, chart row `label` 22.
  build.js is the authority; the spec text is stale. Noted in that repo's STATUS.
- **Europe PMC `fullTextXML` is the reliable way in when PMC blocks scripted PDF
  download.** It carries every table. Say in notes.md that pages are journal pages.
- **The worktree guard rejects Bash commands containing the substring "git"** even
